slides.note: The kidneys do three jobs. They set how much water and salt leave in the urine, which controls blood volume and blood pressure. They excrete wastes such as urea, creatinine and drugs. They also make three hormones. Renin starts the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, which raises blood pressure. Erythropoietin tells the bone marrow to make red cells when O₂ delivery falls. 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D (calcitriol, active vitamin D) is finished in the proximal tubule and raises Ca²⁺ absorption from the gut. Losing these last two explains anemia and low Ca²⁺ in chronic kidney failure (Q5).

Front view of the urinary system. Each kidney sits high on the back wall of the abdomen, one on each side of the spine, with a suprarenal (adrenal) gland (yellow) on top. A renal artery from the abdominal aorta enters each kidney. Urine leaves each kidney through its ureter, which runs down to the bladder for storage. Not drawn here: each renal vein drains its kidney into the inferior vena cava. The three labeled constrictions are the narrow points where kidney stones tend to stick: where the renal pelvis joins the ureter, where the ureter crosses the iliac artery at the pelvic inlet, and where it enters the bladder.

slides.note: Retroperitoneal means behind the peritoneum, the membrane that lines the abdominal cavity. Here the organs that hang inside the peritoneal sac (liver, stomach, most of the intestine) have been removed, and the cut edges of the peritoneum are outlined in white. What is left lies on the back wall of the abdomen, behind the peritoneum. The right and left kidneys sit against the back muscles on either side of the spine, each with a suprarenal (adrenal) gland on top. The abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava, which supply and drain them, run right beside them, also behind the peritoneum. Parts of the duodenum, pancreas and colon, which are also retroperitoneal, lie in front of the kidneys.

slides.note: Front view of the kidneys and their vessels. The yellow glands on top are the suprarenal (adrenal) glands. The red tube in the middle is the abdominal aorta; the blue one beside it, on the body's right, is the inferior vena cava (IVC). Short renal arteries branch off the aorta into each kidney, and the renal veins drain into the IVC. The left renal vein is longer because it must cross in front of the aorta to reach the IVC. To show the vessels behind them, the IVC has been cut and its upper part lifted, and the renal veins have been cut near each kidney (the open blue ends). The box shows a suprarenal gland cut across: outer cortex, inner medulla.

Kidney cut in half. The outer brown layer is the cortex. The dark red cones are the medulla, divided into pyramids. The cortex holds the glomeruli (the filters) and the twisted (convoluted) tubules. The medulla holds the long straight parts: loops of Henle, collecting ducts and the vessels that run beside them. Urine drains from the pyramid tips into the pelvis, a funnel that narrows into the ureter. The renal artery and vein enter and leave at the same notch.

The renal papilla is the tip of a pyramid. Collecting ducts open there, and urine drips into a cup called a minor calyx. Urine path: papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter. The columns between pyramids (renal columns) are strips of cortex that dip down between neighboring pyramids; the interlobar arteries run through them, outward from the renal sinus toward the outer cortex. The renal sinus is the fat-filled space around the calyces and pelvis.

One pyramid with the cortex above it. Follow the blood in: interlobar artery (runs up between pyramids) → arcuate artery (arches along the border between cortex and medulla) → interlobular artery (climbs into the cortex) → afferent arterioles → glomeruli (the round knots in the cortex). Veins run back alongside. Note where each part sits: glomeruli and convoluted tubules are only in the cortex; loops of Henle and collecting ducts run down into the medulla. Many collecting ducts merge and open at the pyramid tip. The vasa recta are the straight vessels running beside the loops.

The nephron is the working unit of the kidney; each kidney has about 1 million. Fluid path: the glomerulus (a knot of capillaries) filters plasma into Bowman's capsule → proximal convoluted tubule → descending limb → loop of Henle (dips into the medulla) → ascending limb → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct. The ascending limb climbs back up and touches its own glomerulus, between the afferent arteriole (blood in) and efferent arteriole (blood out). That contact point is the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA). It senses the salt in the tubule and controls renin release and filtration.

The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries. Bowman's capsule (glomerular capsule) is a double-walled cup around it, like a fist pushed into a balloon. Its inner (visceral) layer is the podocytes that wrap the capillaries; its outer (parietal) layer is the wall. Black arrows = blood: it enters through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole, both at the vascular pole. Plasma is pushed out of the capillaries into the capsular space between the two layers. This fluid is the filtrate (green arrows). It leaves at the tubular pole, straight into the proximal convoluted tubule. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the capillaries. On the right, the distal tubule touches the arterioles: that is the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

Blood enters through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole. Here a capillary bed sits between two arterioles, which is unusual. So the kidney can set the pressure inside the glomerulus by squeezing one or the other. Glomerular capillary pressure is high (about 45 mm Hg) and stays high along the whole tuft, so fluid is pushed out everywhere (yellow arrows) into Bowman's capsule. This glomerular filtrate flows on into the PCT (proximal convoluted tubule). If the efferent arteriole constricts, blood backs up in the glomerulus, so pressure and filtration rise. If the afferent constricts, less blood gets in, so both fall.

Nephrons come in two types, named by where the glomerulus sits. Cortical (superficial) nephrons, about 7 in 8, have glomeruli in the outer cortex and short loops that reach only the outer medulla. Juxtamedullary nephrons (juxta = next to), about 1 in 8, have larger glomeruli deep in the cortex next to the medulla, and long loops that reach the papilla. Long loops build a saltier medulla. A saltier medulla pulls more water out of the collecting ducts, so the urine can become more concentrated. The efferent arterioles of these nephrons also form the vasa recta.

Four views of the renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule). (a) Drawing: blood enters and leaves at the vascular pole (black arrows); filtrate (green arrows) collects in the capsular space and leaves into the proximal tubule at the tubular pole. (b) Stained tissue section: the capillary tuft (G, glomerulus) fills the round capsule. Around it is a clear rim of capsular space (CS), inside the thin parietal layer (PL). Nearby are the macula densa (MD) and cut proximal (PCT) and distal (DCT) tubules. (c) The filter, from capillary blood to capsular space: fenestrated (pored) endothelium → basement membrane → filtration slits between the pedicels. (d) Scanning electron micrograph: podocytes, the cells of the capsule's inner layer, wrap each capillary with interlocking foot processes (pedicels).

Scanning electron micrograph of the outside of a glomerulus (capsule removed). The lumpy surface is the capillary loops, each covered by podocytes. The round bumps are podocyte cell bodies, and their branching arms wrap the capillaries. Everything that is filtered must pass through this podocyte layer to reach Bowman's space.

Cut-away view of one renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule). Blood enters by the afferent arteriole (bottom) and leaves by the efferent arteriole (top). Filtrate collects in the capsular (Bowman's) space, between the podocyte layer and the outer capsule wall, then flows into the proximal tubule (right). On the left, the distal tubule presses against the arterioles; this is the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Macula densa cells in the tubule wall sense how much NaCl is arriving. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells in the afferent arteriole wall release renin. Less NaCl reaching the macula densa → more renin.

Podocytes up close (scanning electron micrograph). The large smooth body is one podocyte. Thick arms reach out and split into tiny foot processes. These interlock like fingers with those of the neighboring podocyte around each capillary. The narrow gaps between foot processes are the filtration slits. The filter has three layers: capillary endothelium (with pores) → basement membrane → podocyte slits. Water and small solutes pass; albumin and blood cells are held back.

Colored scanning electron micrograph. The green bodies and arms are podocytes; the purple carpet is their interlocking foot processes, which cover the glomerular capillary loops. All filtrate passes through the slits between these foot processes.

Higher magnification (scale bar = 1 µm, a thousandth of a millimeter). Foot processes from neighboring podocytes interlock over a capillary loop. The slits between them are only about 25–60 nm wide and are bridged by a thin membrane. The whole filter also carries negative charges. These repel negatively charged proteins such as albumin, so albumin stays in the blood even more completely.

Color key: red = glomerulus, green = Bowman's capsule and PCT (proximal convoluted tubule), blue = loop of Henle, pink = distal convoluted tubule, yellow = collecting duct. The PCT is the first and busiest segment. It reabsorbs (moves out of the tubule fluid and back into the blood) about two-thirds (67%) of the filtered Na⁺ and water, nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids, and most filtered HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate). Its twisting (convoluted) shape packs a long tube into the cortex.

3-D model of a nephron. Green = proximal tubule and the thin limbs of the loop. Yellow = thick ascending limb and distal convoluted tubule. White = collecting duct, which takes fluid from many nephrons. The red vessel at the top is the arteriole pair at the glomerulus. The yellow tubule passes right against its own glomerulus's arterioles; that contact point is the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

Tissue section of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), the spot where the distal tubule touches the arterioles of its own glomerulus. Label key: AA = afferent arteriole (brings blood in); EA = efferent arteriole (takes blood out); JG = juxtaglomerular granular cells, modified smooth-muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall that make renin; D = distal tubule; MD = macula densa, the crowded, tall cells of the distal tubule wall that sense NaCl in the tubule fluid; L = lacis cells (extraglomerular mesangial cells), between the arterioles and the macula densa; G = glomerulus; US = urinary (Bowman's) space; P = proximal tubules. MD + JG cells + lacis cells together make the JGA.

What each segment does (orange arrow = active transport, purple = passive). An arrow pointing out of the tubule means reabsorption: the substance leaves the tubule fluid and goes back into the blood, so it is kept. An arrow pointing into the tubule means secretion: the substance moves from the blood into the tubule fluid, so it ends up in the urine. The blue box (partly cut off) lists the filtrate: water, salts, HCO₃⁻, H⁺, urea, glucose, amino acids, some drugs.
(1) Proximal tubule: reabsorbs most of the NaCl, water, HCO₃⁻, nutrients and K⁺ (arrows out). It secretes H⁺ and NH₃ (ammonia) (arrows in).
(2) Descending limb: reabsorbs only water.
(3) Ascending limb: reabsorbs NaCl but no water. The thick part pumps NaCl out actively; in the thin part it leaks out passively. The tubule fluid gets dilute and the medulla gets salty.
(4) Distal tubule: reabsorbs NaCl and HCO₃⁻ (arrows out). It secretes K⁺ and H⁺ (arrows in). Water leaves here only when ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is present.
(5) Collecting duct: reabsorbs NaCl. It also reabsorbs water and urea when ADH is present. This sets the final urine.

The PCT cell is built to move huge amounts of solute. Its luminal surface (the side facing the tubule fluid) is covered with microvilli (the brush border), which multiply the surface area for transporters. Its base (the side facing the blood) is packed with mitochondria, which make ATP for the Na⁺-K⁺ pumps that drive nearly all reabsorption. Pinocytotic vesicles swallow the small proteins and polypeptides that get filtered, so they are digested in the cell instead of lost in the urine.

Top: electron micrograph of PCT cells. Mv = microvilli (brush border, top); M = mitochondria, lined up in rows toward the base; V = vesicle; L = lysosome; J = junction between cells; Cap = peritubular capillary just under the cells. Bottom: light micrograph of cortex with a pink stain. The fuzzy pink lining inside each tubule is the brush border, the hallmark of the proximal tubule.

Lumen (tubule fluid) on the left, peritubular capillary on the right. Dotted arrows = the two routes from the lumen into the blood. (1) Na⁺ moves from the lumen into the cell, and water follows. (2a) The Na⁺-K⁺ pump (uses ATP) pushes Na⁺ out of the cell's blood-facing (basal) side toward the capillary. (2b) It also pumps Na⁺ out of the cell's sides into the space between neighboring cells. Na⁺ leaving makes the blood side positive compared with the lumen, so negative ions (Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻) follow passively, and water follows the solute by osmosis. (3) This fluid moves on into the capillary, pulled by the capillary's high oncotic pressure (πc, the water-pulling force of its plasma proteins). Water moves in step with solute, so tubule fluid stays isotonic (about 300 mOsm/L, like plasma) all along the PCT. The original slide says K⁺ is also reabsorbed actively; in fact proximal K⁺ reabsorption is passive, carried along with the water.

Correction: the luminal (top) box labeled “pump” for amino acids and glucose is a Na⁺ cotransporter, not an ATP pump: they enter the cell from the lumen riding on the Na⁺ gradient. The top-right “ATPase pump” is misleading too: H⁺ leaves the cell into the lumen mainly in exchange for Na⁺ (next slide), and the proximal tubule does not secrete K⁺. Left: a PCT in cross-section and a PCT cell seen by scanning electron microscope (microvilli on top). Right: one PCT cell, lumen at the top, blood at the bottom. Filtered proteins and polypeptides enter in vesicles and are broken down in lysosomes; the amino acids go on to the blood. At the base, Na⁺ is pumped out of the cell into the blood from deep basal infoldings crowded with mitochondria, so ATP is made right where it is used. Water and Cl⁻ also pass between the cells, from lumen to blood.

How the proximal tubule reabsorbs filtered bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻): it moves from the tubule fluid (lumen, left) back to the blood (right). (1) Inside the cell, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase joins CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), which splits into H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. (2) The Na⁺-H⁺ exchanger (pink circle) sends that H⁺ out of the cell into the lumen and brings one Na⁺ from the lumen into the cell. The Na⁺-K⁺ pump (green ATP circle) keeps cell Na⁺ low, which drives this swap (secondary active transport). (3) The new HCO₃⁻ crosses the blood-side membrane into the blood, carried with Na⁺ (orange circle) or swapped for Cl⁻ (peach circle). (4) In the lumen, the secreted H⁺ meets filtered HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ → CO₂ + H₂O; carbonic anhydrase on the luminal surface speeds this step. The CO₂ diffuses back into the cell. Net result: each H⁺ secreted returns one HCO₃⁻ to the blood, so the body keeps its main buffer.

Close-up of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), where the tubule touches its own arterioles. Three cell types. Macula densa (bottom): crowded tubule cells that sense NaCl in the passing fluid. Granular cells in the afferent arteriole wall: they store and release renin. Lacis cells, also called extraglomerular mesangial cells: they fill the triangle between the two arterioles and the macula densa. The glomerular mesangial cells (top) are their continuation inside the tuft.

Lacis cell = extraglomerular mesangial cell (same cell; "lacis" means lace-like). Their exact role is not settled. They sit between the macula densa and the arteriole cells and are linked to both by gap junctions, so they probably relay the macula densa's signal to the arterioles and renin cells. Don't confuse: lacis cells are part of the JGA, but renin comes from the granular (JG) cells.

Blood route around one nephron: interlobular artery → afferent arteriole → glomerulus (first capillary bed, filters) → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries (second capillary bed, wrapped around the tubules) → interlobular vein → renal vein. Two capillary beds in a row is unusual. The glomerulus runs at high pressure to push fluid out. The peritubular capillaries run at low pressure, and their blood is rich in the protein left behind by filtration. So they pull the reabsorbed fluid from the space around the tubules into the capillary blood. The dashed line is the cortex–medulla border.

Vasa recta ("straight vessels") are the peritubular capillaries of juxtamedullary nephrons. They come off the efferent arteriole and run down and back up beside the long loop of Henle, in the same hairpin shape. They carry the water and solutes reabsorbed from the loop back into the circulation. Going down into the salty medulla, the blood takes in salt from the surrounding fluid and loses water to it; coming back up, it gives that salt back and takes the water back in. So the blood leaves without washing away the medulla's salt gradient, which the kidney needs to concentrate urine (countercurrent exchange). Flow here is slow: only about 5% of renal blood flow reaches the medulla.

Water is 50–70% of body weight, 60% on average. The main reason for the range is fat: fat holds little water, while muscle holds a lot. So women (more fat on average) are about 50% and men about 60%. Thin men are highest among adults (about 70%), and obese or elderly women are lowest. Babies are highest of all (about 75–80%). Clinical use: a sudden weight loss of 1 kg over a day means about 1 L of water lost.

Use the 60-40-20 rule. Total body water (TBW) = 60% of body weight. Intracellular fluid (ICF) = 2/3 of TBW = 40% of body weight. Extracellular fluid (ECF) = 1/3 of TBW = 20%. The ECF splits again: 3/4 is interstitial fluid (the fluid bathing the cells, about 15%) and 1/4 is plasma (about 5%). Example, 70-kg man: TBW = 42 L; ICF = 28 L; ECF = 14 L; interstitial = 10.5 L; plasma = 3.5 L. The cell membrane separates ICF from ECF; the capillary wall separates plasma from interstitial fluid.

Correction: a fetus is not 100% water; early in pregnancy it is about 90%. The 70% shown for a normal adult fits a lean young man; the average adult is about 60%. The point of the picture is the trend: water as a share of body weight falls with age, from about 75–80% at birth to about 60% in a young adult and about 50% in the elderly. Older people lose water-rich muscle and carry relatively more fat. So they have a smaller water reserve and become dehydrated faster.

Correction: the side with more Cl⁻ is the interstitial fluid, not the cell interior (cells have very little Cl⁻). Why: interstitial fluid is plasma filtered through the capillary wall, so it has the same small ions but almost no protein. Plasma proteins such as albumin carry negative charges and cannot leave the capillary. Their charge holds extra cations (Na⁺) in the plasma and pushes small anions (Cl⁻) out of the plasma into the interstitial fluid. Result, the Gibbs-Donnan effect: plasma has slightly more Na⁺ and slightly less Cl⁻ than interstitial fluid.

The same Gibbs-Donnan rule, drawn across a cell membrane. The cytoplasm (right) is full of negatively charged proteins that cannot leave. They hold positive ions (K⁺ here) on their side and repel the small negative ion Cl⁻, which collects on the protein-free left side. The wedges show the result: green = Cl⁻, higher outside; pink = K⁺, higher inside. The trapped negative charge also makes the protein side negative (− signs) compared with the other side (+ signs). Rule to remember: the side with trapped protein has more cations and fewer diffusible anions. The black labels apply this to plasma and interstitial fluid: plasma, with its albumin, is the protein side; interstitial fluid is the protein-free side with more Cl⁻.

This is the dilution method. In words: the volume a marker spreads into equals the amount given divided by the concentration it reaches once it has mixed evenly. Steps: choose a marker that stays only in the compartment you want; inject a known amount; let it mix; measure its plasma concentration; subtract any marker lost in the urine meanwhile. Example: inject 500 mg of mannitol; 50 mg is lost in urine; plasma ends at 30 mg/L. Volume = 450 mg ÷ 30 mg/L = 15 L, which is the ECF.

Each marker measures the space it can reach. Total body water: tritiated water (water made with radioactive hydrogen, ³H), deuterium oxide (D₂O, heavy water) and antipyrine (a fat-soluble drug) cross cell membranes and go everywhere water goes. ECF: inulin (a large sugar polymer), mannitol (a sugar alcohol) and sulfate cross capillary walls but not cell membranes. Plasma: radio-iodinated serum albumin (RISA) and Evans blue (a dye that sticks to albumin) are too big to leave the capillaries. The ICF and interstitial fluid have no marker of their own, so they are found by subtraction: ICF = TBW − ECF; interstitial = ECF − plasma.

Blood is plasma plus cells. The hematocrit (Hct) is the fraction of blood volume made up of red cells (about 0.45). So the plasma fraction is 1 − Hct. In words: blood volume = plasma volume ÷ the fraction of blood that is plasma. Example: plasma volume (measured with RISA or Evans blue) = 3 L and Hct = 0.40. Plasma fraction = 1 − 0.40 = 0.60. Blood volume = 3 ÷ 0.60 = 5 L. The same formula later turns renal plasma flow into renal blood flow.

Answer: C, tritiated water. Step 1: the drug has almost no protein binding, so nothing holds it in the plasma; it can spread through all body water. Step 2: pick the marker with the same space. Tritiated water (³H₂O, shown in the picture) marks total body water. Why not the others: radio-iodinated albumin stays in the plasma; mannitol and inulin cannot enter cells, so they mark only the ECF. "Excreted in the urine" is a distractor: it tells you how the drug leaves, not where it spreads.

Answer: D, 40 liters. Volume = amount ÷ concentration. Amount injected = 800 mCi (millicuries, a unit of radioactivity). Concentration after mixing = 20 mCi per liter. 800 ÷ 20 = 40 L. Check the units: mCi ÷ (mCi/L) leaves liters. Sanity check: 40 L of water fits a person of about 67 kg at 60% water. The trap answer 0.025 L comes from dividing the wrong way (20 ÷ 800).

TBW = total body water. Tritiated water goes everywhere water goes, so the volume it fills is the TBW. If some marker had been lost in the urine before the blood sample, you would subtract that loss from the 800 mCi first. The question gives no urine loss, so 800 mCi is used as is.

Answer: C, 250 mg. Turn the equation around: amount (dose) = volume × concentration wanted. Step 1, volume: the drug fills nearly all body water, and she is a woman, so TBW ≈ 50% × 100 kg = 50 L. Step 2, units: 5 µg/mL (micrograms per milliliter) = 5 mg/L, because a mg is 1000 µg and a liter is 1000 mL. Step 3: 50 L × 5 mg/L = 250 mg. Using 60% (a man) would give 300 mg, which is not offered.

Answer: A, increase. Only free drug (not stuck to protein) can leave the blood, reach the tissues and act. If 95% of a drug binds albumin, only 5% of each dose is free. So a larger total dose is needed to reach a working free level; the bound drug sits in the plasma as a reserve. Clinical flip side: if albumin is low (liver disease, nephrotic syndrome), more of the drug is free, so the usual dose can become toxic.

Answer: A, anemia and hypocalcemia. Fluid overload, metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia (high K⁺) come from losing filtration, so they appear within days in acute kidney failure too. Anemia and hypocalcemia come from losing the kidney's hormones, which takes long-term loss of kidney tissue. Less erythropoietin → fewer red cells; red cells live about 120 days, so anemia takes weeks to show. Less 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D → less Ca²⁺ absorbed from the gut → low blood Ca²⁺.

qs.q: Which hormone made by the kidneys tells the bone marrow to make red cells?
qs.why: Erythropoietin is released when O₂ delivery falls and drives red cell production. Renin starts the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system; calcitriol is active vitamin D.

qs.q: Active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D) from the kidney raises blood Ca²⁺ mainly by doing what?
opts: Increasing Ca²⁺ absorption from the gut
qs.why: Calcitriol, finished in the proximal tubule, raises Ca²⁺ absorption from the gut. Losing it is why chronic kidney failure causes low Ca²⁺.

qs.q: What does it mean that the kidneys are retroperitoneal?
opts: They lie below the pelvic floor
They lie inside the peritoneal sac
qs.why: Retroperitoneal means behind the peritoneum: the kidneys sit against the back muscles beside the spine, outside the peritoneal sac, next to the aorta and vena cava.

qs.q: Why is the left renal vein longer than the right?
opts: It must cross in front of the aorta
It must cross behind the vena cava
The left kidney sits farther from the spine
The left kidney sits lower than the right
qs.why: The vena cava lies on the body's right, so the left renal vein has to cross in front of the aorta to reach it.

qs.q: Which structures are found only in the renal cortex?
opts: Vasa recta and loops of Henle
Loops of Henle and collecting ducts
qs.why: Glomeruli and the twisted (convoluted) tubules sit only in the cortex. The long straight parts, loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta, run down into the medulla.

qs.q: Urine dripping from a renal papilla flows first into what?
qs.why: Urine path: papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter.

qs.q: Which artery arches along the border between the cortex and the medulla?
qs.why: Blood runs interlobar artery (up between pyramids) → arcuate artery (arching along the cortex–medulla border) → interlobular artery (into the cortex) → afferent arterioles.

qs.q: Where is the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)?
opts: Where the proximal tubule leaves Bowman's capsule
Where the distal tubule touches its own arterioles
Where collecting ducts open at the papilla
Where the loop of Henle turns in the medulla
qs.why: The tubule climbs back up to its own glomerulus, where the end of the thick ascending limb (the start of the distal tubule) touches the afferent and efferent arterioles. That contact point senses tubule salt and controls renin release and filtration.

qs.q: What happens to glomerular pressure and filtration when the efferent arteriole constricts?
qs.why: Squeezing the outflow makes blood back up in the glomerulus, so pressure and filtration rise. Afferent constriction does the opposite: less blood gets in, so both fall.

qs.q: About what fraction of nephrons are cortical nephrons with short loops of Henle?
qs.why: About 7 in 8 nephrons are cortical with short loops; only about 1 in 8 are juxtamedullary with long loops.

qs.q: What gives juxtamedullary nephrons their greater power to concentrate urine?
opts: Long loops that reach the papilla
Short loops in the outer medulla
qs.why: Long loops build a saltier medulla, which pulls more water out of the collecting ducts, so the urine can become more concentrated.

qs.q: Podocytes make up which layer of the renal corpuscle?
qs.why: Podocytes form the inner layer of Bowman's capsule; their foot processes interlock around each glomerular capillary. The outer wall is the parietal epithelium.

qs.q: Filtrate crosses the glomerular filter in which order?
qs.why: From blood to Bowman's space: capillary endothelium (with pores), then the basement membrane, then the filtration slits between podocyte foot processes.

qs.q: Besides its size, what keeps albumin from being filtered?
opts: The filter's negative charge repels it
The filter's positive charge binds it
qs.why: The whole filter carries negative charges, which repel negatively charged proteins such as albumin, so albumin stays in the blood even more completely.

qs.q: Less NaCl reaching the macula densa leads to what?
opts: More renin from macula densa cells
qs.why: Macula densa cells only sense the NaCl; the juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall release the renin. Less NaCl → more renin.

qs.q: About what share of filtered Na⁺ and water does the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorb?
qs.why: The PCT, the first and busiest segment, reabsorbs (returns to the blood) about two-thirds of filtered Na⁺ and water, plus nearly all glucose and amino acids and most HCO₃⁻.

qs.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs only water, not NaCl?
qs.why: The descending limb is permeable only to water, so water leaves the tubule fluid into the salty medulla. The ascending limb does the reverse: NaCl leaves the tubule, but water cannot.

qs.q: The ascending limb moves NaCl out of the tubule fluid but lets no water follow. What does that do?
opts: Dilutes both tubule fluid and medulla
Dilutes tubule fluid, makes medulla salty
qs.why: Salt leaves the tubule but water cannot follow, so the fluid inside gets dilute and the salt builds up in the medulla around it.

qs.q: The collecting duct reabsorbs water and urea when which hormone is present?
qs.why: ADH lets the collecting duct reabsorb water and urea (move them out of the duct into the medulla), which sets how concentrated the final urine is.

qs.q: What is the brush border of the proximal tubule?
opts: Microvilli that enlarge the luminal surface
qs.why: The brush border is a carpet of microvilli on the luminal side that multiplies the surface area for transporters; it is the hallmark of the proximal tubule. Mitochondria sit in the basal infoldings.

qs.q: What is the tonicity of fluid along the proximal tubule, and why?
opts: Isotonic, because water follows solute in step
Hypotonic, because salt leaves without water
Hypertonic, because water leaves before salt
qs.why: Na⁺ moves out of the tubule fluid into the blood, anions follow, and water follows by osmosis in step, so the tubule fluid stays about 300 mOsm/L, like plasma, all along the PCT.

qs.q: How do glucose and amino acids enter proximal tubule cells from the lumen?
opts: Riding with Na⁺ down its gradient
Between cells with Cl⁻ and water
qs.why: They are carried in with Na⁺, using the Na⁺ gradient that the basal Na⁺-K⁺ pump maintains. Vesicles take up filtered proteins, not glucose.

qs.q: In proximal tubule HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, what does each H⁺ secreted into the lumen accomplish?
opts: Excretes one HCO₃⁻ in the urine
Returns one HCO₃⁻ to the blood
Adds one H⁺ to the blood
Returns one Cl⁻ to the blood
qs.why: Carbonic anhydrase in the cell makes H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The H⁺ is swapped into the lumen for Na⁺, and the HCO₃⁻ goes to the blood, so each H⁺ secreted saves one HCO₃⁻.

qs.q: Lacis cells are another name for which cells?
qs.why: Lacis cells are extraglomerular mesangial cells, sitting between the two arterioles and the macula densa. They are part of the JGA, but renin comes from the granular cells.

qs.q: After leaving the glomerulus by the efferent arteriole, blood flows into what?
qs.why: Route: afferent arteriole → glomerulus (first capillary bed) → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries (second bed) → interlobular vein → renal vein.

qs.q: Why do peritubular capillaries pull reabsorbed fluid back into the blood?
opts: Low pressure and high protein concentration
High pressure and high protein concentration
High pressure and low protein concentration
Low pressure and low protein concentration
qs.why: Blood leaving the glomerulus has lost fluid but kept its protein, and the peritubular capillaries run at low pressure, so the balance favors fluid moving from around the tubules into the capillaries.

qs.q: Why does blood flowing through the vasa recta not wash out the medullary salt gradient?
opts: Its hairpin path returns salt on the way up
It actively pumps salt into the medulla
It carries about 25% of renal blood flow
Its walls are impermeable to salt
qs.why: Going down, the blood picks up salt; coming back up beside the loop, it gives the salt back (countercurrent exchange). Flow is also slow: only about 5% of renal blood flow reaches the medulla.

qs.q: Why do adult women average a lower percentage of body water than men?
opts: More body fat, which holds little water
More muscle, which holds little water
qs.why: Fat holds little water while muscle holds a lot. Women average more fat, so about 50% water versus about 60% in men.

qs.q: About how much intracellular fluid does a 70-kg man have?
qs.why: TBW = 60% × 70 kg = 42 L; ICF is two-thirds of that, 28 L. 14 L is the ECF, and 10.5 L is the interstitial fluid.

qs.q: Plasma makes up what fraction of the extracellular fluid (ECF)?
qs.why: The ECF is one-quarter plasma and three-quarters interstitial fluid. One-third is the ECF's share of total body water.

qs.q: Because plasma holds trapped negatively charged proteins, how does it compare with interstitial fluid?
opts: Slightly more Na⁺ and more Cl⁻
Slightly less Na⁺, slightly more Cl⁻
Slightly less Na⁺ and less Cl⁻
Slightly more Na⁺, slightly less Cl⁻
qs.why: Gibbs-Donnan effect: the side with trapped protein holds extra cations and repels small anions. So plasma has a bit more Na⁺, and the protein-free interstitial fluid has more Cl⁻.

qs.q: You inject 300 mg of mannitol; 30 mg is lost in urine; plasma mannitol settles at 18 mg/L. What is the volume measured?
qs.why: Volume = amount remaining ÷ concentration = (300 − 30) mg ÷ 18 mg/L = 15 L, the ECF. Forgetting to subtract the urine loss gives 16.7 L.

qs.q: Which marker measures plasma volume?
qs.why: Evans blue sticks to albumin, which is too big to leave the capillaries. Inulin marks the ECF; deuterium oxide and antipyrine mark total body water.

qs.q: How is intracellular fluid (ICF) volume found?
opts: Total body water minus plasma volume
Injecting a marker that stays in cells
qs.why: No marker stays only in cells, so ICF = TBW − ECF. ECF minus plasma gives the interstitial fluid.

qs.q: Plasma volume is 3.6 L and hematocrit is 0.40. What is the blood volume?
qs.why: Blood volume = plasma volume ÷ (1 − Hct) = 3.6 ÷ 0.60 = 6 L. Dividing by the Hct itself gives the wrong 9 L.

qs.q: Why can't mannitol or inulin measure the space of a drug that enters cells?
opts: They cross cell membranes too freely
qs.why: Mannitol and inulin cross capillary walls but not cell membranes, so they mark only the ECF. A drug that enters cells needs a total body water marker such as tritiated water.

qs.q: You inject 900 mCi of tritiated water; after mixing, plasma holds 20 mCi/L, with no urine loss. What is total body water?
qs.why: Volume = amount ÷ concentration = 900 mCi ÷ 20 mCi/L = 45 L. Dividing the wrong way (20 ÷ 900) gives 0.022 L.

qs.q: If some marker is lost in the urine before the blood sample, how do you correct the volume calculation?
opts: Subtract the loss from the plasma concentration
Add the loss to the amount injected
Subtract the loss from the amount injected
qs.why: Only the marker still in the body sets the concentration, so the amount used is the dose injected minus what was lost in urine.

qs.q: A 100-kg man needs a blood level of 5 µg/mL of a drug that fills total body water. What dose is needed?
qs.why: Dose = volume × concentration. A man's TBW ≈ 60% × 100 kg = 60 L, and 5 µg/mL = 5 mg/L, so 60 × 5 = 300 mg. 250 mg would be right for a woman (50% water).

qs.q: A concentration of 5 µg/mL equals what?
qs.why: A mg is 1000 µg and a liter is 1000 mL, so the two factors of 1000 cancel: 5 µg/mL = 5 mg/L.

qs.q: If plasma albumin falls, as in nephrotic syndrome, what can happen with a usual dose of a highly protein-bound drug?
opts: Too little effect, because more is bound
Too little effect, because less is free
Toxicity, because more drug is free
Toxicity, because more drug is bound
qs.why: Only free drug reaches the tissues and acts. Less albumin means more of each dose is free, so the usual dose can become toxic.

qs.q: Anemia and low blood Ca²⁺ in kidney failure come from losing which kidney function?
qs.why: Less erythropoietin → anemia; less 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D → less gut Ca²⁺ absorption. These need long-term tissue loss, so they occur only in chronic failure, unlike fluid overload, acidosis and high K⁺.

slides.note: TBW (total body water) is about 60% of body weight. ICF (intracellular fluid, inside cells) holds 2/3 of it. ECF (extracellular fluid) holds 1/3. The ECF splits into ISF (interstitial fluid, which bathes the cells; 3/4 of ECF) and plasma (the vascular volume; 1/4 of ECF). Example: a 70-kg man has 42 L of TBW = 28 L ICF + 14 L ECF (about 10.5 L ISF + 3.5 L plasma). Here the dashed line only divides the ECF into ISF and plasma. In the shift diagrams that follow, width = volume and height = osmolarity; solid lines are the normal state and dashed lines are the new state. Two rules decide every shift: NaCl stays in the ECF, and water crosses cell membranes freely until ICF and ECF osmolarity are equal.

Answer: A. Fluid enters and leaves the body through the blood. An IV line, absorption from the gut, bleeding and urine all add to or take from plasma first. The change then spreads across capillary walls into the interstitial fluid. The ICF changes last, and only if ECF osmolarity changes, because water moves into or out of cells only to even out osmolarity. (D is a joke choice.)

Answer: A. Read the diagram: only the ECF's right edge moves in, so ECF volume falls. The height (osmolarity) does not change, so no water shifts and the ICF box stays the same. This is isosmotic volume contraction. Diarrhea fluid has about the same osmolarity as ECF, so losing it removes volume without changing concentration. Red cells and proteins stay behind in less plasma, so hematocrit and plasma protein rise. Burns do the same. The other choices change osmolarity: adrenal insufficiency lowers it (Q6). SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH; ADH = antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidney keep water) retains water, so both boxes grow and osmolarity falls. Diabetes insipidus (no ADH effect) loses water, so both shrink and osmolarity rises.

Answer: B. Sweat is hyposmotic: it carries more water than salt. Step by step: (1) losing sweat shrinks the ECF; (2) the salt left behind is now in less water, so ECF osmolarity rises; (3) water moves out of the cells toward the higher osmolarity until the two sides match, so the ICF shrinks too. Result: hyperosmotic volume contraction (both boxes narrower, both taller). Water deprivation, fever and diabetes insipidus look the same. Plasma protein rises, but hematocrit stays the same: red cells become more concentrated, but each one shrinks as it loses water. Hypertonic saline would expand the ECF; burns lose isosmotic fluid, like diarrhea.

Osmolarity is the concentration of dissolved particles that pull water, in mOsm/L (milliosmoles per liter). Serum osmolality (per kg of water) is practically the same number. In words: plasma osmolarity ≈ 2 × plasma sodium + glucose ÷ 18 + BUN ÷ 2.8. Na⁺ is in mEq/L and counts twice because each Na⁺ travels with an anion (Cl⁻ or HCO₃⁻). Glucose and BUN (blood urea nitrogen) are in mg/dL; dividing by 18 and by 2.8 turns them into mOsm/L. Example: Na⁺ 140, glucose 90, BUN 14 → 280 + 5 + 5 = 290 mOsm/L, the normal value (often rounded to 300). Sodium is by far the biggest term, so plasma Na⁺ mostly sets osmolarity.

Answer: D. Eating dry salt adds NaCl, and NaCl stays outside the cells. Step by step: (1) ECF osmolarity rises; (2) water moves out of the cells into the saltier ECF until the osmolarities match; (3) the ECF grows and the ICF shrinks. Result: hyperosmotic volume expansion (ECF wider, ICF narrower, both taller). Infusing hypertonic saline does the same. Hematocrit and plasma protein fall, because the plasma is diluted and red cells shrink. Don't confuse with isotonic saline infusion, which widens only the ECF and leaves osmolarity unchanged (Q5).

Answer: D. Only the ECF's right edge moves out (1); the height and the ICF don't change. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) has the same osmolarity as body fluid, and its NaCl stays outside cells. So all of it stays in the ECF, osmolarity doesn't change, and no water enters or leaves the cells. Result: isosmotic volume expansion, the mirror image of diarrhea. Hematocrit and plasma protein fall by dilution. Free water would spread into both compartments and lower osmolarity. Salt tablets would raise osmolarity. A smaller body would shrink every box.

Answer: C. The adrenal cortex makes aldosterone, the hormone that makes the kidney reabsorb Na⁺. Without it, NaCl is lost in urine. Step by step: (1) the ECF loses more salt than water, so ECF volume and osmolarity both fall (arrow 1 points down and in); (2) the cells now have a higher osmolarity than the ECF, so water moves into them (arrow 2); (3) the ICF swells. Result: hyposmotic volume contraction. Hematocrit rises (less plasma, and each red cell swells). Don't confuse: D5W (5% dextrose in water; the sugar is burned, leaving free water) and half-normal saline (0.45% NaCl) expand both compartments and lower osmolarity. Mannitol stays in the ECF and pulls water out of cells.

Clearance is a volume of plasma per minute (mL/min), not an amount of substance. Picture the plasma flowing through the kidneys. Clearance asks: how many mL of that plasma would have to be emptied completely to supply what appears in urine each minute? That is why it is not just the excretion rate (an amount, in mg/min): clearance divides the excretion rate by how much is in each mL of plasma. A high clearance means the kidney removes the substance well; a clearance of zero means none of it leaves in urine.

In words: clearance of x = urine concentration of x × urine flow rate ÷ plasma concentration of x. In symbols: Cₓ = Uₓ × V ÷ Pₓ. Cₓ = clearance of x (mL/min). Uₓ = urine concentration of x (mg/mL). V = urine flow rate (mL of urine per minute; 'urine volume' in the formula means this). Pₓ = plasma concentration of x (mg/mL). The top, Uₓ × V, is the excretion rate: the mg of x leaving in urine each minute. Example: Uₓ = 10 mg/mL and V = 2 mL/min → 20 mg/min excreted. Pₓ = 0.2 mg/mL, so clearance = 20 ÷ 0.2 = 100 mL/min. Each minute, the kidneys remove all the x held in 100 mL of plasma.

Each analogy counts how much is made completely clean per unit time, not how much dirt is removed. Laundry: count the shirts washed fully clean per hour. Burning house: count the rooms fully emptied per minute. Clearance likewise counts the mL of plasma fully emptied of x per minute. The loan-to-asset ratio stresses that clearance is a ratio: the amount removed per minute divided by the amount in each mL of plasma.

Clearance only says how fast the kidney removes something; whether that is healthy depends on the substance. Normal clearance of glucose and amino acids is zero: they are filtered, then all reabsorbed (returned from the tubule fluid to the blood). Albumin's is near zero because it is too big to be filtered. Clearance above zero signals disease: glucose in urine when blood glucose is so high that the tubule can't reabsorb it all (uncontrolled diabetes), or albumin in urine when the glomerulus is damaged. Excretion = amount filtered − amount reabsorbed + amount secreted (added from the blood into the tubule fluid), and clearance = excretion ÷ plasma concentration. So secretion raises clearance and reabsorption lowers it.

Inulin is a plant fructose polymer (not insulin). It must be infused, so it is used only in research. It passes freely into the filtrate, and the tubules neither reabsorb it (return it to the blood) nor secrete it (add more from the blood). So the amount filtered each minute equals the amount excreted: GFR × plasma inulin concentration = urine inulin concentration × urine flow rate. Rearranged: GFR = urine inulin × V ÷ plasma inulin = inulin clearance (V = urine flow rate). GFR (glomerular filtration rate) is the mL of plasma filtered per minute, normally about 120 mL/min. Clinically, creatinine clearance estimates GFR, because the body makes creatinine itself. A little creatinine is also secreted, so it slightly overestimates GFR.

Inulin clearance equals GFR, so it is the yardstick. Filtered load = GFR × Pₓ: the mg of x filtered per minute. Compare Cₓ with inulin clearance. Cₓ lower: less leaves in urine than was filtered, so the tubules returned some from the tubule fluid to the blood (net reabsorption; e.g., Na⁺, urea, glucose), or x is not filtered at all (albumin). Cₓ higher: more leaves than was filtered, so the tubules added some from the blood into the tubule fluid (net secretion; e.g., PAH). Cₓ equal: x is only filtered, so its clearance also equals GFR. Example: GFR 120 mL/min and Pₓ 1 mg/mL → 120 mg/min filtered. If 60 mg/min is excreted, 60 mg/min was reabsorbed, and Cₓ = 60 mL/min.

PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) is an organic acid used to measure RPF (renal plasma flow: the mL of plasma reaching the kidneys per minute, about 660 mL/min). About 20% of the plasma entering the glomerulus is filtered (the filtration fraction), and it carries 20% of the PAH. The other 80% of the plasma moves on to the peritubular capillaries, where the proximal tubule secretes nearly all the remaining PAH: it moves the PAH out of that blood and into the tubule fluid. So almost all PAH entering the kidney ends up in urine, and renal-vein PAH is near zero. All the plasma that passed through was cleared, so clearance of PAH = RPF. In reality about 90% is removed, so PAH clearance ('effective RPF') underestimates true RPF by about 10%.

qs.q: Diarrhea causes which type of body fluid change?
qs.why: Diarrhea fluid has about the same osmolarity as ECF, so the ECF shrinks with no change in osmolarity, and no water shifts out of the cells.

qs.q: In diarrhea, what happens to hematocrit and plasma protein concentration?
qs.why: Red cells and proteins stay behind in a smaller plasma volume, so both become more concentrated.

qs.q: Why does sweating shrink the intracellular fluid as well as the ECF?
opts: Sweat is hyperosmotic, so ECF osmolarity falls
Sweat carries K⁺ out of the cells
Sweat is hyposmotic, so ECF osmolarity rises
Sweat is isosmotic, so both lose equally
qs.why: Sweat carries more water than salt. The salt left behind raises ECF osmolarity, so water moves out of the cells until the two sides match.

qs.q: Which condition causes the same hyperosmotic volume contraction as sweating?
qs.why: Diabetes insipidus loses water without ADH effect, so both compartments shrink and osmolarity rises, like sweating. SIADH retains water; diarrhea is isosmotic.

qs.q: Plasma Na⁺ is 130 mEq/L, glucose 90 mg/dL and BUN (blood urea nitrogen) 28 mg/dL. What is the estimated plasma osmolarity?
qs.why: Osmolarity ≈ 2 × Na⁺ + glucose ÷ 18 + BUN ÷ 2.8 = 260 + 5 + 10 = 275 mOsm/L. Forgetting to double Na⁺ gives about 145.

qs.q: Eating salt tablets changes the fluid compartments how?
qs.why: The added NaCl stays outside cells and raises ECF osmolarity, so water moves out of the cells into the ECF: hyperosmotic volume expansion.

qs.q: Why does an IV infusion of normal (0.9%) saline expand only the ECF?
opts: It is hyperosmotic and pulls water from cells
It is isosmotic and its NaCl stays outside cells
Its NaCl is pumped into cells
It is hyposmotic and water enters cells
qs.why: Normal saline matches body fluid osmolarity and NaCl stays in the ECF, so osmolarity doesn't change and no water crosses cell membranes: isosmotic volume expansion.

qs.q: In adrenal insufficiency, what happens to the intracellular fluid volume?
opts: It shrinks, as ECF osmolarity falls
It shrinks, as ECF osmolarity rises
It stays the same, as osmolarity is unchanged
It swells, as ECF osmolarity falls
qs.why: Without aldosterone the kidney loses more NaCl than water, so ECF osmolarity falls; the cells now have the higher osmolarity, so water moves into them: hyposmotic volume contraction.

qs.q: Renal clearance of a substance is measured in what units?
qs.why: Clearance is the volume of plasma emptied of the substance each minute. The excretion rate (mg/min) is an amount, not a clearance.

qs.q: Urine concentration of x is 20 mg/mL, urine flow is 1.5 mL/min, and plasma concentration is 0.5 mg/mL. What is the clearance of x?
qs.why: Clearance = Uₓ × V ÷ Pₓ = 20 × 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 60 mL/min. The excretion rate is 30 mg/min; dividing by plasma concentration gives the clearance.

qs.q: Why is the normal clearance of glucose zero?
opts: It is too large to be filtered
It is not present in plasma
It is filtered, then all reabsorbed
It is filtered, then all secreted
qs.why: Glucose is freely filtered but the tubules take all of it back. Albumin's near-zero clearance is the one due to not being filtered.

qs.q: More tubular reabsorption of a substance does what to its clearance?
qs.why: Excretion = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted, and clearance = excretion ÷ plasma concentration. So reabsorption lowers clearance and secretion raises it.

qs.q: Why does inulin clearance equal the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
opts: It is filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted
It is filtered and fully secreted
It is secreted but not filtered
It is filtered and partly reabsorbed
qs.why: With no reabsorption or secretion, the amount filtered each minute equals the amount excreted, so inulin clearance equals GFR.

qs.q: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate GFR?
opts: Creatinine is made by the kidney
qs.why: Secretion adds a little extra creatinine to the urine beyond what was filtered, so its clearance comes out slightly above GFR.

qs.q: A substance's clearance is lower than inulin clearance. What does that show (if it is freely filtered)?
qs.why: Less leaves in urine than was filtered, so the tubules reabsorbed some (returned it from the tubule fluid to the blood). Clearance above inulin's means net secretion; equal means filtration only.

qs.q: Why does PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) clearance slightly underestimate true renal plasma flow?
opts: PAH is made by the tubule
PAH is not filtered at all
Only about 90% of PAH is removed
qs.why: PAH clearance equals RPF only if all PAH entering the kidney ends up in urine. In reality about 90% is removed, so 'effective RPF' runs about 10% low.

slides.note: The kidneys get far more blood than their own tissue needs: 25% of cardiac output (CO) for 1% of body weight. The flow is there to clean the plasma, not to feed the kidney. Worked example: 5 L/min × 0.25 = 1.25 L/min of renal blood flow (RBF). 1.25 L/min × 1,440 minutes in a day = 1,800 L/day. About half of that is plasma, and about 20% of the plasma is filtered, so the kidneys filter about 180 L a day.

Blood flow through the kidney obeys the same rule as any organ. In words: flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. In symbols: Q = ΔP / R, where Q = blood flow, ΔP = renal artery pressure minus renal vein pressure, and R = resistance of the renal vessels. Example: if R doubles while ΔP stays the same, flow halves. Most of the resistance sits in the arterioles, and the kidney has two in a row: the afferent arteriole (into the glomerulus) and the efferent arteriole (out of it). So the body changes RBF mainly by tightening or relaxing these two arterioles.

Graph: x-axis = perfusion pressure (ΔP, arterial minus venous pressure); y-axis = blood flow. Each line is one vessel bed. The slope of each line is 1 ÷ resistance. At the same pressure, the steep red line (low resistance) carries far more flow than the flat blue line (high resistance). So when an arteriole relaxes and its resistance drops, flow jumps even though the pressure has not changed. Resistance depends mostly on vessel radius: halving the radius raises resistance about 16-fold, so small changes in arteriolar tone cause big changes in flow.

Cars = blood; toll booths = narrow vessels (resistors). In series (one booth after another), every car must pass each booth, so the resistances add and total resistance rises. In parallel (booths side by side), cars split among them, so total resistance is lower than any single booth. In the kidney, the afferent arteriole → glomerular capillaries → efferent arteriole are in series. So constricting either arteriole raises total renal resistance and lowers RBF. The million nephrons sit in parallel with each other.

Constrictors raise arteriolar resistance, so RBF falls. Dilators lower resistance, so RBF rises. Catecholamines = norepinephrine and epinephrine, the messengers of the sympathetic nervous system. Endothelin is released by the cells lining blood vessels. In a stress such as bleeding, the body turns on the constrictors to hold blood pressure up. At the same time the kidney makes its own dilators (prostaglandins E₂ and I₂, nitric oxide), so its blood flow does not fall too far.

Renal arterioles carry α1 (alpha-1) receptors, not β receptors. Sympathetic nerves and circulating norepinephrine act on α1 and constrict the arterioles. There are far more α1 receptors on the afferent arteriole, so the afferent constricts most. Less blood and less pressure reach the glomerulus, so both RBF and GFR (glomerular filtration rate) fall. Example: after hemorrhage, the baroreceptor reflex fires the sympathetic nerves. Blood pressure is defended at the kidney's expense. The only β1 receptors in the kidney are on the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, and they trigger renin release.

Angiotensin II (AT II) constricts both arterioles, but the efferent is more sensitive. Low to normal levels squeeze mainly the efferent arteriole. Blood backs up in the glomerulus, so glomerular capillary pressure rises and GFR rises (or is protected when blood pressure is low). Less blood gets through, so RBF falls. Very high levels (e.g., severe hemorrhage) also clamp the afferent arteriole, so less pressure reaches the glomerulus and GFR falls. ACE inhibitors (block the enzyme that makes AT II) and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) remove the efferent squeeze, so glomerular pressure drops.

Prostaglandins (PGE₂ and PGI₂) are made in the kidney itself and dilate both arterioles, the afferent most. They switch on with the same stresses that raise sympathetic activity and AT II (hemorrhage, heart failure, dehydration). This seems contradictory, but it is protective: the dilation offsets the constriction, so RBF and GFR don't crash. NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen) block prostaglandin synthesis. In a healthy person this barely matters. In a stressed kidney (old age, diabetes, heart failure, dehydration), the afferent arteriole constricts unopposed, so RBF and GFR fall and creatinine rises.

Dopamine's effect depends on the dose because it reaches different receptors as its level rises. Low dose: dopamine (D1) receptors dilate renal and splanchnic (gut and spleen) arterioles, so RBF rises. Medium dose: β1 receptors on the heart raise heart rate and force, so cardiac output rises. High dose: α1 receptors constrict arterioles throughout the body, so blood pressure rises. A drug that raises blood pressure this way is called a pressor. At this dose the α1 constriction lowers RBF.

Low-dose ("renal-dose") dopamine raises RBF and urine output, so it was once given to protect the kidneys of very sick patients. Trials showed it does not prevent acute kidney injury, does not reduce the need for dialysis and does not lower deaths. More urine does not mean a healthier kidney. So dopamine is not used to protect the kidneys.

Autoregulation. x-axis = Pa, the pressure in the renal artery (mmHg); y-axis = renal blood flow (RBF) or GFR, which behave the same way. Below about 80 mmHg, RBF and GFR fall as pressure falls. From about 80 to 200 mmHg the line is flat: RBF and GFR stay constant even though pressure changes. It works because the afferent arteriole changes its resistance in step with pressure: pressure rises → afferent constricts → glomerular flow and pressure stay the same. It is local: a transplanted kidney with no nerves autoregulates just as well.

Graph: x-axis = mean pressure in the renal artery. Solid blue line (left axis) = RPF (renal plasma flow); dotted line (right axis) = GFR. Below about 80 mmHg, both rise and fall with pressure. From about 80 to 200 mmHg both lines are flat: that is autoregulation. RPF and GFR are held steady together because the control point is the afferent arteriole, which sits upstream of both. Above about 200 mmHg the afferent arteriole cannot constrict any further, so RPF climbs with pressure again.

Same idea in another experiment. x-axis = renal artery pressure (torr = mmHg). Dashed line = GFR (left axis); red line = RBF (right axis). Both stay nearly flat across the middle pressures (roughly 100 to 200 torr). Dotted line = UFR (urine flow rate, left axis): it is not autoregulated. Urine flow keeps rising as pressure rises, because higher pressure lowers Na⁺ and water reabsorption in the tubules. This pressure diuresis lets the kidney pour out salt and water when blood pressure is high, which brings the pressure back down.

Read the Kidneys row (the arrow hides the first digit: blood flow is 1,260 mL/min). The kidneys weigh only 0.3 kg but get 23% of cardiac output: 420 mL per 100 g per minute, the highest flow per gram of any organ (heart 84, liver 58, brain 54). Yet the arteriovenous O₂ difference (O₂ removed from each liter of blood) is tiny: 14 mL/L, versus 114 in heart muscle. So the kidney's huge flow serves filtration, not its own metabolism. The heart is the opposite: modest flow, but it removes more O₂ per liter than any other single organ in the table.

Myogenic mechanism, step by step: (1) arterial pressure rises; (2) the pressure stretches the wall of the afferent arteriole; (3) stretch opens stretch-activated Ca²⁺ channels in its smooth muscle; (4) Ca²⁺ enters and the muscle contracts ("Don't push me!"); (5) resistance rises in proportion to the pressure, so RBF and GFR stay the same (Q = ΔP/R: ΔP and R both went up). When pressure falls, the muscle relaxes and resistance drops. It is built into the vessel wall, so it needs no nerves.

Blanks: (1) NaCl (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) delivered to the macula densa; (2) adenosine; (3) adenosine. Why, step by step: arterial pressure rises → GFR rises → more fluid and NaCl flow down the tubule → the macula densa (salt-sensing cells in the early distal tubule wall, right beside the same nephron's afferent arteriole) detects the extra NaCl → it releases adenosine → adenosine constricts the afferent arteriole → RBF and GFR fall back to normal. It also works in reverse: less NaCl reaching the macula densa → afferent dilates → GFR rises. This loop is tubuloglomerular feedback.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus is where the early distal tubule touches its own afferent arteriole. The macula densa (the orange ring of tightly packed tubule cells) senses NaCl in the tubular fluid. The JG (juxtaglomerular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall that store and release renin. Renin release rises with three signals: (1) low NaCl at the macula densa; (2) β1 sympathetic stimulation; (3) low blood pressure or fluid volume, sensed as less stretch of the afferent arteriole. The arrows pointing at the JG cells are these three signals; the arrows labeled Renin show renin leaving into the afferent arteriole blood. Renin starts the chain that makes angiotensin II.

Clearance (C) = the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) is infused to measure RPF. The 20% of plasma that is filtered carries 20% of the PAH into the tubule; the tubule secretes nearly all of the other 80%, moving it from the peritubular capillary blood into the tubule fluid. So almost every PAH molecule entering in the renal artery (RA) ends up in urine, and renal vein PAH is about 0. Every mL of plasma reaching the kidney is cleared, so PAH clearance = RPF. In words: RPF = (urine PAH concentration × urine flow rate) ÷ plasma PAH concentration. In symbols: RPF = CPAH = UPAH × V ÷ PPAH (V = urine flow rate). Example: UPAH 6 mg/mL × V 1 mL/min ÷ PPAH 0.01 mg/mL = 600 mL/min.

Follow the PAH dots. (1) PAH arrives in the afferent arteriole. (2) About 20% is filtered into Bowman's space with the filtrate. The other 80% leaves in the efferent arteriole and flows into the peritubular capillaries wrapped around the tubule. There, the tubule cells secrete it: they move it out of the peritubular blood into the tubular fluid (black arrow pointing into the tubule). "100% PAH secreted" means all the PAH still left in that blood. Result: the blood leaving the kidney carries almost no PAH, and all of it ends up in urine. This is why PAH clearance equals RPF.

Glucose is the opposite of PAH. It is filtered with the plasma (20% of the plasma, and so 20% of the glucose, enters the tubule). The proximal tubule then reabsorbs all of it (moves it out of the tubule fluid back into the blood) and secretes none. No glucose reaches urine, so its clearance is 0: no plasma is cleared of glucose. Renal vein glucose equals renal artery glucose, so glucose cannot measure plasma flow. This holds only while plasma glucose is below about 200 mg/dL (the threshold). Above it the transporters saturate and glucose spills into urine, as in uncontrolled diabetes.

Why PAH clearance slightly underestimates RPF, compared with a familiar lung example. In the lung, 2–3% of blood (bronchial veins, and the heart's thebesian veins) drains into the left heart without passing the alveoli, so arterial blood is never fully oxygenated: a normal "shunt." In the kidney, 5–10% of plasma flow goes to tissue that does not secrete PAH (renal fat, capsule, connective tissue). That plasma keeps its PAH, so renal vein PAH is a little above 0. So PAH clearance measures effective RPF, about 10% below the true RPF.

Plasma is only part of blood, so blood flow is larger than plasma flow. Hct (hematocrit) = fraction of blood volume made of red cells; 1 − Hct = fraction that is plasma. In words: renal blood flow = renal plasma flow ÷ fraction of blood that is plasma. In symbols: RBF = RPF / (1 − Hct). Worked example with a normal Hct: RPF 600 mL/min, Hct 0.45 → plasma fraction 0.55 → RBF = 600 / 0.55 ≈ 1,090 mL/min. With Hct 0.5 the math is easy: 600 / 0.5 = 1,200 mL/min. Check: RBF must always come out larger than RPF.

The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries between two arterioles: blood enters by the afferent arteriole and leaves by the efferent arteriole, not by a vein. Because both ends have adjustable resistance, the kidney can set glomerular capillary pressure and flow separately. Fluid filters out of the capillaries into Bowman's space, inside the glomerular capsule (= Bowman's capsule). That space lies between the visceral layer (podocytes hugging the capillaries) and the parietal layer (outer wall of the capsule). The filtrate then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule.

Four processes decide what ends up in urine. (1) Filtration: plasma moves from glomerular capillaries into Bowman's space. (2) Reabsorption: substances move from the tubule back into peritubular capillary blood (arrow pointing out of the tubule). (3) Secretion: substances move from peritubular blood into the tubule (arrow pointing into the tubule). (4) Excretion: what leaves in the urine. In words: excretion = filtration − reabsorption + secretion. Examples: inulin is only filtered; glucose is filtered and fully reabsorbed (none excreted); PAH is filtered and secreted (nearly all excreted).

Cross-section of one glomerular capillary, with blood in the middle. To leave the blood, fluid crosses three layers in order: (1) the fenestrated endothelium (capillary lining full of holes); (2) the GBM (glomerular basement membrane); (3) the podocytes, whose foot processes wrap the outside of the capillary with slits between them. Beyond them is Bowman's space. The mesangium (orange, left) is the stalk of mesangial cells between capillary loops. These cells support the loops, can contract and clear away trapped proteins.

Zoom on the barrier: blood (capillary lumen) at the bottom, Bowman's space at the top, blue arrows = direction of filtration. Endothelial fenestrae are 70–100 nm wide: big enough to pass water, solutes and even proteins, but not blood cells. The GBM is the main barrier to plasma proteins. Between podocyte foot processes are filtration slits (about 40 nm wide) bridged by a thin slit diaphragm, a second size barrier. The glycocalyx is the negatively charged sugar coat on the endothelium.

Top, electron micrograph: Pod = podocyte foot processes; GBM = glomerular basement membrane; GEnC = glomerular endothelial cell; asterisks (*) = slit diaphragms between foot processes. Bottom, the slit diaphragm up close: nephrin molecules from neighboring foot processes zip together across the slit. Podocin and CD2AP anchor nephrin to the actin skeleton inside each foot process. Integrins (α3β1) bolt the foot process onto the GBM. Mutations in nephrin or podocin break the slit diaphragm, so large amounts of protein leak into urine (inherited nephrotic syndrome).

Besides size, the barrier filters by charge. Fixed negatively charged glycoproteins coat the endothelium, the GBM, the podocytes and the slit diaphragms (SD). Like charges repel, so negatively charged molecules are held back and positively charged ones pass more easily. Albumin is close to the pore size and carries a net negative charge, so the barrier's negative charge is a big reason albumin stays in the blood. Red cells are simply too big. If the barrier loses its negative charge (as in early diabetic kidney disease), albumin leaks into urine.

Graph: x-axis = molecular radius in Å (ångström; 10 Å = 1 nm); y-axis = relative filterability (1 = filtered as freely as water, 0 = not filtered). Dextrans are test sugars made in three charges at each size. At every size, cationic (positive) dextran filters best, neutral is in between and anionic (negative) filters worst, because the barrier's negative charge attracts cations and repels anions. The bullets use diameter: neutral molecules under about 4 nm across filter freely; positive ones get through up to about 8 nm; above about 8 nm nothing passes. Radius 20 Å = 4 nm diameter; radius 42 Å ≈ 8 nm diameter.

Same experiment with diameter (nm) on the x-axis and fractional clearance (how freely the molecule is filtered compared with water) on the y-axis. Read up from 6 nm: cationic ≈ 0.8, neutral ≈ 0.35, anionic ≈ 0. Albumin is negatively charged and about 7 nm across, so it sits on the anionic curve near 0: almost none is filtered. Small solutes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, glucose, urea) are far smaller than 4 nm, so charge does not matter for them and they are freely filtered.

GFR is driven by Starling forces, the same pressures that move fluid across any capillary. In words: GFR = filtration coefficient × (pressure pushing fluid out − the pressures holding it back). In symbols: GFR = Kf × [(PGC − PBS) − πGC]. PGC = blood (hydrostatic) pressure in the glomerular capillary, about 45 mmHg; it pushes fluid out. πGC = oncotic pressure, the pull of the plasma proteins that stay in the capillary; it holds fluid in. PBS = pressure of the fluid already in Bowman's space, about 10 mmHg; it pushes back. Oncotic pressure in Bowman's space (πBS) is about 0 because almost no protein is filtered. Kf = filtration coefficient.

Kf (filtration coefficient) = how easily water crosses the barrier × how much surface area there is. Glomerular Kf is more than 100 times that of muscle capillaries, which is why the kidneys filter about 180 L a day. Arrows: yellow PGC points from the capillary toward Bowman's space, pushing fluid out of the capillary; pink πGC and PBS point back toward the capillary, opposing filtration. Anything that lowers Kf lowers GFR even when the pressures are normal. Examples: fewer working glomeruli (scarring), a thickened basement membrane (diabetes), or contracted mesangial cells that shrink the filtering area.

Numbers at the start of the glomerular capillary, in mmHg. Layout: the glomerular capillary (pink) is on top and Bowman's space is below. A plus sign favors filtration (fluid moves from the capillary into Bowman's space); a minus sign opposes it. For filtration: PGC (capillary blood pressure, blue arrow pointing down into Bowman's space) = +45. Against: πGC (protein pull, green arrow pointing up into the capillary) = −19 and PBS (Bowman's space pressure, orange arrow pointing up) = −10, total 29. πBS (oncotic pressure in Bowman's space) = 0 because the filtrate has no protein, so it gets no arrow. Net = 45 − 19 − 10 = +16 mmHg outward, so fluid filters out strongly. PGC stays about 45 along the whole glomerular capillary, unlike body capillaries where pressure falls, because the efferent arteriole downstream holds the pressure up.

Numbers at the end of the capillary. PGC and PBS are unchanged (45 and 10), but πGC (green arrow) has risen from 19 to 35. Why: about 20% of the plasma has filtered out as protein-free fluid, so the proteins left behind are more concentrated and pull harder. Net = 45 − 35 − 10 = 0, so filtration stops: this is filtration equilibrium. Consequences: (1) blood entering the efferent arteriole and peritubular capillaries has a high oncotic pressure, which later helps the proximal tubule reabsorb fluid; (2) the more fluid is filtered (higher filtration fraction), the higher this oncotic pressure gets.

How arteriole changes move GFR, peritubular capillary pressure (blood pressure in the capillaries around the tubules) and RPF. Constrict efferent: blood backs up in the glomerulus, so PGC and GFR rise; less blood gets through, so RPF and downstream pressure fall. FF (filtration fraction = GFR/RPF) rises. Dilate efferent: the reverse; GFR falls, RPF rises, FF falls. Constrict afferent: less blood and pressure reach the glomerulus, so RPF, GFR and peritubular pressure all fall. FF does not change, because GFR and RPF fall together. Dilate afferent: all rise; FF does not change. Examples: sympathetic nerves → afferent constriction; AT II → efferent constriction; ACE inhibitors → efferent dilation; NSAIDs → loss of afferent dilation.

Filtration fraction (FF) = the share of the plasma reaching the glomerulus that gets filtered. In words: FF = GFR ÷ RPF. Worked example: 120 mL/min ÷ 600 mL/min = 0.20. So 20% is filtered, and the other 80% leaves through the efferent arteriole into the peritubular capillaries. If the efferent constricts so GFR rises to 130 and RPF falls to 500, FF = 130 / 500 = 26%. More fluid was filtered, so the plasma left behind carries more protein and has a higher oncotic pressure in the peritubular capillaries.

To measure GFR you need a marker that is freely filtered and then left alone: not reabsorbed, not secreted. Inulin (a plant fructose polymer, infused into a vein) is that marker. Everything filtered appears in urine, so the plasma it clears each minute equals GFR. In words: GFR = (urine inulin concentration × urine flow rate) ÷ plasma inulin concentration. In symbols: GFR = Cinulin = Uinulin × V ÷ Pinulin. Example: 100 mg/mL × 1 mL/min ÷ 1 mg/mL = 100 mL/min. Creatinine is made by muscle, so no infusion is needed, but it is also slightly secreted, so creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR. When GFR falls, plasma creatinine and BUN (blood urea nitrogen) rise.

Step by step: a diabetic with a normal urinalysis still needs a microalbumin test, because the routine dipstick detects protein only once the loss is large (about 300 mg/day or more). Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg albumin per day) is the earliest sign of diabetic kidney damage: albumin starts leaking when the GBM loses negative charge. Finding it early lets you start an ACE inhibitor or ARB, which lowers glomerular pressure and slows the slide to kidney failure. EKG, stress test, chest X-ray and Pap smear do not screen for this.

Answer: B. Albumin is negatively charged and close to the pore size, so normally the barrier's negative charge repels it. In early diabetes, the GBM loses negative charges (heparan sulfate). Albumin is no longer repelled, so small amounts slip through: microalbuminuria. Mesangial expansion (a) and fusion of podocyte foot processes (c) are structural changes that come later and go with heavier proteinuria. Proximal tubule failure (d) spills small proteins and glucose, not albumin first. Prostaglandins (e) change blood flow, not the barrier.

Correction: microalbuminuria is 30–300 mg albumin per day, not 50–300. Answer: C. Step by step: high glomerular pressure forces albumin through the barrier and injures the glomerulus. An ACE inhibitor or ARB removes AT II's squeeze on the efferent arteriole → the efferent dilates → blood leaves the glomerulus more easily → PGC falls → less albumin leaks and the glomerulus is protected. GFR drops a little at first; that is expected. Constricting the efferent (d) would raise PGC. α1 blockers (a) and dopamine (b) do not lower glomerular pressure. Prostaglandin inhibition (e) cuts RBF.

Answer: D. Step by step: an old man with diabetes and hypertension has a kidney that relies on prostaglandins to keep the afferent arteriole open. Ibuprofen (an NSAID) blocks cyclooxygenase, so prostaglandin E₂ and I₂ production stops. Without them, the afferent arteriole constricts under unopposed sympathetic and AT II tone. Less blood and pressure reach the glomerulus → RPF and GFR fall → creatinine, which leaves the body by filtration, builds up in the blood. The other choices are not effects of blocking prostaglandins.

qs.q: Renal blood flow is about what percentage of cardiac output?
qs.why: About 1.25 of 5 L/min goes to the kidneys, though they are only about 1% of body weight. The flow is there to clean plasma, not to feed the kidney.

qs.q: If renal vascular resistance doubles while the pressure difference stays the same, what happens to renal blood flow?
qs.why: Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance (Q = ΔP/R), so doubling R at the same ΔP halves Q.

qs.q: Halving an arteriole's radius raises its resistance about how much?
qs.why: Resistance depends on radius to the fourth power (2⁴ = 16), so small changes in arteriolar tone cause big changes in flow.

qs.q: Why does constricting either renal arteriole lower total renal blood flow?
opts: They are in parallel, so their resistances add
They are in series, so their resistances add
qs.why: Afferent arteriole → glomerular capillaries → efferent arteriole lie one after another, so raising either resistance raises total renal resistance and lowers RBF.

qs.q: Sympathetic nerves constrict renal arterioles through which receptor?
qs.why: Renal arterioles carry α1, not β, receptors. The constriction is strongest on the afferent arteriole, so RBF and GFR fall.

qs.q: What do β1 receptors on juxtaglomerular (JG) cells trigger?
qs.why: The kidney's only β1 receptors are on the JG cells, and they release renin. The arterioles themselves have no β receptors.

qs.q: Low-to-normal angiotensin II constricts mainly which arteriole, with what effect on GFR?
qs.why: The efferent arteriole is more sensitive to AT II. Squeezing it backs blood up in the glomerulus, so glomerular pressure and GFR rise while RBF falls; only very high levels also clamp the afferent and lower GFR.

qs.q: Why can an NSAID lower GFR in a dehydrated older patient?
opts: It removes prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole
It raises pressure in Bowman's space
It blocks α1 receptors on renal arterioles
It constricts the efferent arteriole directly
qs.why: In a stressed kidney, prostaglandins E₂ and I₂ hold the afferent open against sympathetic and AT II tone. NSAIDs block their synthesis, so the afferent constricts unopposed and RBF and GFR fall.

qs.q: Low-dose dopamine raises renal blood flow through which receptor?
qs.why: At low dose, D1 receptors dilate renal and splanchnic arterioles. β1 (heart rate and force) comes in at medium dose and α1 (constriction, lower RBF) at high dose.

qs.q: What does low-dose ("renal-dose") dopamine do for patients at risk of acute kidney injury?
opts: Raises urine output but does not prevent injury
qs.why: It raises RBF and urine output, but trials showed no fewer kidney injuries, dialyses or deaths. More urine does not mean a healthier kidney.

qs.q: Over about what range of mean arterial pressure are RBF and GFR held steady?
qs.why: Between about 80 and 200 mmHg the afferent arteriole changes its resistance in step with pressure. Below about 80 mmHg, RBF and GFR fall with pressure.

qs.q: Which renal quantity keeps rising with arterial pressure even within the autoregulatory range?
qs.why: Higher pressure lowers tubular Na⁺ and water reabsorption, so urine flow rises (pressure diuresis) while RBF and GFR stay flat. This helps bring blood pressure back down.

qs.q: The kidney has the highest blood flow per gram of any organ but a tiny arteriovenous O₂ difference. What does this show?
opts: Its flow is set by its metabolic rate
It extracts more O₂ than heart muscle
Its flow serves filtration, not its own metabolism
It has the highest O₂ demand per gram
qs.why: Kidney flow is about 420 mL/100 g/min, yet it removes only about 14 mL O₂ per liter of blood, versus about 114 in heart muscle.

qs.q: In the myogenic response, stretch of the afferent arteriole opens channels for which ion?
qs.why: Stretch-activated Ca²⁺ channels let Ca²⁺ into the smooth muscle, which contracts. Resistance rises with pressure, so RBF and GFR stay the same, with no nerves needed.

qs.q: When more NaCl reaches the macula densa, what does it release to constrict the afferent arteriole?
qs.why: Tubuloglomerular feedback: high NaCl delivery → macula densa releases adenosine → afferent constricts → GFR falls back to normal.

qs.q: Which signal increases renin release from juxtaglomerular (JG) cells?
opts: More stretch of the afferent arteriole
Low NaCl at the macula densa
High NaCl at the macula densa
α1 stimulation of the JG cells
qs.why: Renin rises with low NaCl at the macula densa, β1 sympathetic stimulation, and low blood pressure sensed as less afferent stretch.

qs.q: Why does PAH clearance approximately equal renal plasma flow?
opts: It is filtered and then fully reabsorbed
It is secreted but not filtered at all
It is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted
It is filtered and secreted, so renal vein PAH is near 0
qs.why: About 20% of PAH is filtered and the tubule secretes nearly all the rest, moving it from peritubular blood into the tubule fluid, so every mL of plasma reaching the kidney is cleared. Filtered-only describes inulin, which measures GFR.

qs.q: What is the normal renal clearance of glucose?
qs.why: Glucose is filtered, but below about 200 mg/dL the proximal tubule reabsorbs all of it. None reaches urine, so no plasma is cleared of glucose.

qs.q: Why does PAH clearance slightly underestimate true renal plasma flow?
opts: PAH is partly trapped inside red blood cells
Some filtered PAH is reabsorbed by the proximal tubule
5–10% of flow perfuses tissue that does not secrete PAH
PAH is not freely filtered at the glomerulus
