qs.why: Plasma perfusing renal fat, capsule and connective tissue keeps its PAH, so renal vein PAH is slightly above 0. PAH clearance gives effective RPF, about 10% below true RPF.

qs.q: RPF is 600 mL/min and hematocrit is 0.40. What is renal blood flow?
qs.why: RBF = RPF ÷ (1 − Hct) = 600 ÷ 0.60 = 1,000 mL/min. Dividing by Hct (1,500) uses the red-cell fraction instead of the plasma fraction.

qs.q: Blood leaves the glomerular capillaries through which vessel?
qs.why: The glomerulus sits between two arterioles, so the kidney can set glomerular pressure and flow by adjusting resistance at both ends.

qs.q: Which expression gives the amount of a substance excreted in urine?
qs.why: Reabsorption moves a substance out of the tubule fluid back into the blood, so it is subtracted; secretion moves it from the blood into the tubule, so it is added. Glucose is filtered and fully reabsorbed; PAH is filtered and secreted.

qs.q: In order from blood to Bowman's space, which layers does the filtrate cross?
qs.why: The capillary lining comes first, then the glomerular basement membrane (GBM, the main barrier to plasma proteins), then the slits between podocyte foot processes.

qs.q: Mutations in nephrin or podocin cause what?
qs.why: Nephrin zips the slit diaphragm closed and podocin anchors it to the foot process. When either fails, the slit diaphragm breaks and large amounts of protein leak into urine.

qs.q: Of three dextrans of the same size, which is filtered least?
opts: They filter equally; only size matters
qs.why: The barrier's fixed negative charges repel anions and attract cations, so at every size cationic > neutral > anionic.

qs.q: Above about what molecular diameter are even cationic molecules not filtered?
qs.why: Neutral molecules pass freely below about 4 nm and cations up to about 8 nm; nothing larger gets through. 70–100 nm is the size of the endothelial fenestrae.

qs.q: Besides its size, what keeps albumin out of the glomerular filtrate?
opts: Its binding to red blood cells
qs.why: Albumin (about 7 nm) is close to the pore size and negatively charged, so the barrier's negative charge repels it and almost none is filtered.

qs.q: Which force favors glomerular filtration?
qs.why: PGC (about 45 mmHg) pushes fluid out. πGC (the pull of plasma proteins) and PBS (about 10 mmHg) hold it back.

qs.q: A thickened glomerular basement membrane in diabetes lowers GFR by lowering which factor?
qs.why: Kf = water permeability × filtering area. A thicker membrane, fewer working glomeruli or contracted mesangial cells lower Kf, and GFR falls even with normal pressures.

qs.q: PGC = 50, πGC = 25 and PBS = 10 mmHg (oncotic pressure in Bowman's space = 0). What is the net filtration pressure?
qs.why: Net = PGC − πGC − PBS = 50 − 25 − 10 = +15 mmHg outward. +25 forgets PBS; +40 forgets πGC.

qs.q: Why does glomerular capillary oncotic pressure rise from about 19 to 35 mmHg along the capillary?
opts: Filtered albumin is returned to the capillary
Podocytes add protein to the capillary blood
Protein-free fluid filters out, concentrating the proteins left
Hydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary
qs.why: About 20% of the plasma leaves as protein-free filtrate, so the proteins left behind pull harder. By the end, net pressure is 0 (filtration equilibrium).

qs.q: Constricting the efferent arteriole does what to GFR and RPF?
qs.why: Blood backs up in the glomerulus, raising PGC and GFR, while less blood gets through, so RPF falls and filtration fraction rises.

qs.q: Constricting the afferent arteriole does what to the filtration fraction?
qs.why: Less blood and pressure reach the glomerulus, so GFR and RPF fall together and FF = GFR ÷ RPF does not change. Efferent constriction is what raises FF.

qs.q: GFR is 150 mL/min and RPF is 500 mL/min. What is the filtration fraction?
qs.why: FF = GFR ÷ RPF = 150 ÷ 500 = 0.30. The other 70% of the plasma leaves through the efferent arteriole.

qs.q: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate GFR?
opts: Creatinine is slightly reabsorbed by the tubule
Creatinine is slightly secreted by the tubule
Creatinine is made by the kidney
qs.why: Inulin is filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR. Creatinine's small secretion adds to the amount in urine, so its clearance runs a bit high.

qs.q: Microalbuminuria means albumin excretion of about how much?
qs.why: Albumin loss of 30–300 mg/day is the earliest sign of diabetic kidney damage, starting when the GBM loses negative charge.

qs.q: Why can a routine urine dipstick be normal in early diabetic kidney disease?
opts: It detects protein only above about 300 mg/day
It detects glucose but not protein
It detects only positively charged proteins
Albumin cannot cross the barrier in diabetes
qs.why: The dipstick turns positive only once protein loss is large, so a diabetic with a normal urinalysis still needs a microalbumin test.

qs.q: Right after an ACE inhibitor is started, what is the expected change in GFR?
opts: A sharp fall, as the afferent arteriole constricts
A rise, as the efferent arteriole constricts
A rise, as the afferent arteriole dilates
A small fall, as glomerular pressure drops
qs.why: Removing AT II's squeeze dilates the efferent arteriole, so PGC falls. GFR drops a little at first, which is expected, and less albumin leaks.

qs.q: Ibuprofen lowers renal prostaglandin production by blocking which enzyme?
qs.why: Blocking cyclooxygenase stops PGE₂ and PGI₂ synthesis, so the afferent arteriole constricts unopposed; GFR falls and creatinine rises.

slides.note: GFR (glomerular filtration rate) is the volume of plasma both kidneys filter each minute, about 120 mL/min. Multiply by the minutes in a day: 120 mL/min × 1440 min = 172,800 mL, about 180 L/day. Plasma volume is only about 3 L, so the kidneys filter the whole plasma about 60 times a day. Yet urine is only about 1.5 L/day. So more than 99% of the filtrate must be reabsorbed (moved out of the tubule fluid back into the blood), which is why reabsorption is the tubule's biggest job.

Freely filtered means a substance crosses the glomerular barrier as easily as water. So its concentration in Bowman's space (the cup that collects the filtrate) equals its concentration in plasma. All small molecules and ions pass. Big proteins such as albumin and the hormone-binding globulins are held back by their size and negative charge. Inulin (a plant sugar used to measure GFR) and PAH (para-aminohippuric acid, used to measure renal plasma flow) are test substances. Myoglobin (17 kDa, about a quarter of albumin's size) also passes, so muscle breakdown puts it into the urine.

Filtration is bulk flow. Pressure pushes plasma through the barrier like water through a sieve, and small solutes ride along. No carrier protein binds the solute, so there is nothing to fill up: filtration never saturates. No ATP is spent on the solute. So the amount filtered depends on only two things: how much plasma is filtered (GFR) and the solute's concentration in it. Double the plasma glucose and the glucose filtered doubles. Reabsorption is the opposite: it uses carriers, so it has a ceiling.

TF/P = concentration of a substance in tubular fluid (TF) ÷ its concentration in plasma (P). In Bowman's space TF/P = 1 for anything freely filtered, because the filtrate is plasma minus the big proteins. TF/P = 0 for anything held back. Filtration fraction (FF) = GFR ÷ RPF (renal plasma flow, the plasma reaching the kidneys per minute), about 120 ÷ 600 = 20%. So only one-fifth of the plasma volume is filtered, but that fifth carries every small solute at plasma concentration. The listed exceptions are the big proteins that are not filtered (TF/P ≈ 0): albumin and the globulins that carry cortisol, thyroid hormone and sex hormones. Hormone bound to these globulins stays in the blood with them. Further down the tubule TF/P changes, because water and solutes are removed at different rates.

Follow the filtrate: blood in the glomerular capillaries (the tuft of loops) → through the podocyte layer → Bowman's space → straight into the proximal tubule, where most reabsorption happens. Small solutes cross this barrier freely, so the fluid entering the proximal tubule has the same small-solute concentrations as plasma. The macula densa (top, where the distal tubule touches the glomerulus) senses tubular NaCl; it plays no part in filtration itself.

Filtered load is the amount of a substance (mg or meq) that enters Bowman's space each minute. In words: filtered load = filtration rate × plasma concentration. In symbols: filtered load = GFR × Pₓ, where Pₓ is the plasma concentration of substance x. GFR is in mL/min, so first convert Pₓ to per mL: mg/dL ÷ 100 (1 dL = 100 mL); meq/L ÷ 1000. Example: plasma Na⁺ 140 meq/L = 0.14 meq/mL, so filtered Na⁺ = 120 mL/min × 0.14 meq/mL = 16.8 meq/min.

Excretion rate is the amount of a substance leaving in the urine each minute. In words: excretion rate = urine concentration × urine flow rate. In symbols: excretion = Uₓ × V̇, where Uₓ is the urine concentration of x and V̇ is the urine flow rate (mL/min): the "quantity of urine" made per minute, not the total volume. Convert units first, as for filtered load. Example: urine glucose 300 mg/dL = 3 mg/mL and urine flow 2 mL/min, so excretion = 3 × 2 = 6 mg/min. Comparing excretion with filtered load tells you whether the tubule reabsorbed or secreted the substance.

Answer: E. Step 1, units: GFR is per mL, so convert K⁺ to per mL: 4 meq/L ÷ 1000 = 0.004 meq/mL. Step 2: filtered load = GFR × plasma K⁺ = 120 mL/min × 0.004 meq/mL = 0.48 meq/min. Choice D (480) is the trap: 120 × 4 without converting liters to mL, which is 1000 times too big.

Answer: B. Step 1, units: 500 mg/dL ÷ 100 = 5 mg/mL. Step 2: filtered load = GFR × plasma glucose = 120 mL/min × 5 mg/mL = 600 mg/min (the choice leaves out 'per minute'). Why polyuria and polydipsia: the glucose carriers can reabsorb at most about 375 mg/min (Tm, transport maximum). So about 225 mg/min stays in the tubule. That glucose holds water in the tubule by osmosis, so urine volume rises (osmotic diuresis), the patient loses water and becomes thirsty.

In words: amount reabsorbed = amount filtered − amount excreted. In symbols: reabsorption = (GFR × Pₓ) − (Uₓ × V̇). Normal plasma glucose is about 100 mg/dL = 1 mg/mL. Filtered load = 120 mL/min × 1 mg/mL = 120 mg/min. Normal urine has no glucose, so excretion = 0. So all 120 mg/min went back to the blood. Whenever the result is positive (filtered more than excreted), the tubule has reabsorbed the substance.

Substances the body must keep, such as glucose, amino acids and lactate, are freely filtered and then reabsorbed (moved out of the tubule fluid back into the blood) by Na⁺-coupled carrier proteins in the proximal tubule. At normal plasma levels these carriers have spare capacity, so they return 100% to the blood and urine contains none. 'Energy dependent' here means carrier transport powered by the Na⁺ gradient. If one of these appears in urine, either the plasma level is so high that the filtered load exceeds the carriers' maximum (Tm), or the carriers are defective.

Correction: the subtraction is off: 56 − 18 = 38 g/day secreted. Secretion moves a substance from the peritubular capillary blood into the tubule, on top of what was filtered. In words: amount secreted = amount excreted − amount filtered. In symbols: secretion = (Uₓ × V̇) − (GFR × Pₓ). PAH is filtered (18 g/day) and then pumped into the proximal tubule by organic-anion carriers, so the urine carries three times the filtered amount. Rule: excreted more than filtered means net secretion.

The four processes, colored boxes left to right. Filtration: plasma moves from the glomerulus into the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule. Reabsorption: substances move from the tubule back into the peritubular capillary (arrow pointing up, out of the proximal convoluted tubule into the capillary). Secretion: substances move from the peritubular capillary into the tubule (arrow pointing down, out of the capillary into the distal convoluted tubule; secretion also happens in the proximal tubule, e.g. PAH). Excretion: whatever reaches the renal pelvis. Together: amount excreted = amount filtered − amount reabsorbed + amount secreted. The H₂O arrows point out of the loop and the collecting duct: water is reabsorbed there, leaving the tubule for the blood.

Glucose is a small molecule, so it is freely filtered: no carrier, no ATP, no limit. Filtered load = GFR × plasma glucose. Normal plasma glucose is about 100 mg/dL = 1 mg/mL, so the filtered load is 120 mL/min × 1 mg/mL = 120 mg/min. 'Filtration cannot be maximized' means the filtered load keeps rising in a straight line as plasma glucose rises: 300 mg/dL gives 360 mg/min, 500 mg/dL gives 600 mg/min. At normal levels all 120 mg/min is reabsorbed.

Reabsorbing glucose (moving it out of the tubule fluid, through the tubule cell, into the blood) is the opposite of filtering it. It needs a carrier protein, and carriers can all be busy, so reabsorption has a ceiling (Tm). Moving glucose into the cell is uphill (against its concentration gradient), so it needs energy. The energy comes from Na⁺: glucose rides into the cell with Na⁺ on the same carrier (cotransport). The glucose carrier itself does not split ATP. The ATP is split by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the blood side, which keeps Na⁺ inside the cell low.

Graph of the transport maximum. x-axis: glucose filtered load. y-axis: glucose reabsorbed. Both are scaled to Tm, so 1.0 = Tm (about 375 mg/min). Left part: reabsorption rises one-for-one with load, because free carriers catch every filtered glucose. At a load of 1.0 every carrier is busy, so the line goes flat: reabsorption cannot rise any further. Any glucose filtered beyond Tm stays in the tubule and ends up in urine. The dots are real measurements: near the corner they fall a little below the sharp line (splay), and the dashed line just under 1.0 marks their average plateau.

Glucose crosses the proximal tubule cell in two steps. Step 1, lumen side (apical membrane): SGLT2 (sodium–glucose cotransporter 2) carries Na⁺ and glucose into the cell together. Na⁺ flows downhill and pulls glucose in uphill. Step 2, blood side (basolateral membrane): GLUT2 (glucose transporter 2) lets glucose leave by facilitated diffusion, downhill, with no energy. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the blood side pumps that Na⁺ out of the cell into the blood (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ into the cell). The SGLT spends no ATP itself; it uses the Na⁺ gradient the pump builds (secondary active transport). S1 = the first segment of the proximal tubule.

Correction: S3 cells (last segment of the proximal tubule) release glucose to the blood through GLUT1; GLUT2 is right for the intestinal cell and for S1. Both cells work the same way: a Na⁺–glucose cotransporter (SGLT1 or SGLT2) brings glucose in from the lumen, and a GLUT lets it out into the blood. 200 and 350 are plasma glucose levels (mg/dL); 375 mg/min is Tm, the maximum reabsorption rate. Below about 200 mg/dL the carriers have spare capacity and catch all the glucose. Above 200, the carriers of some nephrons are full, so glucose first appears in urine (threshold). Above about 350 mg/dL all carriers are full, and reabsorption is fixed at Tm ≈ 375 mg/min. The curved stretch in between is the splay.

Secondary active transport, step by step. (1) The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the blood side splits ATP and pumps 3 Na⁺ out of the cell for 2 K⁺ in. (2) This keeps Na⁺ inside the cell low and the cell interior negative. (3) So Na⁺ in the tubular lumen is pulled into the cell. (4) SGLT2 lets Na⁺ in only together with glucose, so glucose is dragged in against its gradient. ATP powers the pump directly (primary active) and glucose uptake only indirectly (secondary). If the pump stops, the Na⁺ gradient fades and glucose reabsorption stops too. Interstitium = the fluid between the tubule and the peritubular capillaries.

The same two steps drawn on a real cell outline. Glucose (hexagons) enters with Na⁺ (red dots) through SGLT on the brush border (luminal) membrane. It exits through GLUT on the basolateral membrane into the blood. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump sends the Na⁺ out of the cell into the blood and brings K⁺ into the cell. Glucose takes the path through the cell (transcellular); it does not slip between cells across the tight junctions. No Na⁺ in the lumen means no glucose uptake.

Along the proximal tubule, glucose in the tubular fluid falls as it is reabsorbed (fewer blue dots further down). The blue arrows pointing out of the tubule wall are glucose leaving the tubule fluid for the blood; the last one is dotted because little glucose is left. In the two cells, the lumen is on top and the blood is at the bottom. Early tubule: SGLT2, 1 Na⁺ per glucose. Glucose is plentiful here, so a high-capacity carrier takes most of it. Late tubule: SGLT1, 2 Na⁺ per glucose. Little glucose is left, so the carrier needs twice the Na⁺ energy to pull the last molecules in. Insulin has no effect on SGLTs or GLUT2: kidney glucose uptake does not need insulin (only GLUT4 in muscle and fat does). So in diabetes, glucose spills into urine only because the filtered load exceeds Tm.

'1005' means 100%. The proximal tubule has three segments. S1 (first part, next to the glomerulus) has SGLT2 + GLUT2 and reabsorbs about 90% of the filtered glucose. S2 is the middle. S3 (last part) has SGLT1 + GLUT1 and reabsorbs the last ~10%. So at normal plasma glucose no glucose is left by the end of the proximal tubule. Later segments (loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct) have no glucose carriers, so any glucose that gets past the proximal tubule ends up in urine.

Electron micrograph of proximal tubule cells (brown circles = nuclei). The blue-green fringe facing the lumen at the top is the brush border: thousands of microvilli. They multiply the luminal surface area many times over and carry the SGLT carriers. That is why the proximal tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered Na⁺ and water and all of the glucose. Proximal tubule cells are also packed with mitochondria, which make the ATP for the Na⁺/K⁺ pumps.

Correction: glucose first appears in urine (renal threshold) at plasma glucose about 200 mg/dL, not 300 mg/100 mL as the small label says. Axes: x = plasma glucose; y = glucose handled per minute. Filtered (red) rises in a straight line, since filtration never saturates. Reabsorbed (black dashed) equals filtered until the carriers fill, then stays flat at Tm. Excreted (green dotted) = filtered − reabsorbed: zero below threshold, then rising parallel to red. "Everything >350–375 spills" means every extra mg filtered beyond Tm is excreted; the carriers still reabsorb their full 375 mg/min. In a real kidney the bend is gradual, not a sharp corner (splay), so glucose spills before Tm is reached: nephrons differ in their Tm, and near saturation a glucose that lets go of its carrier finds no free carrier to grab it.

The glucose titration curve with real numbers. x-axis: plasma glucose (mg/dL). y-axis: glucose filtered, reabsorbed or excreted (mg/min). Filtered (purple) rises in a straight line. Reabsorbed (orange dashed) follows it, then levels off at the transport maximum (Tm, about 375 mg/min). Excreted (green dashed) = filtered − reabsorbed. At a normal ~100 mg/dL, filtered = reabsorbed ≈ 120 mg/min, and excretion is 0. At the threshold, about 200 mg/dL, glucose first appears in urine. The blue hatched areas are the splay, where some nephrons' carriers are full and others' are not; above about 350 mg/dL all are full, so every extra mg filtered is excreted and the green line runs parallel to the purple. (The drawing puts the threshold and the end of the splay a little to the right of 200 and 350.) Example: at 600 mg/dL, filtered = 720 mg/min, reabsorbed = 375, excreted ≈ 345 mg/min.

Correction: intestinal cells release glucose to the blood through GLUT2, not GLUT1. Kidney and gut take up glucose with the same design: a Na⁺–glucose cotransporter on the lumen side (uphill entry, powered by the Na⁺ gradient) and a GLUT on the blood side (downhill exit by facilitated diffusion). The early proximal tubule uses SGLT2; the small intestine uses SGLT1. That is why SGLT2-inhibitor drugs (the '-gliflozins') make the kidney spill glucose into urine without blocking glucose absorption from food.

The same titration curve in mmol units (1 mM glucose ≈ 18 mg/dL; 28 mM ≈ 500 mg/dL). x-axis: plasma glucose. y-axis: glucose flux, i.e. glucose moved per minute (mmol/min). Dashed grey line = filtered. Shaded blue area = reabsorbed, flat at Tmax (= Tm). Solid blue line = excreted. The right axis gives the same flux in mg/min: glucose weighs 180 mg per mmol, so 1.7 mmol/min × 180 ≈ 300 mg/min. 'Appearance threshold' = plasma level where glucose first shows up in urine; 'saturation threshold' = level where every nephron is at Tm; the curved stretch between them is the splay. This data set runs lower (Tmax ≈ 300 mg/min; appearance 8.3 mM ≈ 150 mg/dL; saturation 13.3 mM ≈ 240 mg/dL). The standard values to learn: threshold ≈ 200 mg/dL, full saturation ≈ 350 mg/dL, Tm ≈ 375 mg/min.

qs.q: About how much plasma do the kidneys filter per day?
qs.why: GFR 120 mL/min × 1,440 min ≈ 173 L, about 180 L/day. Urine is only about 1.5 L/day, so more than 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT freely filtered at the glomerulus?
qs.why: Only big proteins such as albumin and the hormone-binding globulins are held back. Myoglobin (17 kDa) passes, so muscle breakdown puts it into urine.

qs.q: Why can glomerular filtration of a small solute never saturate?
opts: It is bulk flow with no carrier to fill up
Glomerular carriers have a very high Tm
Insulin raises its rate as needed
qs.why: Pressure pushes plasma through the barrier like a sieve, so the amount filtered depends only on GFR and plasma concentration. Reabsorption uses carriers and has a ceiling.

qs.q: For a freely filtered solute, what is TF/P (tubular fluid ÷ plasma concentration) in Bowman's space?
qs.why: The filtrate is plasma minus the big proteins, so freely filtered solutes enter at plasma concentration. 0.2 is the filtration fraction, a share of plasma volume, not a concentration ratio.

qs.q: The filtered load of a substance equals what?
qs.why: Filtered load is the amount entering Bowman's space each minute. Urine concentration × urine flow rate is the excretion rate.

qs.q: GFR is 100 mL/min and plasma concentration of substance X is 20 mg/dL. What is the filtered load of X?
qs.why: Convert first: 20 mg/dL ÷ 100 = 0.2 mg/mL. Then 100 mL/min × 0.2 mg/mL = 20 mg/min; 2,000 comes from skipping the dL-to-mL conversion.

qs.q: Urine glucose is 100 mg/dL and urine flow is 4 mL/min. What is the glucose excretion rate?
qs.why: Excretion = urine concentration × urine flow. 100 mg/dL = 1 mg/mL, and 1 mg/mL × 4 mL/min = 4 mg/min.

qs.q: Why does a plasma glucose of 500 mg/dL cause polyuria?
opts: Glucose is secreted into the tubule with water
Glucose above Tm stays in the tubule and holds water
qs.why: The filtered load (600 mg/min) exceeds the carriers' maximum (about 375 mg/min). The leftover glucose holds water in the tubule by osmosis (osmotic diuresis), so the patient loses water and gets thirsty.

qs.q: Reabsorption moves a substance from where to where?
qs.why: Reabsorption returns substances to the blood. The reverse direction, peritubular capillary to tubule, is secretion.

qs.q: Filtered load of a substance is 20 mg/min and its excretion is 60 mg/min. What is its net secretion?
qs.why: Excreted more than filtered means net secretion: secretion = excreted − filtered = 60 − 20 = 40 mg/min.

qs.q: Which of these is normally 100% reabsorbed?
qs.why: Glucose, amino acids and lactate are reabsorbed (moved out of the tubule fluid back into the blood) by Na⁺-coupled carriers in the proximal tubule. At normal plasma levels the carriers have spare capacity, so urine contains none.

qs.q: PAH is secreted into the proximal tubule by which carriers?
qs.why: PAH is filtered and then pumped from peritubular blood into the proximal tubule by organic-anion carriers, so urine carries about three times the filtered amount.

qs.q: As plasma glucose rises, what happens to the filtered glucose load?
opts: Rises in a straight line with no ceiling
qs.why: Filtration uses no carrier, so filtered load = GFR × plasma glucose keeps rising in a straight line. It is reabsorption that plateaus at Tm.

qs.q: Why does glucose reabsorption have a maximum rate (Tm)?
opts: Tubule cells run out of ATP
GFR falls when glucose is high
Uptake needs insulin, which is limited
qs.why: Reabsorption needs carriers. Once every carrier is busy, extra filtered glucose stays in the tubule and ends up in urine.

qs.q: In the early proximal tubule (S1), which transporter moves glucose out of the cell into the blood?
qs.why: SGLT2 brings glucose in from the lumen with Na⁺. GLUT2 on the blood side lets it leave downhill by facilitated diffusion, with no energy.

qs.q: What directly powers SGLT2's uphill uptake of glucose?
qs.why: SGLT2 spends no ATP: Na⁺ flowing downhill pulls glucose in (secondary active transport). The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase splits the ATP that keeps cell Na⁺ low.

qs.q: At about what plasma glucose does glucose first appear in urine?
qs.why: Above about 200 mg/dL (threshold) the carriers of some nephrons are full. By about 350 mg/dL all are full and reabsorption is fixed at Tm.

qs.q: If the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is blocked, what happens to glucose reabsorption?
opts: No change, since GLUT2 is passive
It rises, as cell Na⁺ rises
It stops, as the Na⁺ gradient fades
No change, since SGLT2 splits its own ATP
qs.why: The pump keeps cell Na⁺ low. Without it, the Na⁺ gradient that drives SGLT2 fades, so glucose uptake stops.

qs.q: How many Na⁺ ions does SGLT1 in the late proximal tubule move with each glucose?
qs.why: Early SGLT2 uses 1 Na⁺ per glucose. Late SGLT1 uses 2, giving twice the energy to pull in the last glucose from fluid where little is left.

qs.q: In diabetes, why does glucose appear in urine?
opts: Renal SGLTs need insulin to work
The filtered load exceeds the transport maximum
qs.why: Kidney SGLTs and GLUT2 work without insulin (only GLUT4 in muscle and fat needs it), so glycosuria reflects a filtered load above Tm.

qs.q: Which proximal tubule segment reabsorbs about 90% of filtered glucose, and with which carriers?
qs.why: S1 does the bulk with SGLT2 + GLUT2; S3 takes the last ~10% with SGLT1 + GLUT1. Later segments have no glucose carriers, so any glucose that escapes ends up in urine.

qs.q: About what is the renal transport maximum (Tm) for glucose?
qs.why: Above about 350 mg/dL plasma glucose, reabsorption is flat at about 375 mg/min, and every extra mg filtered is excreted. 120 mg/min is the normal filtered load.

qs.q: Why does glucose spill into urine before every carrier is full (splay)?
opts: Nephrons differ in their individual Tm
SGLT2 reverses direction at high glucose
qs.why: Some nephrons fill up before others, and near saturation a glucose that lets go of its carrier may find no free carrier, so the bend in the curve is gradual.

qs.q: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria without blocking glucose absorption from food?
opts: Food glucose crosses the gut by simple diffusion
The gut absorbs glucose with GLUT4
The gut absorbs glucose with SGLT1, not SGLT2
The drugs act only on GLUT2
qs.why: The early proximal tubule relies on SGLT2, while the small intestine uses SGLT1, so the '-gliflozins' make the kidney spill glucose but leave intestinal uptake intact.

slides.note: Urea is the body's main nitrogen waste. When amino acids from protein are broken down, the liver turns their NH₃ (ammonia) into urea, so more protein eaten means more urea made. Urea is small and not protein-bound, so it is freely filtered: filtered load (amount filtered per minute) = GFR (glomerular filtration rate) × plasma urea. This rises in a straight line with blood urea and never hits a ceiling, because filtration is bulk flow through pores with no carrier to saturate. After filtration, urea crosses the tubule only by diffusion, downhill, using no ATP. A low-protein diet leaves less urea in the inner medulla, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine as well.

Correction: in dehydration, water reabsorption goes up, not down, because ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is high, and urea reabsorption rises with it. As water leaves the tubule, the urea left behind becomes more concentrated and diffuses back into blood. Creatinine is not reabsorbed. So BUN (blood urea nitrogen) rises much more than creatinine, and the BUN:creatinine ratio goes above 20 (prerenal azotemia: a healthy kidney that gets too little blood). In kidney failure both rise together, so the ratio stays normal. Urea supplies about half the osmolality of the inner medulla, which helps the kidney concentrate urine. Uremia = the symptoms of urea and other wastes building up in kidney failure.

Urea reabsorption is passive: urea simply diffuses down its concentration gradient. Simple diffusion goes straight through the cells; facilitated diffusion goes through a urea channel protein (UT1, urea transporter 1, in the inner medullary collecting duct), still downhill and with no ATP. Why is there a gradient? Filtrate starts with the same urea concentration as plasma. In the proximal tubule water is reabsorbed and urea lags behind, so luminal urea becomes a bit more concentrated than blood urea and diffuses out of the tubule into the blood. By the end of the proximal tubule 50% is reabsorbed. Rule: urea reabsorption follows water reabsorption. Picture: 56 g/day filtered, half reabsorbed, 28 g/day excreted (net totals).

Follow the % of filtered urea along the nephron: 100% filtered → 50% left after the proximal tubule → 110% at the bend of the loop. The rise happens because the inner medulla is full of urea, so urea diffuses into the thin descending limb (passive secretion). The thick ascending limb, distal tubule and cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts are closed to urea. With ADH, water leaves the late distal tubule and these collecting ducts but urea stays, so urea becomes very concentrated. The inner medullary collecting duct then lets urea diffuse out through UT1 into the medulla. That urea re-enters the loop and goes around again (urea recycling), which keeps the inner medulla concentrated.

Axes: x = urine flow rate (ml/min); y = clearance (ml of plasma cleared of the substance per minute). Inulin is flat at 100 because it is filtered and never reabsorbed or secreted, so its clearance equals GFR at any flow. Creatinine sits a bit higher (~120) because a little is also secreted, so it slightly overestimates GFR. Urea is always below inulin because part of it is reabsorbed. Its curve drops at low urine flow: when more water is reabsorbed, tubular urea gets more concentrated and more of it diffuses back into blood. So in dehydration urea is retained and BUN rises.

Correction: 110% is the urea present at the bend of the loop (after urea diffuses into the thin descending limb), not the amount in urine. With no ADH, far less urea is reabsorbed and urea excretion is at its highest, but it still stays below the filtered load. With ADH, water is pulled out of the collecting ducts, so the urea left behind becomes concentrated, and ADH also turns on UT1 in the inner medullary collecting duct. Urea diffuses out into the medulla, so only 20–40% of the filtered urea is excreted. The rest builds the medullary gradient that lets ADH concentrate the urine.

Answer: D. Step 1: BUN is high (34) but creatinine is normal (0.9). Step 2: BUN ÷ creatinine = 34 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 38, well above 20. Step 3: a ratio above 20 points to a prerenal cause (too little blood reaching a healthy kidney), such as dehydration. Low volume → low urine flow → more urea reabsorbed, while creatinine is not reabsorbed and barely rises. Confusion and light-headedness fit low blood volume. Kidney damage from hypertension or diabetes would raise BUN and creatinine together, keeping the ratio normal.

Answer: B. In dehydration, ADH acts on the inner medullary collecting duct in two ways: it opens water channels, and it turns on UT1, the urea transporter. The water entering the medulla would dilute it, but urea enters along with the water. Because urea supplies about half the osmolality of the inner medulla, adding urea keeps the medulla concentrated, so the kidney can keep pulling water out of the urine. Na⁺ reabsorption in the collecting duct is small and is controlled mainly by aldosterone, so (a) cannot do this job.

Answer: D. Marginal nutrition means little protein is eaten. Fewer amino acids are broken down, so the liver makes less urea and BUN falls. Free access to water rules out dehydration, so there is no prerenal rise in BUN. Creatinine comes from muscle; an elderly, wheelchair-bound patient has low muscle mass, so creatinine tends to be low, not high (c is wrong). Nothing in the case changes sodium, potassium or calcium.

Clearance = the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. In words: urine concentration × urine flow ÷ plasma concentration; Cₓ = Uₓ × V ÷ Pₓ (Uₓ = urine concentration of x, V = urine flow rate, Pₓ = plasma concentration of x). PAH is filtered, and almost all PAH left in the blood is then secreted, so blood leaving the kidney carries almost no PAH. Every ml of plasma that passes through is cleared, so PAH clearance = RPF (renal plasma flow; strictly ‘effective RPF’, about 10% below true RPF). Example: U = 6 mg/ml, V = 1 ml/min, P = 0.01 mg/ml → 6 × 1 ÷ 0.01 = 600 ml/min. Penicillin uses the same carrier; probenecid blocks it, so penicillin stays in the blood longer.

Correction: plasma PAH here should read 100 mg/L, not mEq/L (180 L/day × 100 mg/L = 18 g/day). Follow PAH through the picture. Blue arrow: PAH is filtered from the glomerular capillary into Bowman's space. Green arrow: more PAH is secreted from the peritubular capillary, through the tubule cells, into the lumen. Yellow arrow: excretion = filtered + secreted, because PAH is not reabsorbed. The numbers are only a worked example. In a real kidney about 20% of the plasma is filtered (filtration fraction = GFR ÷ RPF ≈ 0.2), so about 20% of the arriving PAH is filtered and nearly all of the other 80% is secreted. Plasma leaving in the renal vein is therefore almost free of PAH, which is why PAH clearance measures RPF (renal plasma flow).

PAH secretion uses the same kind of machinery as glucose reabsorption, run in the opposite direction. In the picture, the pink Reabsorption arrow points from the tubule lumen into the peritubular capillary: that is the glucose direction. The green Secretion arrow points the other way, from the capillary into the lumen: that is the PAH direction. Both need a carrier protein and energy. ‘ATP split’ means ATP pays for it indirectly: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump burns ATP to build a Na⁺ gradient, and that gradient drives the carrier (secondary active transport). Because there is a fixed number of carriers, both saturate at a Tm (transport maximum, the fastest rate the carriers can run).

Axes: x = unbound plasma PAH concentration; y = the amount of PAH filtered, secreted or excreted per minute. Filtered (solid purple line): filtered load = GFR × plasma PAH, a straight line that keeps climbing because filtration has no carrier to saturate. Secreted (orange dashed line): secretion rises steeply, then goes flat. That plateau is the Tm (transport maximum): every carrier is busy. Excreted (green dashed line) = filtered + secreted. Before Tm it climbs steeply because both parts rise. After Tm only filtration still rises, so the excreted line runs parallel to the filtered line. Consequence: at high plasma PAH, PAH clearance falls below RPF, so RPF must be measured at low PAH levels.

Correction: at the symporter, Na⁺ moves into the cell together with PAH, so its arrow should point left like the PAH arrow; a symporter carries both the same way. Read the cell from right (blood, red) to left (tubular fluid, blue); the green cells are proximal tubule cells. Step 1: the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase (yellow ATP) pumps Na⁺ out of the cell into blood, keeping cell Na⁺ low. Step 2: Na⁺ flows back into the cell through a symporter and drags PAH with it from the blood, even against PAH's own gradient. Step 3: PAH leaves the cell into the lumen through an antiporter, swapping for another anion that moves into the cell. ‘Competitive secretion’: many organic anions (penicillin, probenecid, salicylate) share these carriers, so one drug can slow another's secretion and raise its blood level.

Secretion moves a substance from blood into the tubule. It runs on carriers powered by the Na⁺ gradient, so it has a transport maximum and can be blocked by competing drugs. Creatinine is mostly filtered but also slightly secreted, by a carrier for organic cations. Cimetidine (a stomach-acid H₂ blocker) and trimethoprim (an antibiotic) compete for that carrier. Less creatinine is secreted, so serum creatinine rises a little even though GFR has not changed. Don't mistake this small rise for kidney injury.

A weak acid exists as HA (uncharged) ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ (charged). In alkaline urine (few H⁺) it gives up its H⁺ and becomes charged A⁻; in acid urine it keeps its H⁺ and stays uncharged. A weak base is the mirror image: B + H⁺ ⇌ BH⁺, so it is charged in acid urine. Why it matters (non-ionic diffusion): only the uncharged form can cross the tubule cells and leak back into blood. The charged form is trapped in the urine and excreted. So alkaline urine speeds excretion of weak acids, and acid urine speeds excretion of weak bases. The pH numbers are rough; the real switch point is each drug's pKa (the pH at which half of it is charged).

Aspirin overdose is treated by ion trapping. Salicylic acid (a weak acid) is filtered and also secreted, so it reaches the urine at high concentration. In acid urine much of it is uncharged and diffuses back into blood. Giving IV (intravenous) sodium bicarbonate makes the urine alkaline → salicylic acid becomes charged salicylate (A⁻) → it cannot cross back → it is excreted. Aspirin is the main drug for which this trick is used.

TF/Pₓ = concentration of x in tubular fluid ÷ concentration of x in plasma. Plasma concentration stays constant, so changes in the ratio show what the tubule did. In Bowman's space a freely filtered substance has the same concentration as plasma: TF/P = 1. Big proteins are not filtered: TF/P = 0. A ratio of 1 later on can still hide reabsorption, if solute and water leave in the same proportion (Na⁺ in the proximal tubule). To correct for water, divide by inulin: (TF/P)ₓ ÷ (TF/P)inulin = fraction of the filtered x still in the tubule. Example, end of proximal tubule: Na⁺ 1 ÷ inulin 3 = 0.33, so one-third of the filtered Na⁺ is left and two-thirds was reabsorbed.

Concentration = amount of solute ÷ volume of water, so the ratio depends on how fast the solute leaves compared with water. TF/P below 1: solute left faster than water (glucose, HCO₃⁻ = bicarbonate). TF/P above 1: solute left slower than water, so it got concentrated, or it was secreted (added). Inulin is filtered but never reabsorbed or secreted, so its ratio rises only because water leaves. Worked example: start with 100 ml of filtrate; the proximal tubule reabsorbs two-thirds of the water (67 ml). The same inulin now sits in 33 ml, so its concentration triples: TF/P inulin = 3. In general, fraction of water reabsorbed = 1 − 1 ÷ (TF/P)inulin.

Q4 answers. Axes: x = distance along the proximal tubule (start → end); y = TF/P. All lines start at 1 (Bowman's space) and are judged against inulin (B), which climbs to 3 only because water leaves. Above B = secreted (red arrow): A, PAH. Below B = reabsorbed (yellow arrow), even if the line is still above 1. D stays at 1: Na⁺ (the ‘salt’ line; total osmolarity also stays at 1), reabsorbed exactly in step with water. C rises slightly above 1: Cl⁻, which lags behind water early on because HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed first. E falls to about 0.5: HCO₃⁻. F drops to 0 in the early proximal tubule: glucose (and amino acids), all reabsorbed.

Answer: B. Step 1: filtered load (amount filtered per minute) = GFR × plasma concentration = 100 ml/min × 0.1 mg/ml = 10 mg/min. Step 2: excretion is 20 mg/min, twice the filtered load. Step 3: the extra 10 mg/min must have been added by the tubule, so the drug is secreted, like PAH. Check with clearance: 20 ÷ 0.1 = 200 ml/min, more than GFR. Inulin would give excretion = filtered load (10 mg/min); glucose ≈ 0 (all reabsorbed); albumin ≈ 0 (not filtered).

Answer: B. Creatinine is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, but a small amount is also secreted. So the creatinine in urine is a bit more than what was filtered, and creatinine clearance comes out about 10–20% higher than the true GFR. Inulin is neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR exactly. Reabsorption (a) would make clearance read low, not high.

Answer: D. The clues point to salicylate (aspirin) poisoning. Ringing in the ears (tinnitus) is classic. Salicylate stimulates the breathing center in the brainstem → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis. Salicylic acid is itself an acid and also makes lactic and keto acids build up; they use up HCO₃⁻ → anion-gap metabolic acidosis, so serum bicarbonate is low. A normal EKG argues against tricyclic antidepressants, which widen the QRS and cause arrhythmias. Early acetaminophen overdose causes few symptoms (liver injury comes later), and PPIs (proton pump inhibitors) are not dangerous in overdose.

Answer: A. Treatment is IV sodium bicarbonate to make the urine alkaline. Salicylic acid is a weak acid. In alkaline urine it loses its H⁺ and becomes charged salicylate. Charged molecules cannot cross the tubule cells back into blood, so salicylate is trapped in the urine and excreted. Filtration and secretion do not change (c, d); the gain comes only from less back-diffusion, which is less reabsorption.

qs.q: What creates the gradient for passive urea reabsorption in the proximal tubule?
opts: Water reabsorption concentrates urea in the lumen
Na⁺ cotransport pulling urea into the cells
An ATP-driven urea pump on the blood side
Urea secretion from the peritubular capillaries
qs.why: Water leaves the proximal tubule and urea lags behind, so luminal urea rises above plasma urea and diffuses out. About 50% of filtered urea is reabsorbed this way, with no ATP used.

qs.q: About what share of the inner medulla's osmolality does urea supply?
qs.why: Urea supplies about half the osmolality of the inner medulla, which helps the kidney concentrate urine. That is why a low-protein diet impairs concentrating ability.

qs.q: In dehydration, why does the BUN (blood urea nitrogen) to creatinine ratio rise above 20?
opts: Urea filtration rises while creatinine filtration falls
The liver makes extra urea when volume is low
More creatinine is secreted; urea is not
More urea is reabsorbed; creatinine is not reabsorbed
qs.why: High ADH raises water reabsorption, concentrating tubular urea so more diffuses back into blood. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, so BUN rises much more than creatinine (prerenal azotemia).

qs.q: In which segment does urea enter the tubule by passive secretion?
opts: Thin descending limb of the loop
Thick ascending limb of the loop
qs.why: The inner medulla is full of urea, so urea diffuses into the thin descending limb, bringing it to about 110% of the filtered amount at the bend. The thick ascending limb, distal tubule and cortical collecting duct are closed to urea.

qs.q: What happens to urea clearance when urine flow is low?
opts: It falls, as more urea is reabsorbed
It rises, as more urea is secreted
It stays equal to inulin clearance
qs.why: When more water is reabsorbed, tubular urea becomes more concentrated and more of it diffuses back into blood. So low flow retains urea and BUN rises.

qs.q: With ADH present, about what share of the filtered urea is excreted in urine?
qs.why: ADH concentrates collecting-duct fluid and turns on UT1, so urea diffuses into the medulla and only 20–40% is excreted. 110% is the urea present at the bend of the loop, not the amount in urine.

qs.q: Besides opening water channels, what does ADH do in the inner medullary collecting duct?
opts: Raises urea filtration at the glomerulus
Blocks urea movement into the medulla
qs.why: ADH activates UT1, so urea follows the water into the inner medulla. This keeps the medulla concentrated instead of letting the reabsorbed water dilute it.

qs.q: Why does poor protein intake lower BUN?
opts: Less creatinine is made by muscle
More urea is secreted into the urine
Fewer amino acids are broken down into urea
qs.why: The liver makes urea from the nitrogen of broken-down amino acids. Less protein eaten means less urea made, so BUN falls; low muscle mass lowers creatinine, not BUN.

qs.q: PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) clearance is used to measure which quantity?
qs.why: PAH is filtered and almost all that remains in the blood is secreted, so renal venous plasma is nearly PAH-free. Every ml of plasma passing through is cleared, so PAH clearance equals renal plasma flow (plasma, not whole blood).

qs.q: Of the PAH reaching the kidney, about how much enters the tubule by secretion rather than filtration?
qs.why: Only about 20% of the plasma is filtered (filtration fraction ≈ 0.2). The other 80% of the PAH flows on to the peritubular capillaries, where proximal tubule cells secrete it.

qs.q: PAH secretion uses the same kind of carrier mechanism as which process, run in reverse?
qs.why: Both use a carrier powered by the Na⁺ gradient and both saturate at a transport maximum (Tm); glucose moves lumen → blood, PAH moves blood → lumen. Urea and water move passively.

qs.q: Why must renal plasma flow be measured at a low plasma PAH level?
opts: PAH binds plasma proteins at high levels
Secretion saturates at high levels, so clearance falls
PAH is reabsorbed at high levels
qs.why: Above the Tm every carrier is busy, so extra PAH is only filtered and excretion runs parallel to filtration. PAH clearance then falls below renal plasma flow.

qs.q: How does probenecid prolong penicillin's blood level?
opts: It slows penicillin's breakdown in the liver
qs.why: Penicillin, probenecid and PAH share the organic anion secretory carriers. Probenecid competes for them, so less penicillin is secreted and it stays in blood longer.

qs.q: Why do cimetidine and trimethoprim raise serum creatinine slightly?
opts: They increase creatinine production by muscle
qs.why: Both compete for the organic cation carrier that secretes a small amount of creatinine. Serum creatinine rises even though GFR is unchanged, so the rise does not mean kidney injury.

qs.q: In alkaline urine, a weak acid in the tubular fluid is mostly…
opts: Uncharged and trapped in the urine
Charged and trapped in the urine
qs.why: With few H⁺ around, the acid gives up its H⁺ and becomes charged A⁻. Only the uncharged form can cross tubule cells back into blood, so the charged form stays in the urine and is excreted.

qs.q: Which treatment speeds salicylate excretion in aspirin overdose?
qs.why: Bicarbonate makes the urine alkaline, so salicylic acid becomes charged salicylate that cannot diffuse back into blood. Acidifying the urine would do the opposite.

qs.q: Inulin TF/P (tubular fluid ÷ plasma concentration) is 3 at the end of the proximal tubule. What fraction of filtered water has been reabsorbed?
qs.why: Inulin is never reabsorbed or secreted, so its concentration triples only because water leaves. Fraction of water reabsorbed = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3.

qs.q: Na⁺ TF/P stays at 1 along the proximal tubule. What does this show?
opts: Na⁺ is reabsorbed faster than water
Na⁺ is reabsorbed in step with water
Na⁺ is secreted into the lumen
qs.why: A ratio of 1 can hide a lot of reabsorption when solute and water leave in the same proportion. Dividing by inulin (1 ÷ 3) shows only one-third of the filtered Na⁺ is left.

qs.q: A substance's TF/P climbs higher than inulin's TF/P. What is the tubule doing to it?
opts: Reabsorbing it in step with water
qs.why: Inulin rises only because water leaves. A curve above inulin means solute was added to the lumen, as with PAH; any curve below inulin is being reabsorbed, even if it is still above 1.

qs.q: For a freely filtered drug, which finding shows that the tubule secretes it?
qs.why: Clearance above GFR means more leaves in the urine than was filtered, so the tubule added some. Clearance equal to GFR fits inulin; below GFR means net reabsorption.

qs.q: Because creatinine is slightly secreted, how does creatinine clearance compare with true GFR?
qs.why: Urine creatinine includes a small secreted amount on top of what was filtered, so its clearance overestimates GFR. Reabsorption would make it read low instead.

qs.q: What acid–base pattern does salicylate (aspirin) poisoning cause?
opts: Respiratory alkalosis plus anion-gap metabolic acidosis
qs.why: Salicylate stimulates the brainstem breathing center, so hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis. Salicylic, lactic and keto acids use up HCO₃⁻, giving an anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

slides.note: Answer: B. Each day the kidneys filter about 25,000 mEq (milliequivalents) of Na⁺ and must reabsorb over 99% of it (return it to the blood). Every reabsorbed Na⁺ is finally pumped out of a tubule cell into blood by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, so this step uses most of the kidney's ATP and oxygen. Filtration is pushed by blood pressure from the heart, so it costs the kidney no ATP. Water reabsorption is passive: water follows solute. Secretion uses far less energy, and the kidney does no muscular work.

Water follows Na⁺, so the amount of Na⁺ in the body sets the ECF volume (extracellular fluid: plasma plus the fluid between cells), and with it blood volume and blood pressure. Keep more Na⁺ than you eat → ECF expands → hypertension and edema. Lose more than you eat → ECF shrinks → hypotension. Example: eat 150 mEq/day → must excrete exactly 150 mEq/day. Filtered Na⁺ = GFR (glomerular filtration rate, 180 L/day) × plasma Na⁺ (140 mEq/L) = 25,200 mEq/day. So the urine carries only 0.6% of the filtered Na⁺.

Each curved arrow leaves the tubule. It shows the share of filtered Na⁺ reabsorbed in that segment: the Na⁺ leaves the tubule fluid and returns to the blood. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs 67%, the thick ascending limb (TAL) 25%, the distal convoluted tubule 5% and the collecting duct 3%. The box at the bottom is different: it is excretion, the less than 1% of filtered Na⁺ left in the urine. The small late segments still matter most for balance, because they make the final, hormone-controlled adjustments (aldosterone).

Where each diuretic acts (− = blocks, + = stimulates). Red arrows show Na⁺ leaving the tubule fluid for the blood (reabsorption). At the collecting duct the blue K⁺ H⁺ arrow points into the tubule (secretion). The further along the nephron a drug acts, the smaller the share of filtered Na⁺ it can affect.

  • PCT (proximal convoluted tubule): carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) block NaHCO₃ reabsorption. The effect is mild, because later segments reabsorb much of the extra Na⁺.
  • TAL (thick ascending limb): loop diuretics such as furosemide block the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter, which reabsorbs ~25% of filtered Na⁺. These are the strongest diuretics.
  • DCT (distal convoluted tubule): thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide block the Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter (~5%).
  • Collecting duct: aldosterone (Aldo) increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ and H⁺ secretion. K⁺-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone block this (only 1–2% of Na⁺). ADH (antidiuretic hormone) adds water reabsorption here.

Early PCT = the first half of the proximal tubule. Na⁺ enters the cell from the lumen on carriers that bring something with it: amino acids, glucose, phosphate, lactate, citrate. HCO₃⁻ is returned to the blood differently: Na⁺ entering on the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger pushes H⁺ into the lumen, and that H⁺ recovers filtered HCO₃⁻ (next slides). PTH (parathyroid hormone) blocks the Na⁺–phosphate cotransporter, so more phosphate is lost in urine. Don't confuse: in the distal tubule PTH increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

Left = tubular lumen (urine side); right = blood side. Start at the right: the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out of the cell into blood and 2 K⁺ into the cell. This keeps Na⁺ inside the cell low and the cell interior negative (the − inside and + outside at top right). Na⁺ in the lumen therefore tends to flow in, and the luminal carriers harness that flow. One brings amino acids (AA) or glucose in together with Na⁺. The other swaps H⁺ out into the lumen as Na⁺ comes into the cell. The secreted H⁺ is used to reclaim HCO₃⁻, which then exits to blood on the right.

Secondary active transport: these carriers burn no ATP themselves. They move glucose, amino acids, phosphate, lactate and citrate uphill into the cell by coupling them to Na⁺ flowing downhill. That Na⁺ gradient is made by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase (primary active transport). Na⁺–glucose and Na⁺–amino acid carriers move net positive charge into the cell and leave negative charge behind. So the lumen of the early proximal tubule is slightly negative (about −4 mV) compared with blood.

CA = carbonic anhydrase, the enzyme that turns CO₂ + H₂O into H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) and back. Follow the steps: (1) the green Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger secretes H⁺ into the lumen; (2) H⁺ joins filtered HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃, and CA on the brush border splits it → CO₂ + H₂O; (3) CO₂ diffuses into the cell; (4) inside, CA rebuilds H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; (5) HCO₃⁻ leaves to blood with Na⁺ (yellow carrier), and the H⁺ is secreted again. Net: filtered HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed (returned to the blood), and no H⁺ is excreted. Bottom: glutamine splits into NH₄⁺ (ammonium, secreted into urine) and α-ketoglutarate, whose breakdown makes a new HCO₃⁻ for the blood.

Same proximal tubule cell with more carriers. Yellow (left) = lumen; blue (right) = blood. Red octagons: Na⁺ cotransporters that bring amino acids and glucose into the cell with Na⁺. Blue circles: exchangers. One swaps Cl⁻ into the cell for X⁻ out into the lumen (X⁻ = an organic anion such as formate; this one works mainly in the late proximal tubule). The other swaps Na⁺ into the cell for H⁺ out into the lumen, and the secreted H⁺ reclaims HCO₃⁻ through CA as in the previous diagram. On the blood side the ATP-driven pump moves Na⁺ out of the cell into blood (and K⁺ in), which powers everything on the lumen side.

'Proximal PCT' here means the early (first) half of the proximal tubule. Its Na⁺ cotransporters are so efficient that all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed by its end, so normally none reach the urine. Glucose appears in urine when the filtered amount exceeds the carriers' maximum rate, as in uncontrolled diabetes. 85% of HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed here by the H⁺/CA cycle; the rest is reabsorbed further along the nephron.

Correction: fluid entering the late PCT is rich in Cl⁻, not lacking it. What it lacks is glucose, amino acids and HCO₃⁻ to carry Na⁺ in. Why Cl⁻ is high: the early PCT reabsorbed HCO₃⁻ instead of Cl⁻, and water left along with the absorbed solute, so the Cl⁻ left behind became more concentrated than in plasma. That Cl⁻ gradient now drives NaCl reabsorption in two ways. (1) Through the cells: the Cl⁻–formate exchanger (Cl⁻ into the cell, formate out to the lumen) runs beside the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger, so NaCl enters the cell. (2) Between the cells: Cl⁻ diffuses out of the lumen into the blood, leaving the lumen positive (about +4 mV compared with blood), which pushes Na⁺ out of the lumen the same way.

Formate (HCOO⁻) is the anion the late PCT trades for Cl⁻. It is recycled, so it never runs out. Formate leaves the cell into the lumen and picks up an H⁺ that the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger has secreted, becoming uncharged formic acid. Formic acid diffuses back into the cell and splits into H⁺ and formate again. Net result of the two exchangers together: one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻ enter the cell, with no loss of formate or H⁺.

In red cells this anion exchanger is band 3. CO₂ from the tissues enters the red cell, and carbonic anhydrase turns it into H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Band 3 swaps that HCO₃⁻ out into plasma for Cl⁻ moving into the cell (the chloride shift), which is why most CO₂ travels in blood as plasma HCO₃⁻. Band 3 also anchors the red cell's membrane skeleton, so a defect makes small, round, fragile cells that the spleen destroys: hereditary spherocytosis. In the kidney, a Cl⁻–HCO₃⁻ exchanger of the same family returns new HCO₃⁻ to blood from α-intercalated cells.

The proximal tubule is very leaky to water (many water channels, and its 'tight' junctions are loose). So whenever solute is reabsorbed, water follows right away by osmosis, in the same proportion. Removing 67% of the NaCl together with 67% of the water leaves the remaining fluid at the same concentration as plasma (about 300 mOsm/L, milliosmoles per liter). The proximal tubule therefore changes the fluid's volume, not its concentration. Diluting and concentrating the urine happen later, in the loop of Henle and beyond.

Answer: C (sodium). Step by step: (1) the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase pumps Na⁺ out of the cell and keeps cell Na⁺ low; (2) Na⁺ flows in from the lumen, dragging glucose, amino acids and phosphate along and pushing H⁺ out to reclaim HCO₃⁻; (3) solute leaving the lumen makes it slightly dilute, so water follows by osmosis. Water and HCO₃⁻ reabsorption both depend on Na⁺ moving first. K⁺ is a distractor: in the proximal tubule it is mostly reabsorbed passively, following Na⁺ and water.

Water moves only by osmosis, so a solute difference must come first. Solute (mostly Na⁺) is transported out of the lumen. This makes the lumen slightly dilute and the spaces between the cells, next to the capillary, slightly concentrated. Water then flows the same way: out of the lumen toward the blood. Solute transport is always the primary event; water moves only because of it. Proof: a solute that cannot be reabsorbed (mannitol, or extra glucose in diabetes) holds water in the tubule, so urine volume rises (osmotic diuresis).

The proximal tubule reabsorbs a constant fraction (~67%) of whatever is filtered, not a fixed amount. Why it matters: filtered Na⁺ = GFR × plasma Na⁺ = 180 L/day × 140 mEq/L = 25,200 mEq/day. If GFR rose just 1% with no extra reabsorption, an extra 252 mEq/day would be lost in urine, a big hit to the ~1,960 mEq of Na⁺ in the whole ECF. How it works: a higher GFR filters more water out of the same plasma. The blood leaving the glomerulus (which becomes peritubular capillary blood) then has more concentrated protein, and its stronger oncotic pull draws more of the fluid reabsorbed from the tubule into the blood.

Answer: D. Step by step: Na⁺ and water leave the tubule cells into the spaces between cells. From there, the Starling forces of the peritubular capillary decide whether the fluid enters blood. The biggest is the capillary's oncotic pressure (πc, the pull of plasma proteins). It is high because this blood just came from the glomerulus, where about 20% of its plasma water was filtered off while all of its protein stayed. Wrong choices: (a) the fluid is isosmotic, so there is no osmotic gradient; (b) tubular fluid has almost no protein; (c) pressure inside the tubule is small.

'More filtration' means a higher filtration fraction: the share of plasma flowing through the kidney that gets filtered. FF = GFR ÷ RPF (glomerular filtration rate ÷ renal plasma flow). Example: 120 mL/min ÷ 600 mL/min = 0.20, so 20% of plasma is filtered. If FF rises to 0.25, more water leaves the same plasma, so the protein left behind is more concentrated → higher πc. FF usually rises because the efferent arteriole constricts (e.g., angiotensin II). Less pressure then reaches the peritubular capillary → lower Pc (capillary hydrostatic pressure, the push of fluid out of the vessel). Stronger pull in plus weaker push out = more reabsorption.

Thick black arrows: reabsorbed fluid moving from the tubule (purple) into the red capillaries wrapped around it. The thin arrows show blood entering at the top and leaving at the left. These peritubular capillaries get their blood from the efferent arteriole, so it has just been filtered: low pressure, concentrated protein, high πc. That pull keeps clearing reabsorbed fluid away from the tubule. The label at right refers to the vasa recta, the long straight capillaries beside the loop of Henle, which carry the water and solute reabsorbed from the loop back into the blood the same way.

Low ECF volume (vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding) changes both capillary forces: (1) plasma proteins become more concentrated → πc rises; (2) blood pressure falls → Pc falls. Both favor movement into the capillary, so the proximal tubule reabsorbs more than the usual 67% of filtered Na⁺ and water. The kidney is holding on to volume. Volume expansion (e.g., IV saline) does the opposite: proteins are diluted (πc falls) and Pc rises. Less is reabsorbed, some fluid leaks back into the tubule, and the extra NaCl and water are excreted.

A second effect of low volume. In the picture, ‘in’ means from the lumen into the blood and ‘out’ means into the lumen. (1) Low blood pressure turns on the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. (2) ATII (angiotensin II) stimulates the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger of the proximal tubule. (3) More H⁺ is secreted into the lumen, and each H⁺ reclaims one filtered HCO₃⁻ into blood along with Na⁺ (the CA cycle). The kidney saves Na⁺ and water, but blood HCO₃⁻ rises → metabolic alkalosis, called contraction alkalosis (e.g., after vomiting or diuretics). Aldosterone adds to it by increasing H⁺ secretion in the collecting duct.

Thin limbs have no pumps: water and solute move passively (the descending limb loses water, the thin ascending limb loses NaCl). The TAL reabsorbs ~25% of filtered Na⁺ actively. Its luminal Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (one Na⁺, one K⁺, two Cl⁻ together) is not itself a pump; it runs on the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase. Some K⁺ leaks back into the lumen and leaves it positive (+7 mV compared with blood). This charge pushes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ out of the lumen, between the cells, into the blood. Furosemide binds the carrier's Cl⁻ site and stops it, so Na⁺ is lost, and with the positive charge gone Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ are lost too. Load dependent: more Na⁺ arriving → more reabsorbed. No water follows, so the fluid becomes dilute.

Early distal tubule = the first part of the DCT. Its luminal Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter carries one Na⁺ with one Cl⁻, powered by the Na⁺ gradient. Thiazides (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) bind its Cl⁻ site and block it. This segment is also water-impermeable, so it dilutes the fluid further (the cortical diluting segment). Here Ca²⁺ is reabsorbed by its own route, separate from Na⁺: PTH increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption, and thiazides increase Ca²⁺ reabsorption too, so less Ca²⁺ ends up in urine. That is the opposite of furosemide, and it is why thiazides help prevent calcium kidney stones.

Two cell types. Principal cells: Na⁺ enters the cell from the lumen through ENaC (epithelial Na⁺ channel) and is pumped to blood; this leaves the lumen negative compared with blood, which drives K⁺ secretion into urine. Aldosterone boosts both by making more ENaC and more Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase. α-intercalated cells: secrete H⁺ into urine. Each H⁺ made inside the cell leaves behind a HCO₃⁻ that goes to blood, a new bicarbonate rather than a reclaimed one. Drugs: spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor; amiloride and triamterene plug ENaC. All three are K⁺-sparing: less Na⁺ entry → less K⁺ and H⁺ secretion → risk of high blood K⁺.

qs.q: Why does glomerular filtration cost the kidney no ATP?
opts: Blood pressure from the heart drives it
The Na⁺ gradient across tubule cells drives it
Water following reabsorbed Na⁺ drives it
qs.why: Filtration is bulk flow pushed by blood pressure the heart creates. It is Na⁺ reabsorption, via the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, that uses most of the kidney's ATP.

qs.q: Na⁺ intake keeps exceeding Na⁺ excretion. What results?
opts: ECF unchanged: Na⁺ moves into cells
qs.why: Water follows Na⁺, so body Na⁺ sets the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume. Keeping more Na⁺ than you eat expands ECF and blood volume, raising blood pressure and causing edema.

qs.q: Which segment reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered Na⁺?
qs.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds, the thick ascending limb about a quarter, and the distal tubule and collecting duct only a few percent each.

qs.q: Why is acetazolamide only a mild diuretic, even though it acts in the proximal tubule?
opts: It works only when aldosterone is high
Later segments reabsorb much of the extra Na⁺
The proximal tubule reabsorbs little Na⁺
It weakly blocks the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter
qs.why: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block NaHCO₃ reabsorption, but later segments reabsorb much of the Na⁺ that escapes the proximal tubule. Loop diuretics, blocking about 25% of filtered Na⁺ in the thick ascending limb, are the strongest.

qs.q: What does PTH (parathyroid hormone) do in the proximal tubule?
qs.why: PTH blocks the Na⁺–phosphate cotransporter, so more phosphate is lost in urine. Increasing Ca²⁺ reabsorption is what PTH does in the distal tubule.

qs.q: Why is Na⁺–glucose cotransport called secondary active transport?
opts: It runs on the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase
It needs no energy source at all
It is driven by water leaving the lumen
qs.why: The carrier burns no ATP itself; it couples glucose moving uphill to Na⁺ flowing downhill. The Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase on the blood side (primary active transport) creates that Na⁺ gradient.

qs.q: What is the net result of proximal tubule H⁺ secretion working with carbonic anhydrase?
opts: Filtered HCO₃⁻ is excreted as CO₂
HCO₃⁻ is secreted into the urine
New HCO₃⁻ is made; H⁺ is excreted in urine
Filtered HCO₃⁻ returns to blood; no net H⁺ is excreted
qs.why: Secreted H⁺ turns filtered HCO₃⁻ into CO₂ + H₂O; CO₂ enters the cell, HCO₃⁻ is rebuilt and sent to blood, and the H⁺ is secreted again. The HCO₃⁻ is recovered, not newly made.

qs.q: Breakdown of which molecule in the proximal tubule yields NH₄⁺ for the urine and a new HCO₃⁻ for the blood?
qs.why: Glutamine splits into NH₄⁺ (ammonium), which is secreted into urine, and α-ketoglutarate, whose breakdown makes a new HCO₃⁻.

qs.q: Normally, how much of the filtered glucose is left by the end of the proximal tubule?
qs.why: The early proximal tubule's Na⁺ cotransporters reabsorb 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids. Glucose spills into urine only when the filtered load exceeds the carriers' maximum rate, as in uncontrolled diabetes.

qs.q: Compared with plasma, which solute is more concentrated in the fluid entering the late proximal tubule?
qs.why: The early proximal tubule reabsorbs HCO₃⁻ rather than Cl⁻, and water leaves with the absorbed solute, so the Cl⁻ left behind becomes concentrated. That Cl⁻ gradient drives NaCl reabsorption in the late proximal tubule.

qs.q: In the late proximal tubule, the luminal anion exchanger brings Cl⁻ into the cell in exchange for which anion?
qs.why: The Cl⁻–formate exchanger runs beside the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger; formate is recycled as formic acid, so net NaCl enters the cell. The Cl⁻–HCO₃⁻ exchanger is band 3 of red cells.

qs.q: A defect in band 3, the red cell Cl⁻–HCO₃⁻ exchanger, causes which disorder?
qs.why: Band 3 also anchors the red cell's membrane skeleton. Without it the cells become small, round and fragile, and the spleen destroys them.

qs.q: Why does fluid in the proximal tubule stay isosmotic to plasma as it is reabsorbed?
opts: Water follows solute at once across the leaky epithelium
No solute is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
ADH holds water in the proximal lumen
Urea is added as Na⁺ is removed
qs.why: The proximal tubule is very permeable to water, so water follows reabsorbed solute in the same proportion (67% of each). Volume falls but concentration stays about 300 mOsm/L.

qs.q: What happens when a solute that cannot be reabsorbed, such as mannitol, is in the tubule?
opts: Urine volume falls as water is pulled out
Urine volume rises as water stays with it
Na⁺ reabsorption rises and urine volume falls
qs.why: Water moves only by osmosis, following solute. A solute held in the lumen holds water with it, so urine volume rises (osmotic diuresis).

qs.q: Glomerulotubular balance means the proximal tubule reabsorbs…
opts: A constant fraction of the filtered load
A fixed amount regardless of GFR
qs.why: It reabsorbs about 67% of whatever is filtered, so a rise in GFR brings a matching rise in reabsorption. Without this, a 1% rise in GFR would lose about 252 mEq of Na⁺ a day.

qs.q: A rise in filtration fraction (GFR ÷ renal plasma flow) does what to proximal reabsorption?
opts: Increases it via higher peritubular oncotic pressure
Decreases it via lower peritubular oncotic pressure
Increases it via higher peritubular hydrostatic pressure
qs.why: Filtering more water from the same plasma concentrates the protein left behind, so peritubular oncotic pressure rises and pulls more fluid back into the blood.

qs.q: Peritubular capillaries receive their blood directly from which vessel?
qs.why: Their blood comes straight from the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole, so it has just been filtered: low pressure and concentrated protein.

qs.q: In ECF volume contraction, how do peritubular capillary oncotic pressure (πc) and hydrostatic pressure (Pc) change?
qs.why: Plasma proteins become more concentrated (πc up) and blood pressure falls (Pc down). Both favor uptake into the capillary, so the proximal tubule reabsorbs more than its usual 67%.

qs.q: In volume contraction, angiotensin II stimulates which proximal tubule transporter, causing contraction alkalosis?
qs.why: More H⁺ secretion reclaims more filtered HCO₃⁻ into blood along with Na⁺. The kidney saves Na⁺ and water, but blood HCO₃⁻ rises: metabolic alkalosis.

qs.q: Why does furosemide increase urinary loss of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺?
opts: It removes the lumen-positive voltage in the TAL
It blocks Ca²⁺ channels in the distal tubule
qs.why: In the thick ascending limb (TAL), K⁺ leaking back into the lumen makes it positive (+7 mV compared with blood), which pushes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ out of the lumen between the cells into blood. Blocking the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter removes that voltage.

qs.q: Why does fluid leaving the thick ascending limb become dilute?
opts: It reabsorbs NaCl but is impermeable to water
It secretes water into the lumen
Urea enters it from the medulla
qs.why: The TAL actively reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na⁺ with no water following, so the tubular fluid becomes dilute. The early distal tubule dilutes it further.

qs.q: What do thiazide diuretics do to urinary Ca²⁺?
opts: Lower it, helping prevent Ca²⁺ stones
qs.why: Thiazides block the distal tubule's Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter and increase Ca²⁺ reabsorption there, so less Ca²⁺ reaches the urine. This is the opposite of loop diuretics.

qs.q: Which K⁺-sparing diuretic directly plugs ENaC (the epithelial Na⁺ channel) in principal cells?
qs.why: Amiloride (and triamterene) plug ENaC. Spironolactone is also K⁺-sparing, but it works by blocking the aldosterone receptor.

slides.note: Almost all K⁺ (98%) sits inside cells, in the ICF (intracellular fluid), at about 150 mEq/L. The ECF (extracellular fluid: plasma plus the fluid between cells) holds only about 4.5 mEq/L (normal blood K⁺ 3.5–5). The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in every cell keeps this gap: each cycle pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. Because the store inside is so big, a small shift matters. Example: if just 1% of cell K⁺ leaked out, blood K⁺ would jump from about 4.5 to about 7 mEq/L. Moving K⁺ between cells and ECF is internal balance. Matching urine K⁺ to the K⁺ you eat is external balance, the kidney's job.

Correction: K⁺ does not share a carrier with glucose. Insulin moves K⁺ into cells by turning up the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Normally this clears the K⁺ from each meal: food triggers insulin, and insulin moves the new K⁺ into cells so blood K⁺ stays normal. Without insulin (untreated type 1 diabetes) the K⁺ stays outside, giving hyperkalemia. In DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis) blood K⁺ is high from the missing insulin plus the very high glucose, which pulls water and K⁺ out of cells. As treatment, insulin lowers K⁺ within minutes; glucose (dextrose) is given with it only to prevent low blood sugar.

Cells can buffer extra H⁺, but H⁺ cannot cross the cell membrane alone. To keep charges balanced it swaps places with another cation, and that cation is K⁺. In acidosis there is too much H⁺ outside. H⁺ moves into cells, K⁺ comes out, and blood K⁺ rises (hyperkalemia). In alkalosis there is too little H⁺ outside. H⁺ leaves cells, K⁺ moves in (the last line should read K⁺), and blood K⁺ falls. Little shift happens in respiratory acid–base disorders (CO₂ crosses membranes freely) or in lactic acidosis and ketoacidosis (the acid's anion enters the cell with the H⁺).

This is acidosis. The ECF is full of extra H⁺ (white balls). H⁺ moves into the cell's ICF to be buffered by cell proteins (white arrow). To keep the charge balanced, a K⁺ (green) moves out (green arrow). Repeat this across all the body's cells and blood K⁺ climbs, even though total body K⁺ has not changed.

The mirror image: alkalosis. With too little H⁺ in the blood, cells release H⁺ to replace it. K⁺ moves into the cells to balance the charge, so blood K⁺ falls. This kidney tubule cell (lumen on the left, blood on the right) shows the same kind of swap at its lower carrier: H⁺ goes out into the lumen (urine side) and K⁺ comes into the cell. CA (carbonic anhydrase) makes the H⁺ inside the cell from CO₂ and water, leaving HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate), which exits to the blood on the right in exchange for Cl⁻. Separately, alkalosis makes principal cells (a different cell type) secrete more K⁺ into urine, so the two effects add up to hypokalemia.

Epinephrine acting on β₂ receptors switches on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. The pump moves more K⁺ into cells, so blood K⁺ falls. Example: high-dose albuterol (a β₂ agonist inhaled for asthma) lowers blood K⁺ and is even used to treat hyperkalemia. β-blockers (e.g., propranolol) remove this push. Less K⁺ enters cells, more stays outside, and blood K⁺ rises. This matters most after a K⁺ load, during exercise, or in kidney failure.

α-adrenergic stimulation does the opposite of β₂: it shifts K⁺ out of cells and raises blood K⁺. α-blockers let K⁺ move into cells and lower it. Epinephrine hits both receptor types, but the β₂ effect wins, so a surge of epinephrine during severe stress lowers blood K⁺. Memory aid: β₂ moves K⁺ in, α moves K⁺ out.

Hyperosmolarity means the ECF has too many dissolved particles, for example very high blood glucose in uncontrolled diabetes, or IV mannitol. Water leaves the cells by osmosis. As water leaves, the K⁺ left inside becomes more concentrated. Its gradient to diffuse out gets steeper, so K⁺ leaks out; the outflowing water also drags K⁺ with it. Net result: blood K⁺ rises. Low ECF osmolarity does the opposite and moves K⁺ into cells.

When cells burst, their K⁺ (98% of body K⁺) pours into the blood at once. Hemolysis is red blood cells breaking. Rhabdomyolysis is skeletal muscle breaking down (crush injury, burns, extreme exercise). Tumor lysis is chemotherapy killing many cancer cells at once. Prevention: IV fluids keep urine flowing so the kidney can flush out the K⁺ (and the uric acid from dead cells). Bicarbonate makes the blood alkaline, which shifts K⁺ back into cells.

This is the reverse of lysis. Each new cell fills itself with K⁺ (about 150 mEq/L inside), taking it from the blood. Normally cells are made too slowly for this to matter. But when B12 or folate is given to someone with megaloblastic anemia (too few, oversized blood cells), the marrow suddenly makes huge numbers of new cells within days. They soak up K⁺ from the blood, and hypokalemia can follow.

Working muscle uses up its ATP. Low ATP opens K⁺ channels in the muscle membrane, so K⁺ leaks out of the cells. This K⁺ is useful: it acts on the muscle's own arterioles and dilates them, so more blood reaches the working muscle. The rise in blood K⁺ is small and reverses with rest. It can become dangerous if the person also takes a β-blocker or has kidney failure, because K⁺ is then not moved back into cells (β-blocker) or not excreted (kidney failure).

One rule ties the table together. Anything that turns up the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (insulin, β₂ agonists) or makes H⁺ leave cells (alkalosis) pulls K⁺ into cells and lowers blood K⁺. The opposite of each raises it. Lysis, high osmolarity and exercise raise K⁺ by letting it escape from cells. Low osmolarity (the empty box opposite high osmolarity) shifts K⁺ in. All of these move K⁺ between cells and ECF without changing total body K⁺.

K⁺ outside the cell sets the resting membrane potential of nerve, skeletal muscle and heart. High or low blood K⁺ shifts this potential, which changes how easily these cells fire. The result is muscle weakness (even paralysis) and arrhythmias, the part that kills. Item 3 belongs to hypokalemia: low K⁺ makes the collecting duct resist ADH (antidiuretic hormone), so it cannot concentrate urine. This is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: large volumes of dilute urine and thirst.

K⁺ is not bound to plasma proteins, so all plasma K⁺ is filtered at the glomerulus. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 67% of the filtered K⁺, along with water. The thick ascending limb reabsorbs another 20% through the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ carrier. These two percentages stay constant, whatever the diet. All the adjusting to diet happens in the distal tubule and collecting duct. On a low-K⁺ diet, α-intercalated cells reabsorb more. On a normal or high-K⁺ diet, principal cells secrete K⁺. Urine K⁺ can range from 1% to 110% of the filtered amount (110% means more was secreted than filtered).

These cells work mainly on a low-K⁺ diet, when the body must save K⁺. On the lumen (urine) side sits the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, the same pump as in the stomach. "ATP splitting" means the pump burns ATP directly. It pushes H⁺ into the urine and pulls K⁺ from the urine into the cell. The K⁺ then leaves through the blood side, so it is reabsorbed. Each H⁺ secreted was made from CO₂ and water, leaving one HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) behind, which enters the blood as a new bicarbonate. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the ATP-splitting pump on the blood side.

This α-intercalated cell reabsorbs K⁺, mainly on a low-K⁺ diet. Lumen (urine) is on the left at −50 mV; blood is on the right at 0 mV, so the lumen is 50 mV more negative than blood. Lumen side: the blue pump is the H⁺-ATPase; it pushes H⁺ into the urine. The pink pump is the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase; it pushes H⁺ into the urine and pulls K⁺ from the urine into the cell. Blood side: K⁺ then leaves the cell into the blood (lower-right arrow), which completes K⁺ reabsorption. The green pump is the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (Na⁺ out to blood, K⁺ into the cell). The H⁺ is made inside the cell from CO₂ and water by carbonic anhydrase, leaving an HCO₃⁻ that goes to the blood (not drawn here; see the next slide).

The same α-intercalated cell, now with the urine buffer. Lumen on the left, blood on the right. Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase turns CO₂ + H₂O into H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), which splits into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. Two ATP pumps push the H⁺ into the urine: the blue H⁺-ATPase and the purple H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which also brings K⁺ into the cell. In the urine, filtered HPO₄²⁻ picks up H⁺ and becomes H₂PO₄⁻, which is excreted (titratable acid).
