The HCO₃⁻ leaves the cell into the blood through the pink Cl⁻–HCO₃⁻ exchanger (Cl⁻ comes into the cell); it is a new HCO₃⁻. The green pump is the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Not drawn here: NH₃ in the urine also picks up H⁺ to become NH₄⁺ (ammonium), and aldosterone stimulates the H⁺-ATPase.

A third view of the same cell, turned so the urine side is on top. Top: the two pumps on the apical (urine) side, the H⁺-ATPase and the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase. The second one pulls K⁺ in from the urine. Bottom right: the pink carrier moves K⁺ (with Cl⁻) out the basolateral (blood) side, completing K⁺ reabsorption. Bottom left: kAE1 (kidney anion exchanger 1) moves HCO₃⁻ into blood in exchange for Cl⁻.

Principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct secrete K⁺ into the urine. Step by step: the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the blood side pumps K⁺ into the cell, keeping cell K⁺ high. Na⁺ enters from the urine through Na⁺ channels, which leaves the lumen electrically negative compared with blood. K⁺ then flows out of the cell into the lumen through K⁺ channels, pushed by its high concentration in the cell and pulled by the negative lumen. The bigger this push, the more K⁺ is secreted. Secretion is "extremely variable" because it rises and falls with diet and the factors on the next two slides.

Rule: secretion rises when K⁺ inside the cell rises or K⁺ in the lumen falls. Diet: a high-K⁺ meal fills the cells with K⁺, so more is secreted; a low-K⁺ diet does the reverse. Acid–base: alkalosis moves K⁺ into cells, so secretion rises (hypokalemia); acidosis lowers it (hyperkalemia). Loop and thiazide diuretics block Na⁺ reabsorption upstream, so more Na⁺ and fluid reach the principal cells. More Na⁺ enters, the pump brings in more K⁺, and the fast flow washes lumen K⁺ away. The result is hypokalemia. K⁺-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride) block secretion instead.

Aldosterone acts on principal cells in three ways. It adds Na⁺ channels on the lumen side, so more Na⁺ enters. It adds Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps, which push that Na⁺ to the blood and bring more K⁺ into the cell. It adds K⁺ channels on the lumen side, so the extra K⁺ exits into urine. Net: Na⁺ (and water) kept, K⁺ lost. It also boosts H⁺ secretion by α-intercalated cells. Too much aldosterone gives hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis; too little gives the opposite, including hyperkalemia.

Answer: A. A dialysis patient has almost no working kidneys, so K⁺ builds up. Insulin turns up the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which moves K⁺ from the blood into cells within minutes. It does not remove K⁺ from the body, so urinary (B) and GI (C) routes are wrong, and the effect is temporary: dialysis is still needed. Dextrose is given only to prevent low blood sugar from the insulin. Storing glucose as glycogen (D) is not what lowers K⁺.

Answer: A. A blood-pressure drug that slows the heart is a β-blocker. Step 1: β₂ stimulation normally turns up the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and keeps K⁺ moving into cells. Step 2: a β-blocker removes this push, so more K⁺ stays in the blood. Step 3: β-blockers also lower renin release, so there is less aldosterone and less K⁺ secretion by the kidney. Both effects raise blood K⁺.

Answer: A. Chemotherapy kills a large lymphoma quickly (tumor lysis syndrome). The dying cells spill K⁺, phosphate and nucleic acids; the nucleic acids are broken down to uric acid, which is why uric acid rises. Uric acid crystals can block the kidneys (B) and form stones (D) over days, and gout (C) is slow and not deadly. High K⁺ can stop the heart through an arrhythmia within hours, so it kills first.

Answer: C. Low counts with big cells (high MCV, mean corpuscular volume) mean megaloblastic anemia. High methylmalonic acid points to B12 deficiency (folate deficiency raises homocysteine but not methylmalonic acid). Giving B12 lets the marrow suddenly make huge numbers of new cells. Each new cell takes K⁺ in from the blood, so blood K⁺ falls: hypokalemia. Neuropathy (A) comes from the B12 deficiency itself, not from treating it.

Answer: C. An aldosterone-secreting adenoma causes primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). In principal cells, aldosterone raises Na⁺ reabsorption, so ECF volume and blood pressure rise. It also raises K⁺ secretion, so blood K⁺ falls; low K⁺ explains the weakness. In α-intercalated cells it raises H⁺ secretion, which adds new HCO₃⁻ to the blood (metabolic alkalosis), and the alkalosis drives K⁺ even lower. A renal artery bruit (D) points to renal artery stenosis, which raises renin (secondary hyperaldosteronism), not to an adrenal adenoma.

qs.q: About what share of total body K⁺ is inside cells?
qs.why: About 98% of K⁺ is intracellular at about 150 mEq/L; the ECF holds only about 4.5 mEq/L. So even a small shift out of cells raises blood K⁺ a lot.

qs.q: How does insulin move K⁺ into cells?
opts: It swaps K⁺ in for H⁺ out
It carries K⁺ in with glucose
qs.why: Insulin turns up the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which pumps K⁺ into cells. K⁺ does not share a carrier with glucose.

qs.q: In acidosis, extra H⁺ moves into cells. What happens to blood K⁺?
opts: Unchanged, as Na⁺ leaves cells instead
qs.why: To balance the charge of H⁺ entering cells, K⁺ moves out, so blood K⁺ rises without any change in total body K⁺. Alkalosis does the reverse.

qs.q: Why does respiratory acidosis cause little K⁺ shift out of cells?
opts: The lungs excrete the extra K⁺
The acid's anion enters with the H⁺
qs.why: CO₂ diffuses straight into cells, so no H⁺–K⁺ swap is needed. Lactic acidosis and ketoacidosis also cause little shift, but for a different reason: the anion enters the cell with the H⁺.

qs.q: What does high-dose inhaled albuterol, a β₂ agonist, do to blood K⁺?
opts: Raises it by moving K⁺ out of cells
Lowers it by raising urine K⁺
Raises it by blocking K⁺ secretion
Lowers it by moving K⁺ into cells
qs.why: β₂ stimulation turns on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, pulling K⁺ into cells. That is why albuterol can be used to treat hyperkalemia.

qs.q: During a surge of epinephrine, which way does blood K⁺ usually go, and why?
opts: Rises; β₂ stimulation moves K⁺ out of cells
Falls; α stimulation moves K⁺ into cells
Falls; the β₂ effect outweighs the α effect
Rises; the α effect outweighs the β₂ effect
qs.why: α stimulation shifts K⁺ out of cells and β₂ shifts it in. Epinephrine hits both, but the β₂ effect wins, so blood K⁺ falls during severe stress.

qs.q: Why does severe hyperosmolarity, such as very high blood glucose, raise blood K⁺?
opts: Glucose carries K⁺ out of cells
Water leaving cells concentrates and drags out K⁺
qs.why: Water leaves cells by osmosis, so the K⁺ left inside becomes more concentrated and diffuses out, and the outflowing water drags K⁺ along. Low ECF osmolarity does the opposite.

qs.q: Which of these raises blood K⁺ by bursting cells?
qs.why: Rhabdomyolysis breaks down skeletal muscle and spills its stored K⁺ (98% of body K⁺ is inside cells). The other three move K⁺ into cells and lower blood K⁺.

qs.q: Why can a sudden burst of new blood-cell production lower blood K⁺?
opts: New cells release K⁺ into the blood
Each new cell fills itself with K⁺ from blood
qs.why: Each new cell loads up to about 150 mEq/L of K⁺ inside. When B12 or folate triggers huge marrow output within days, the new cells soak up blood K⁺ and hypokalemia can follow.

qs.q: What does the K⁺ released by exercising muscle do locally?
qs.why: Low ATP opens muscle K⁺ channels, and the K⁺ that leaks out dilates nearby arterioles, raising blood flow to the working muscle.

qs.q: Hypokalemia impairs urine concentration by causing which condition?
qs.why: Low K⁺ makes the collecting duct resist ADH, so it cannot concentrate urine: large volumes of dilute urine and thirst. ADH itself is present, so it is not central.

qs.q: About what share of filtered K⁺ does the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorb?
qs.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 67% along with water, and the thick ascending limb another 20%. These amounts stay constant whatever the diet.

qs.q: Which part of the nephron adjusts K⁺ excretion to match dietary K⁺?
qs.why: Proximal and thick ascending limb reabsorption stay fixed; all the adjusting happens distally, where α-intercalated cells reabsorb K⁺ and principal cells secrete it.

qs.q: In the distal tubule and collecting duct, which cells reabsorb K⁺ on a low-K⁺ diet?
qs.why: α-intercalated cells save K⁺ when intake is low. Principal cells do the opposite: they secrete K⁺ on a normal or high-K⁺ diet.

qs.q: Which luminal pump lets α-intercalated cells pull K⁺ from the urine?
qs.why: The luminal H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the same pump as in the stomach) burns ATP to push H⁺ into urine and pull K⁺ in; each H⁺ leaves a new HCO₃⁻ for the blood. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase sits on the blood side, and the V-type pump moves only H⁺.

qs.q: What drives K⁺ out of principal cells into the urine?
opts: A luminal H⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumping K⁺ out
A lumen-positive voltage from Cl⁻ entry
High cell K⁺ plus a lumen-negative voltage
qs.why: The blood-side Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase keeps cell K⁺ high, and Na⁺ entering through luminal Na⁺ channels leaves the lumen negative compared with blood. K⁺ then flows out through luminal K⁺ channels.

qs.q: What is the biggest determinant of K⁺ secretion by principal cells?
qs.why: A high-K⁺ meal fills the cells with K⁺ and raises secretion; a low-K⁺ diet does the reverse. Aldosterone, acid–base status and diuretics also act, but diet matters most.

qs.q: Why do loop and thiazide diuretics cause hypokalemia?
opts: They block K⁺ reabsorption in the proximal tubule
More Na⁺ and flow reach the principal cells
qs.why: Blocking Na⁺ reabsorption upstream delivers more Na⁺ to principal cells. More Na⁺ entry drives more K⁺ secretion, and the fast flow washes luminal K⁺ away.

qs.q: Which three changes does aldosterone make in principal cells?
opts: More water channels, urea transporters and Cl⁻ channels
More Na⁺ channels, Na⁺/K⁺ pumps and K⁺ channels
Fewer Na⁺ channels, more K⁺ channels and H⁺ pumps
More H⁺/K⁺ pumps, fewer Na⁺ and K⁺ channels
qs.why: Aldosterone adds luminal Na⁺ channels, blood-side Na⁺/K⁺ pumps and luminal K⁺ channels. Na⁺ (and water) is kept and K⁺ is lost in the urine.

qs.q: Why is dextrose given along with insulin to treat hyperkalemia?
qs.why: Insulin lowers K⁺ by turning up the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; the dextrose only prevents the hypoglycemia the insulin would cause. The shift is temporary because no K⁺ leaves the body.

qs.q: Besides blocking β₂-driven K⁺ uptake into cells, how do β-blockers raise blood K⁺ through the kidney?
opts: More renin, so more aldosterone-driven K⁺ secretion
Blocked K⁺ filtration at the glomerulus
Less renin, so less aldosterone-driven K⁺ secretion
qs.why: β-blockers reduce renin release, so aldosterone falls and principal cells secrete less K⁺. This adds to the effect of less K⁺ moving into cells.

qs.q: Which lab result points to B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency?
qs.why: Both deficiencies cause large cells (high MCV) and raise homocysteine, but only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.

qs.q: How does an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma cause metabolic alkalosis?
opts: More K⁺ uptake by α-intercalated cells
More H⁺ secretion by α-intercalated cells
More HCO₃⁻ secretion by principal cells
Less Na⁺ reabsorption in the collecting duct
qs.why: Aldosterone boosts H⁺ secretion by α-intercalated cells, and each H⁺ secreted leaves a new HCO₃⁻ for the blood. The alkalosis then pushes blood K⁺ even lower.

slides.note: Phosphate is stored mostly in bone (85%). About 15% is in the ICF (intracellular fluid, inside cells), where it is part of DNA, RNA, ATP and many metabolic intermediates. Under 0.5% is in the ECF (extracellular fluid: plasma plus the fluid between cells). That tiny ECF share is what the kidney controls, by deciding how much phosphate to let out in urine. Phosphate that reaches the urine also binds secreted H⁺, so it works as a urinary acid buffer.

One proximal tubule cell: tubular lumen (urine side) on the right, blood side (basolateral membrane) on the left. Filtered phosphate can enter the cell only together with Na⁺, on Na⁺–phosphate cotransporters (NaPi-IIa, NaPi-IIc and PiT-2; NaPi-IIa carries most of it). The Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase on the blood side pumps Na⁺ out and keeps cell Na⁺ low, so Na⁺ keeps flowing in from the lumen and drags phosphate along. Phosphate then exits to the blood by a route not yet identified (the green '?'). Phosphate exists as HPO₄²⁻ or H₂PO₄⁻; adding H⁺ turns HPO₄²⁻ into H₂PO₄⁻. PTH (parathyroid hormone) lowers phosphate reabsorption by pulling these cotransporters out of the membrane.

About 10% of plasma phosphate is bound to proteins and can't cross the glomerular filter; the other 90% is filtered. The proximal tubule reabsorbs most of it (moves it out of the tubule fluid and back into the blood): 70% of the filtered load in the PCT (proximal convoluted tubule) and 15% in the proximal straight tubule. Later segments reabsorb little or none, so the proximal tubule alone decides how much is excreted. The Na⁺–phosphate cotransporter has a Tm (transport maximum), a top rate it can't exceed. Below the Tm, almost all filtered phosphate is reabsorbed. Once the Tm is reached, every extra bit spills into the urine, just as glucose does in diabetes. Normally the filtered load sits just above the Tm, which is why some phosphate is always excreted.

Add up the proximal tubule: 70% + 15% = 85% reabsorbed, so about 15% of filtered phosphate is excreted. That is a large share; Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻ and glucose are almost fully reabsorbed. The leftover phosphate has a job. In the urine it binds H⁺ secreted by the tubule (HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻), so the kidney can excrete acid without the urine pH falling too far. H⁺ excreted on urinary buffers, mainly phosphate, is called titratable acid. The name comes from how it is measured: urine is titrated with base back to blood pH (7.4), and the base needed equals the H⁺ carried.

PTH binds its receptor on the blood side of the proximal tubule cell → the receptor activates a Gs protein → Gs turns on adenylyl cyclase → adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP (cyclic AMP, a second messenger) from ATP → cAMP activates protein kinases → these shut down Na⁺–phosphate cotransport. Less phosphate is reabsorbed, and later segments can't reabsorb it either, so it is lost in urine (phosphaturia). Some cAMP also leaves the cell into the lumen, so a rise in urine cAMP shows that PTH is acting. In pseudohypoparathyroidism the receptor, Gs or adenylyl cyclase is defective, so the kidney ignores PTH. Blood PTH is high, but urine phosphate and urine cAMP stay low; blood phosphate rises and Ca²⁺ falls, as if PTH were missing.

When blood phosphate falls, less phosphate is filtered. The filtered load (GFR × plasma phosphate; GFR = glomerular filtration rate, the volume of plasma filtered per minute) drops below the Tm, so the cotransporters can reabsorb (return to the blood) every bit that is filtered. The proximal tubule also inserts more Na⁺–phosphate cotransporters into its luminal membrane. Result: reabsorption approaches 100% and urine phosphate falls to nearly zero. Example: normally about 15% of filtered phosphate is more than the carriers can handle and spills into urine. Halve plasma phosphate and the filtered load halves; it now fits under the Tm, so almost nothing spills.

Answer: C (low Ca²⁺, high phosphate). (1) In end-stage renal failure few nephrons work, so the GFR is very low. Little phosphate is filtered and excreted, but food keeps adding it, so blood phosphate rises. (2) The kidney makes active vitamin D (calcitriol). Damaged kidneys make little, so the gut absorbs less Ca²⁺ and blood Ca²⁺ falls. (3) The extra phosphate also binds Ca²⁺ and lowers free Ca²⁺ further. A and B are wrong because nothing here raises Ca²⁺; D is wrong because phosphate can't get out.

Answer: D. Vitamin D becomes active in two steps: the liver adds a 25-OH group, then the proximal tubule adds a 1-OH group (enzyme 1α-hydroxylase), making 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Calcitriol's main job is to make the gut absorb Ca²⁺. Failing kidneys can't make enough, so Ca²⁺ absorption drops and blood Ca²⁺ falls. Why not the others: the gut itself works (A). PTH is actually high, not low (B), and high PTH raises Ca²⁺, so it is the body's response, not the cause (C). Urine Ca²⁺ loss is low, not high, because little is filtered (E).

Answer: C. The kidney is the main exit for phosphate absorbed from food. Phosphate is filtered, and the proximal tubule decides how much to keep; what it doesn't keep is excreted. 'Failure of excretion' means too little phosphate gets into the urine. In renal failure the GFR falls, so much less phosphate is filtered. Even when the proximal tubule reabsorbs (returns to the blood) very little of it, too little is left in the tubule fluid to be excreted. Intake continues, so blood phosphate rises. This happens even though PTH is high and is telling the proximal tubule to reabsorb less (so B is wrong). The gut doesn't absorb extra (A), low Ca²⁺ doesn't release phosphate (D), and the liver doesn't make phosphate (E).

Answer: B. Chain of events: kidney failure → low calcitriol (less gut Ca²⁺ absorption) plus high phosphate → low blood Ca²⁺ → the parathyroid glands sense it and secrete much more PTH. This is secondary hyperparathyroidism: 'secondary' because the glands are normal and only respond to the low Ca²⁺ (losing calcitriol, which normally holds PTH down, adds to it). High PTH keeps osteoclasts (bone-dissolving cells) busy pulling Ca²⁺ out of bone, so the bone becomes soft and weak. Low calcitriol also leaves too little Ca²⁺ to mineralize new bone, which adds to the softening. C is false: vitamin D doesn't hold osteoclasts back. D can't explain soft bone: less vitamin D would mean less osteoclast activity. E is false: phosphate doesn't dissolve bone. A is wrong: renal failure causes acidosis, not alkalosis.

Hyperphosphatemia = high blood phosphate, the rule in kidney failure. Because the kidney can't excrete phosphate, treatment stops it from being absorbed. Phosphate binders are taken with meals: in the gut they bind phosphate from food into a compound that can't be absorbed and leaves in the stool. Calcium carbonate and calcium acetate bind it with Ca²⁺. They also add Ca²⁺, which helps low Ca²⁺, but too much can raise Ca²⁺ and deposit calcium phosphate in blood vessels. Sevelamer (a resin) and lanthanum (a metal) bind phosphate without adding Ca²⁺, so they are used when Ca²⁺ is high.

Total plasma Ca²⁺ is about 10 mg/dL (5 mEq/L). About 40–45% is bound to plasma proteins (mostly albumin), 10–15% is paired with small anions such as phosphate and citrate, and about half is free, ionized Ca²⁺. Only the free form acts on nerves, muscle, heart and the parathyroid glands, so it is the form the body senses and regulates. The protein-bound part matters for the kidney because it can't be filtered.

Protein-bound Ca²⁺ is too big to cross the glomerular filter. Free Ca²⁺ and Ca²⁺ on small anions pass, so only ~60% is filterable. Filtered load (amount filtered per day) = GFR × plasma Ca²⁺ × 0.6. Example: 180 L/day × 5 mEq/L × 0.6 = 540 mEq/day. Over 99% of that is reabsorbed; under 1% is excreted. The proximal tubule (67%) and thick ascending limb (25%) reabsorb Ca²⁺ in step with Na⁺: whatever raises or lowers Na⁺ reabsorption there does the same to Ca²⁺. The distal tubule reabsorbs only 8%, but it has its own control (PTH), so it fine-tunes how much Ca²⁺ ends up in urine.

In the thick ascending limb (TAL), the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter moves Na⁺, K⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ from the lumen into the cell. Much of that K⁺ leaks straight back into the lumen through K⁺ channels, leaving the lumen about +7 mV compared with the blood side (lumen-positive). Positive repels positive, so this voltage pushes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ out of the lumen between the cells into the blood. Furosemide (a loop diuretic) blocks the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter → no K⁺ to recycle → no positive voltage → Ca²⁺ stays in the tubule. So loop diuretics increase Ca²⁺ excretion, which is why they are used to treat high blood Ca²⁺ (hypercalcemia).

In the proximal tubule and TAL, Ca²⁺ reabsorption follows Na⁺. In the distal tubule the two are uncoupled: Ca²⁺ reabsorption can rise while Na⁺ reabsorption falls. This is the segment PTH controls: PTH → receptor → Gs → cAMP → more Ca²⁺ reabsorbed → less Ca²⁺ in urine. Thiazide diuretics block the Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter here, so more Na⁺ is lost. But less Na⁺ enters the cell, so cell Na⁺ falls; the Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger on the blood side then pushes more Ca²⁺ out of the cell into the blood, and more Ca²⁺ enters from the lumen to replace it. Net: thiazides lower urine Ca²⁺. Don't confuse: loop diuretics lose Ca²⁺; thiazides keep it.

PTH acts on two nephron sites, both through the same cAMP signal. In the proximal tubule it blocks Na⁺–phosphate cotransport, so phosphate is lost in urine (its phosphaturic action). In the distal tubule it increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption, so less Ca²⁺ is lost (its hypocalciuric action). Net effect: blood Ca²⁺ rises and blood phosphate falls. Excreting phosphate also helps free Ca²⁺ rise, because phosphate left in the blood would bind Ca²⁺.

Answer: A. Most kidney stones are calcium stones (calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate), and a common cause is too much Ca²⁺ in the urine (hypercalciuria). Thiazides make the distal tubule reabsorb more Ca²⁺, so less Ca²⁺ reaches the urine and fewer stones form. Furosemide (B) does the opposite: it removes the TAL's lumen-positive voltage, raises urine Ca²⁺ and makes stones more likely. Spironolactone (C) blocks aldosterone in the late distal tubule and collecting duct and barely affects Ca²⁺. Oral vitamin D (D) increases gut Ca²⁺ absorption, which raises urine Ca²⁺ and worsens stones.

An early distal tubule cell: lumen (urine) on the left, interstitial space (blood side) on the right. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ enter together on the Na⁺–Cl⁻ symporter (cotransporter), the transporter thiazides block. On the blood side the Na⁺–K⁺ pump sends Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, and Cl⁻ leaves through Cl⁻ channels. This segment is water-tight, so removing NaCl from the tubule fluid here, without water, dilutes that fluid. Ca²⁺ isn't drawn: it enters through its own luminal channel and leaves on the blood-side Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger. A thiazide lowers cell Na⁺, which speeds that exchanger and raises Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

Correction: loop diuretics block only the thick ascending limb (TAL) share of Mg²⁺ reabsorption, not the proximal or distal share. Because the TAL share is the biggest, they still cause large urine Mg²⁺ losses and can cause low blood Mg²⁺ (hypomagnesemia). Mg²⁺ differs from Na⁺ and Ca²⁺: the proximal tubule takes only 30% (versus 67% for Na⁺ and Ca²⁺), and the TAL is the main site (60%). About 20–30% of plasma Mg²⁺ is protein-bound, so roughly 75% is filtered. Overall 95% is reabsorbed and 5% is excreted, a high share compared with Na⁺ or Ca²⁺ (under 1%).

A thick ascending limb cell: urine on the left, blood on the right. Read it top to bottom. (1) The Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter brings Na⁺, K⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ from the urine into the cell; furosemide blocks it (top label). (2) The Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase pumps Na⁺ to the blood; K⁺ and Cl⁻ also exit on the blood side. (3) Some K⁺ leaks back into the lumen through a K⁺ channel, making the lumen positive compared with the blood side. (4) That (+) potential pushes Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ between the cells into the blood. Block step 1 and steps 3–4 stop (bottom label), so Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ stay in the urine.

The main force behind Mg²⁺ reabsorption is the lumen-positive voltage in the TAL, because the TAL reabsorbs most filtered Mg²⁺. Anything that removes this voltage, such as a loop diuretic, wastes Mg²⁺ in the urine and can cause hypomagnesemia. Low Mg²⁺ makes nerve and muscle membranes over-excitable. The results are neurologic signs (tremor, confusion, seizures), tetany (involuntary muscle spasms) and cardiac arrhythmias. Low Mg²⁺ also drags blood Ca²⁺ and K⁺ down, which adds to the tetany and arrhythmias.

Mg²⁺ is a cofactor for about 300 enzymes, including every enzyme that uses or makes ATP (ATP works mostly as an Mg²⁺–ATP complex). About 60% of body Mg²⁺ sits in the skeleton. Two links to other electrolytes: (1) The parathyroid glands need Mg²⁺ to release PTH. In severe Mg²⁺ deficiency PTH falls and tissues respond poorly to it, so blood Ca²⁺ drops and won't correct until Mg²⁺ is replaced. (2) Inside late distal tubule and collecting duct cells, Mg²⁺ plugs the K⁺ channels that secrete K⁺ into urine. With low Mg²⁺ they stay open, K⁺ is wasted, and low K⁺ won't correct until Mg²⁺ is given.

qs.q: Where is most of the body's phosphate stored?
qs.why: About 85% of phosphate is in bone, 15% in the ICF and under 0.5% in the ECF.

qs.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs nearly all of the phosphate that is reabsorbed?
qs.why: The proximal convoluted tubule takes 70% and the proximal straight tubule 15% of filtered phosphate; later segments take little or none.

qs.q: About what fraction of filtered phosphate is normally excreted?
qs.why: 70% + 15% = 85% is reabsorbed, so about 15% is excreted, a large share compared with Na⁺ or glucose. 85% is the reabsorbed share, not the excreted one.

qs.q: H⁺ excreted bound to urinary phosphate (HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻) is called what?
qs.why: H⁺ carried on urinary buffers, mainly phosphate, is titratable acid: it is measured by titrating urine with base back to pH 7.4.

qs.q: PTH's signal to block Na⁺–phosphate cotransport in the proximal tubule runs through which pathway?
qs.why: PTH's receptor activates Gs, which turns on adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP; cAMP-activated kinases shut down Na⁺–phosphate cotransport, so phosphate is lost in urine.

qs.q: In pseudohypoparathyroidism, what are blood PTH and urine cAMP?
qs.why: The receptor, Gs or adenylyl cyclase is defective, so the kidney ignores PTH: PTH is high, but no cAMP is made and urine cAMP and phosphate stay low.

qs.q: Why does urine phosphate fall to nearly zero when plasma phosphate is low?
opts: Filtered load falls below the transport maximum
The distal tubule reabsorbs the remainder
qs.why: Filtered load = GFR × plasma phosphate. When it drops below the Tm, the proximal cotransporters (now more numerous) reabsorb all of it (return it to the blood).

qs.q: Which proximal tubule enzyme completes activation of vitamin D to calcitriol?
qs.why: The liver adds the 25-OH group; the proximal tubule's 1α-hydroxylase adds the 1-OH group, making 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

qs.q: What is calcitriol's main job in Ca²⁺ balance?
qs.why: Calcitriol mainly makes the gut absorb Ca²⁺, so failing kidneys that make little of it cause low blood Ca²⁺. It does not hold osteoclasts back, and it normally holds PTH down.

qs.q: In renal failure, what makes the hyperparathyroidism 'secondary'?
opts: Normal glands respond to low blood Ca²⁺
A tumor secretes a PTH-like peptide
A parathyroid adenoma secretes PTH autonomously
Kidney tubules fail to respond to PTH
qs.why: The parathyroid glands are normal; they secrete more PTH because low calcitriol and high phosphate lower blood Ca²⁺.

qs.q: Which phosphate binder is chosen when blood Ca²⁺ is already high?
qs.why: Sevelamer (and lanthanum) bind dietary phosphate without adding Ca²⁺; calcium salts add Ca²⁺ and can push it higher.

qs.q: Why is only about 60% of plasma Ca²⁺ filterable at the glomerulus?
qs.why: About 40% of plasma Ca²⁺ is bound to proteins (mostly albumin), which can't cross the filter. Free Ca²⁺ and Ca²⁺ on small anions like phosphate and citrate are filtered.

qs.q: Which segment reabsorbs the largest share of filtered Ca²⁺?
qs.why: The proximal tubule takes about 67%, the thick ascending limb about 25% and the distal tubule about 8%.

qs.q: How does furosemide increase urine Ca²⁺?
opts: It blocks Ca²⁺ channels in the distal tubule
It abolishes the lumen-positive voltage in the TAL
It inhibits the basolateral Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger
qs.why: Blocking the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter stops K⁺ recycling into the lumen, so the +7 mV that pushes Ca²⁺ between the cells is lost and Ca²⁺ stays in the urine.

qs.q: In which segment is Ca²⁺ reabsorption uncoupled from Na⁺ and controlled by PTH?
qs.why: In the proximal tubule and TAL, Ca²⁺ follows Na⁺; in the distal tubule it is regulated separately, by PTH.

qs.q: How do thiazides and loop diuretics change urine Ca²⁺?
opts: Thiazides lower it; loop diuretics raise it
Thiazides raise it; loop diuretics lower it
qs.why: Thiazides increase distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, so they keep Ca²⁺; loop diuretics remove the TAL voltage, so they lose Ca²⁺.

qs.q: Why does a thiazide increase Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule?
opts: Lower cell Na⁺ speeds the basolateral Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger
qs.why: Blocking the Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter lowers cell Na⁺, so the Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger pushes more Ca²⁺ out to the blood and more enters from the lumen.

qs.q: What are PTH's net renal effects on blood Ca²⁺ and blood phosphate?
qs.why: PTH blocks proximal phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia) and increases distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, so blood Ca²⁺ rises and phosphate falls.

qs.q: Which segment reabsorbs the largest share of filtered Mg²⁺?
qs.why: The TAL takes about 60% of filtered Mg²⁺; unlike Na⁺ and Ca²⁺, the proximal tubule takes only about 30%.

qs.q: What is the main driving force for Mg²⁺ reabsorption?
opts: Na⁺–Mg²⁺ cotransport in the proximal tubule
qs.why: K⁺ leaking back into the TAL lumen makes the lumen positive compared with the blood, and that voltage pushes Mg²⁺ between the cells into the blood. Loop diuretics remove it and waste Mg²⁺.

qs.q: Why does hypokalemia often not correct until low Mg²⁺ is replaced?
opts: Distal K⁺ channels stay open and secrete K⁺
qs.why: Inside late distal tubule and collecting duct cells, Mg²⁺ plugs the K⁺ secretory channels; without it they stay open and K⁺ is wasted in urine.

qs.q: Why can severe Mg²⁺ deficiency cause low blood Ca²⁺?
opts: Low Mg²⁺ increases Ca²⁺ binding to albumin
Low Mg²⁺ speeds Ca²⁺ uptake into bone
The parathyroid glands need Mg²⁺ to release PTH
qs.why: Without Mg²⁺, PTH release falls and tissues respond poorly to PTH, so Ca²⁺ drops and won't correct until Mg²⁺ is given.

lectures.title: Water Balance, ADH & Disorders of ADH

slides.note: Osmolarity is the concentration of all dissolved particles that pull water, in mOsm/L (milliosmoles per liter). Normal plasma is about 290, rounded to 300 mOsm/L for easy math. Na⁺ and the anions that travel with it supply most of it. The body guards this number closely because water crosses cell membranes freely. If plasma osmolarity drifts, water rushes into or out of cells, and brain cells swell or shrink. The kidney's tool is water: it changes how much water it keeps, not how much salt, to hold osmolarity steady.

Plasma stays fixed near 300, but urine can range from 50 (very dilute) to 1,200 mOsm/L (very concentrated, 4 times plasma). That wide urine range is what lets plasma stay constant. Hyposmotic urine (below 300) means the kidney is getting rid of extra water. Hyperosmotic urine (above 300) means it is saving water. Urine equal to plasma is isosmotic. The 1,200 ceiling is the osmolarity deep in the medulla. The 50 floor comes from nephron segments that remove salt without water (later slides).

Graph: x-axis = minutes after drinking 1 L; y-axis = urine flow (mL/min). Water (black): it dilutes the plasma, so osmolarity falls → the hypothalamus shuts off ADH (antidiuretic hormone) → the collecting ducts stop reabsorbing water → urine flow jumps from about 1 to 15 mL/min, peaks at about an hour, and stops once the extra water is gone. Saline (blue, isotonic salt water): it adds volume but does not change osmolarity, so ADH stays on and urine barely rises. Salty pretzels with a sports drink work the same way: the salt keeps osmolarity up, so ADH stays on and the water is kept.

Step by step. Water keeps leaving in sweat and breath, so plasma osmolarity rises. Osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus sense a rise of about 1% and do two things: they trigger thirst, and they make the posterior pituitary release ADH. ADH acts on the principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct and makes them permeable to water. Water leaves the urine and returns to the blood, so urine becomes small in volume and concentrated, and plasma osmolarity falls back to normal (negative feedback). In the drawing, SON = supraoptic nucleus, where ADH is made. ETOH (alcohol) blocks ADH release, which is why drinking alcohol makes you urinate.

The mirror image of water deprivation. Extra water dilutes the plasma, so the osmoreceptors are inhibited: thirst stops and ADH release stops. Without ADH the late distal tubule and collecting duct are impermeable to water. The water that reaches them is not reabsorbed and leaves as a large volume of dilute urine (as low as about 50 mOsm/L). Because more water than salt is lost, plasma osmolarity rises back toward normal. The cartoon's '260' is a plasma osmolarity well below normal, a level at which ADH should be fully off.

The whole loop in one picture. ADH is made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary into the blood, and carried to the kidney. At the collecting duct, ADH (green dots) arrives from the peritubular capillary side and opens water channels in the duct wall. Water then moves out of the duct by osmosis, into the peritubular capillaries and back into the circulation. Less water is left in the urine.

ADH is made in the hypothalamus, not in the pituitary. Left column: a hypothalamic neuron makes ADH (pink circles) in its cell body. ADH travels down the axon into the posterior lobe of the pituitary. The nerve ending releases it into the blood, which carries it to its target (the kidney). Right column, a different system: other hypothalamic neurons release releasing hormones (yellow circles, e.g., TRH = thyrotropin-releasing hormone) into the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels. These carry them to the anterior lobe, whose own gland cells then make hormones (blue triangles, e.g., TSH = thyroid-stimulating hormone). Don't confuse them: posterior pituitary = nerve endings that release hypothalamic hormones (ADH, oxytocin); anterior pituitary = gland cells controlled by portal blood.

Follow the dots: blue = vasopressin (ADH), red = oxytocin. (1) Neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus make the hormones. (2) The hormones travel down the axons through the hypothalamic–posterior pituitary stalk. (3) The nerve endings in the posterior pituitary release them into the systemic blood when the neurons fire. ADH comes mainly from the supraoptic nucleus; oxytocin comes mainly from the paraventricular nucleus.

Correction: the two labels are swapped. The supraoptic nucleus mainly makes ADH, and the paraventricular nucleus mainly makes oxytocin (each makes some of both). The rest of the picture is right. The hormones travel down the axons through the infundibulum (pituitary stalk). Axon terminals release them into the capillary bed of the posterior pituitary, and the blood carries them out through the vein.

Water balance = water in versus water out. Intake is controlled by thirst, which the same hypothalamic osmoreceptors switch on when plasma osmolarity rises. Output is controlled mainly by ADH acting on the kidney. When the two match, plasma osmolarity stays near 300. ADH responds first: it starts rising at about 280. Thirst starts a little higher (about 290) and backs it up. The kidney can only slow further water loss; only drinking can replace water that is already gone.

This is the corticopapillary osmotic gradient: the fluid between the tubules (the interstitium) gets saltier the deeper you go. It is about 300 mOsm/L in the cortex and rises to about 1,200 at the papilla (the inner tip of the medulla). The loops of Henle and the collecting ducts dip down into this gradient. The collecting duct passes through it last. With ADH, water leaves the duct until the urine matches the surrounding fluid, so urine can reach 1,200. The next slides show how the loop builds the gradient.

Gold numbers = interstitium; blue numbers = fluid inside the tubes. Descending limb: only water leaves. It moves out into the salty interstitium, so the fluid concentrates on the way down (400 → 1,200). Ascending limb: NaCl leaves (pumped out in the thick part, leaking out passively in the thin part near the bend), but water cannot follow, so the fluid dilutes on the way up (1,200 → 200). That pumped salt keeps the interstitium salty. Collecting tubule (right): with ADH, it loses water at each level until it matches the interstitium, so the urine leaves at 1,200. Correction: the key's 'active water absorption' is wrong. Water is never pumped; it always moves passively by osmosis, here through water channels that ADH inserts.

Left: the nephron. Right (b): the vasa recta (blood vessels of the medulla). Follow the numbers. Proximal tubule: fluid stays at 300 (isosmotic). Descending limb (blue arrows = passive): only water leaves, so the fluid rises to 1,200 at the bend. Ascending limb (red arrows = active): NaCl is pumped out without water, so the fluid falls to 100 by the time it returns to the cortex. Here the collecting duct stays at 100 all the way down. That is the no-ADH state: the duct is water-tight, so the urine leaves dilute. With ADH it would lose water and reach 1,200. Vasa recta: blood going down gains NaCl and loses water; going up it does the reverse. It leaves at about 300, so it carries off reabsorbed water without washing out the gradient.

Correction: at site 5, urea does not leave the thin ascending limb. Urea moves the other way, from the interstitium into the thin limbs (urea recycling); only NaCl leaves at 5. The numbered sites: (1) The TAL (thick ascending limb) takes NaCl out of the tubule fluid with the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) and deposits it in the interstitium. This is the only active step and the engine of the whole gradient. Loop diuretics such as furosemide block it, so the kidney can no longer concentrate urine. (2) Water leaves the cortical collecting duct (with ADH). Urea cannot leave here, so it becomes more concentrated inside the duct. (3) In the inner medulla, urea diffuses out of the collecting duct and adds to the gradient. (4) Water leaves the thin descending limb, pulled out by the salty interstitium. (5) NaCl leaks passively out of the thin ascending limb.

Countercurrent multiplication (right panel, A–F). A: the loop fills with 300 fluid. B, pump: the TAL moves NaCl out of the ascending limb. This makes a 200 mOsm difference at each level (ascending 200; descending limb and interstitium 400). This step is called the single effect. C, flow: new 300 fluid enters and pushes the 400 fluid down to the bend and around. D–F: pump, flow, pump again. With each cycle the bend gets saltier (400 → 500 → 600) and the fluid leaving the top gets more dilute. Repeated many times, a 200 step 'multiplies' into a 1,200 gradient. Overall the TAL reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na⁺, and the more NaCl reaches it, the more it reabsorbs.

The four transport steps, by number. (1) Active (red): the TAL pumps Na⁺ and Cl⁻ into the interstitium. (2) Diffusion (green): that NaCl spreads through the interstitium toward the descending limb, raising the osmolarity around it. (3) Osmosis (blue): water leaves the descending limb because the interstitium is now saltier, so the descending fluid concentrates (300 → 1,200). (4) Diffusion (green): in the thin ascending limb, NaCl leaks out passively, down its concentration gradient. Memory line: salt leaves the ascending limb, water leaves the descending limb. No salt leaves the descending limb, and no water leaves the ascending limb.

The same multiplication, step by step, with osmolarities in mOsm/L. Each U has three columns: descending limb (left), interstitial fluid (middle) and ascending limb (right; heavy outline = water-tight). Initial state: everything is 300. 1, single effect: the thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out of its fluid into the interstitium. The ascending limb drops to 200, the interstitium rises to 400, and the descending limb matches the interstitium (400). That is a 200 difference at each level. 2, flow of fluid: fresh 300 fluid enters the descending limb (down arrow) and pushes the 400 fluid down and around the bend (up arrow). 3, single effect again: the bottom rises to 500, while the top of the ascending limb falls to 150. 4, flow again. Each repeat makes the bottom saltier and the top more dilute. With enough repeats the bend reaches about 1,200.

Three drawings. Top right (loop of Henle): the descending limb loses water (H₂O arrow out). The ascending limb pumps NaCl out, and water cannot follow (the curved H₂O arrow bounces back because the wall is water-tight). Top left (labeled countercurrent exchange, the vasa recta idea): solute moves from the up-flowing side to the down-flowing side, so it is trapped deep in the medulla. Flow in opposite directions is what 'countercurrent' means. Bottom: the result. Fluid in the loop and in the CD (collecting duct) gets more concentrated toward the bottom. Don't confuse: countercurrent multiplication = active, done by the loop, builds the gradient; countercurrent exchange = passive, done by the vasa recta, preserves it.

Urea supplies up to about half of the inner-medulla osmolarity. Read down the collecting duct (far right). Cortex and outer medulla: ADH opens water channels (AQP2, AQP3 = aquaporins), but this part of the duct has no urea channels. Water leaves and urea stays, so the urea concentration inside the duct climbs. Inner medulla ('Urea comes IN here' = urea is reabsorbed, out of the duct into the body): ADH also turns on UT-A1 and UT-A3 (urea transporters), so the now very concentrated urea diffuses out into the interstitium. Some of it re-enters the thin limbs (UT-A2) and the descending vasa recta (UT-B) and circles back: this is urea recycling. Other labels: AQP1 = water channel of the descending limb; NKCC2 = Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter; ROMK1 = K⁺ channel; ClC-K1 = Cl⁻ channel.

Along the collecting duct, urea transporters exist only in the inner medullary part, so only there does ADH increase urea reabsorption (along with water). In the cortex and outer medulla, ADH raises only water permeability. That split is the point. Removing water first concentrates the urea; letting it leave the duct deep in the medulla then deposits it in the interstitium where the gradient must be highest. ADH strengthens the gradient in two ways: more urea recycling and more NaCl transport in the TAL. When ADH is low (water drinking, central diabetes insipidus), the gradient gets smaller.

Dialysis works by diffusion across a semipermeable membrane. Small molecules such as urea pass through the membrane's pores and move from where they are concentrated (the blood) to where they are not (the bath). Large molecules such as proteins, and blood cells, cannot pass, so they stay in the blood. In Kolff's first test, all the urea had left the sausage casings within about five minutes. Modern hemodialysis uses the same principle. Fresh dialysate (cleaning fluid) keeps flowing past the membrane, so the gradient for urea and K⁺ stays high.

Correction: the loop (thick ascending limb) reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na⁺ and about 20% of filtered K⁺; the Na⁺ and K⁺ values above are swapped. The Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ values above are a little high: the usual figures are about 25% of filtered Ca²⁺ and about 60% of filtered Mg²⁺. Why it matters: the loop is the main site for Mg²⁺, while the proximal tubule reabsorbs the largest share of the others. Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ pass between the cells, pushed by the lumen-positive voltage (lumen positive compared with the blood side) that the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter creates. So loop diuretics (furosemide) increase the loss of Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in the urine.

The vasa recta ('straight vessels') are long hairpin capillaries. They come off the efferent arterioles of the deep (juxtamedullary) nephrons and run down beside the loops into the medulla. Only about 5% of renal blood flow goes to the medulla, and it flows slowly. That is useful: fast flow would carry away the salt and urea and wash out the gradient. Their job is to pick up the water and solute reabsorbed in the medulla (from the descending limb and collecting duct) and return it to the circulation, while leaving the gradient in place.

Countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta (the hairpin capillaries of the medulla). Thick light-blue arrows = blood flow: in at the left, out at the right. The middle is the interstitial fluid, which gets saltier with depth (300 → 600 → 1,200). Solid dark-blue arrows = solute (NaCl and urea); dashed green arrows = water. Blood enters the descending side at 300 mOsm/L. On the way down it meets saltier and saltier interstitium, so solute diffuses in and water diffuses out. At the bend it is 1,200. On the way up the reverse happens: solute diffuses out and water diffuses in. Blood leaves at only about 325, a little above where it started. So the blood carries off the reabsorbed water and only a little solute, and the gradient survives. All of this is passive diffusion; the vessels have no pumps.

Three tubes side by side. Left (descending limb): the filtrate loses water and concentrates from 300 to 1,200. Middle (vasa recta): blood enters at 300, matches the interstitium on the way down and back up, and leaves at about 300. Right (ascending limb): Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ are pumped out but water cannot follow, so the filtrate leaves the loop hyposmotic (100). Key point: the water that leaves the descending limb moves into the vasa recta and is carried away in the blood. If it stayed in the interstitium, it would dilute the gradient.

ADH and vasopressin are the same hormone (AVP, arginine vasopressin). The two names come from its two jobs. Triggers: hypothalamic osmoreceptors respond to about a 1% rise in osmolarity, so osmolarity is the everyday control. Baroreceptors (stretch sensors in the atria and large arteries) respond only after about a 10% fall in blood volume or pressure, but then they drive ADH very high. Receptors: V2 on the principal cells of the collecting duct raises cAMP and inserts water channels, so water is kept ('antidiuretic'). V1 on vascular smooth muscle raises cell Ca²⁺ and constricts arterioles, so blood pressure rises ('vasopressin').

With ADH high, follow the numbers (mOsm/L) around the nephron. The proximal tubule stays at 300: it reabsorbs water (big arrow, top left) but only in step with solute. The descending limb concentrates to 1,200 at the bend. The thick ascending limb and early distal tubule (heavy outline = water-tight) remove salt without water, so the fluid falls to 100, then 80. In the late distal tubule and collecting duct, ADH opens water channels. Water leaves at every level (arrows out) into the saltier interstitium, and the fluid rises with its surroundings: 300 in the cortex, 600 in the medulla, 1,200 at the papilla tip. 'Increased water permeability' means the water goes back into the body: urine volume falls and water is retained. In the inner medulla, ADH also lets urea leave the collecting duct into the interstitium.

Principal cells line the late distal tubule and collecting duct. They carry the V2 receptors, so they are where ADH acts. With ADH they become water-permeable, and the salty medulla pulls water out of the urine by osmosis (back 'in' to the body). In the inner medullary duct, urea also leaves the duct (it 'comes in' to the body) and stays in the interstitium, which keeps the gradient high. 'Hypertonic out here' points to the bend of the loop, where tubular fluid and interstitium are most concentrated (about 1,200). The result is a small volume of concentrated urine.

Correction: the three H₂O arrows at the bottom right point into the loop, but water never enters the loop. Water only leaves the descending limb, into the salty interstitium, and the ascending limb lets no water through. Read the rest as one tube. Fluid enters at 290 (top left), runs down the descending limb (outer channel), and reaches 1,000 at the bend. It then rises in the inner channel, the ascending limb (thick black wall = impermeable to water). Active pumps move NaCl out of it, into the descending side and the interstitium, while water stays behind. So the fluid leaves the loop very dilute (50). In the distal segment at top right, ADH lets water leave until the fluid matches the cortex (290).

ADH's action inside a principal cell of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, by number. The lumen (urine side) is on the left; the blood side is on the right. (1) ADH from the blood binds R, the V2 receptor on the basolateral (blood-side) membrane. (2) Through Gs (a stimulatory G protein), the receptor switches on AC (adenylyl cyclase), which converts ATP to cAMP (cyclic AMP). (3) cAMP activates protein kinase A. (4) Protein kinase A phosphorylates the proteins that move vesicles. (5) Vesicles holding AQP2 (aquaporin-2, the ADH-controlled water channel) move toward the lumen. (6) They fuse with the luminal membrane, so AQP2 channels now sit in the urine-side wall. Water then flows from the urine through AQP2 into the cell and out the blood side. If ADH stays high, cAMP also makes the cell build more AQP2. When ADH falls, the channels are pulled back into vesicles.

The same nephron with ADH off (a) and on (b). The loops look the same: the descending limb loses water and the ascending limb pumps NaCl out, so the fluid reaching the DCT (distal convoluted tubule) is dilute either way. The difference is the collecting duct. (a) No ADH: the duct wall is water-tight (no H₂O arrows leave it), so water stays in. Result: a large volume of dilute urine. (b) ADH present: water leaves at every level, drawn out by the salty medulla. Result: a small volume of concentrated urine. So ADH decides urine concentration only at the last step.

Why urine ranges from 50 to 1,200. Maximum: with ADH, collecting-duct fluid can only come to equal its surroundings, so the most concentrated urine equals the osmolarity at the loop tip and papilla (about 1,200). Minimum: the TAL and early distal tubule remove salt without water (the diluting segments), so the fluid reaching the late distal tubule is about 50–100 whether or not ADH is present. Without ADH, nothing concentrates it again, so urine leaves at 50–100. With ADH, it climbs to 1,200. Anything that disables the TAL (loop diuretics) limits both ends: the kidney can neither dilute nor concentrate well.

The same chain as the previous cell diagram, drawn more simply. (1) ADH reaches its receptor (red box, V2) on the blood side of a collecting duct cell. (2) The receptor switches on adenylyl cyclase, which turns ATP into cAMP. (3) cAMP activates protein kinase A. (4) The kinase sends water channels (aquaporin-2) to the urine-side membrane. (5) Water flows from the urine into the cell through those channels. (6) Water leaves the cell on the blood side, into the medullary interstitium and blood. Urea too: in the inner medullary collecting duct, ADH also turns on urea transporters, so urea follows the same route, from the urine into the interstitium.

SIADH = syndrome of inappropriate ADH. ADH is released without an osmotic stimulus, so it keeps acting even when the plasma is already dilute. Step by step: the collecting ducts keep reabsorbing water → body water rises → plasma Na⁺ and osmolarity fall (hyponatremia) → the urine stays inappropriately concentrated. Causes: brain (head injury, stroke, meningitis); lung disease (pneumonia); drugs (e.g., carbamazepine, SSRIs, cyclophosphamide); cancer, classically small-cell lung cancer, which makes ADH itself. Treatment: restrict water; demeclocycline blocks ADH's action on the principal cells.

Two graphs, two triggers. Top: x-axis = plasma osmolarity; y-axis = plasma ADH (pg/mL, picograms per milliliter). ADH is near zero below about 280, then rises steeply in a straight line. A few mOsm make a big change, so osmolarity is the sensitive everyday control. Thirst starts a bit higher (arrow). Bottom: x-axis = % of blood volume lost. ADH changes little until about 10% is lost, then rises steeply to about 40 pg/mL, far above anything osmolarity produces. So volume loss is the less sensitive but more powerful trigger. A large volume loss drives ADH up even when the plasma is dilute.

x-axis = plasma osmolality; y-axis = plasma ADH. Point a (about 280) is where ADH secretion starts. Point b (about 290) is where thirst starts. Normal plasma (about 285) gives an ADH of about 4 pg/mL. Below 280, ADH should be zero. So measurable ADH with plasma osmolality under 280 is inappropriate: that is SIADH, unless low blood volume explains it. Lab pattern: low serum Na⁺ and osmolality, high urine osmolality, high urine Na⁺. Urine Na⁺ is high because the retained water expands volume a little. That lowers aldosterone and raises ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide), so Na⁺ is excreted.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) = the kidney cannot concentrate urine because ADH is missing or does not work. 'Insipidus' (tasteless) contrasts with diabetes mellitus (sweet, glucose-filled urine); both cause large urine volumes and thirst. Central DI: the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary releases too little ADH. Nephrogenic DI: ADH is released (even more than normal), but the principal cells do not respond, e.g., because of a defect in the V2 receptor, Gs or adenylyl cyclase. To tell them apart, give desmopressin (dDAVP, a synthetic ADH). In central DI the urine becomes concentrated; in nephrogenic DI nothing changes.

x-axis = plasma osmolarity; y-axis = plasma ADH; gray zone = thirst. In DI, water loss pushes plasma osmolarity above 300. On the normal curve, ADH should then be very high. Use that to read a measured ADH level. Low ADH with high plasma osmolarity means the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary are not releasing ADH: central DI. High ADH with high osmolarity, but the urine is still dilute, means the kidney cannot respond: nephrogenic DI.

Central DI: the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary is damaged, so no ADH is released. Causes: head trauma, a pituitary or brain tumor (or surgery), brain hypoxia. Without ADH, the late distal tubule and collecting duct stay water-tight. The patient makes huge volumes of dilute urine (often more than 10 L a day) and must drink the same amount to keep up. If the patient cannot drink (unconscious, no access to water), free water keeps pouring out and serum Na⁺ climbs. The resulting hypernatremia shrinks brain cells and can kill. Treatment: desmopressin (dDAVP), an ADH analog that acts on V2 receptors.

Why these results. In DI the collecting duct cannot reabsorb water, so large amounts of pure water are lost. The salt stays behind, so serum Na⁺ and osmolarity rise. The urine is mostly water. Urine osmolarity is low (below plasma, often under 100–200), and urine Na⁺ concentration is low because the salt is diluted in a large volume. Key pattern: high serum osmolarity with dilute urine is never normal, because a healthy kidney would make concentrated urine. SIADH is the exact opposite: low serum osmolarity with concentrated urine.

Nephrogenic DI: ADH is present (high), but the principal cells do not respond. Causes: hypercalcemia and hypokalemia (both reduce aquaporin-2 and the duct's response to ADH); chronic kidney disease (damaged medulla and gradient); lithium (the classic drug cause); inherited V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 defects. Desmopressin does not help, because the problem is the response, not the hormone. Thiazides reduce urine volume in two ways. (1) They block NaCl reabsorption in the early distal tubule, a diluting segment, so the urine is less dilute. (2) They shrink the ECF (extracellular fluid) volume, so GFR (glomerular filtration rate) falls and the proximal tubule reabsorbs more water. Less water reaches the collecting duct.

In words: plasma osmolarity ≈ 2 × sodium + BUN ÷ 2.8 + glucose ÷ 18. Na⁺ (in mEq/L) is doubled because each Na⁺ travels with an anion (Cl⁻ or HCO₃⁻). BUN (blood urea nitrogen) and glucose are reported in mg/dL; dividing by 2.8 and by 18 converts them to mOsm/L. Example: Na⁺ 140, BUN 14, glucose 90 → 280 + 5 + 5 = 290 mOsm/L. Sodium dominates, so serum Na⁺ is a quick stand-in for osmolarity, unless glucose (uncontrolled diabetes) or BUN (kidney failure) is very high.

Use the formula at the top to decide whether the serum is dilute. If serum osmolarity is low, a healthy body shuts off ADH and gets rid of water, so urine osmolarity should be low (dilute, under about 100). It also holds on to Na⁺, so urine Na⁺ should be low. In SIADH both are high. ADH keeps the urine concentrated, and the slight volume expansion turns off aldosterone and turns on ANP, so Na⁺ is lost in the urine. Example: serum Na⁺ 120 with urine osmolarity 500 and urine Na⁺ 60 → SIADH.

Na⁺ problems show up in the brain, because Na⁺ sets ECF osmolarity and water follows osmolarity across cell membranes. Low Na⁺ (hyponatremia, e.g., SIADH): the ECF is dilute, so water moves into brain cells and they swell (cerebral edema). High Na⁺ (hypernatremia, e.g., DI without water): water moves out of brain cells and they shrink. Both give the same progression: confusion → disorientation → lethargy → obtundation (reduced alertness) → stupor → coma, often with seizures. Fast changes are worse than slow ones, because brain cells need time to adjust.

Free water = pure water with no solute. Free-water clearance asks: compared with urine that matches plasma, how much extra pure water is the kidney getting rid of, or keeping? Compare Uosm (urine osmolarity) with Sosm (serum osmolarity). Uosm < Sosm: the urine carries extra pure water, so free water is being cleared (positive value), as in water drinking and both types of DI. Uosm > Sosm: pure water is being kept in the body (negative value), as in dehydration and SIADH. Uosm = Sosm: zero.

The equations in words. Osmolar clearance (Cosm) = urine flow × urine osmolarity ÷ plasma osmolarity: the volume of plasma cleared of all solutes per minute. Free-water clearance (CH₂O) = urine flow − Cosm. In symbols: Cosm = (U̇ × OSMu) ÷ OSMp, and CH₂O = U̇ − Cosm. U̇ (U with a dot) = urine flow rate (mL/min); OSMu = urine osmolarity; OSMp = plasma osmolarity. Example: urine flow 10 mL/min, urine osmolarity 100, plasma 290. Cosm = 10 × 100 ÷ 290 = 3.45 mL/min. CH₂O = 10 − 3.45 = +6.55 mL/min. Meaning: 3.45 mL of each minute's urine carries all the solute at plasma strength, and the other 6.55 mL is pure water added on top. Positive = low ADH (water drinking or DI).

The same formula in one line. In words: free-water clearance = urine flow − (urine osmolarity ÷ plasma osmolarity) × urine flow. In symbols: CH₂O = V − (Uosm ÷ Posm) × V, which equals V × (1 − Uosm ÷ Posm). CH₂O = free-water clearance; V = urine flow rate (mL/min); Uosm = urine osmolarity; Posm = plasma osmolarity. Example of concentrated urine: V = 1 mL/min, Uosm 1,200, Posm 300. CH₂O = 1 × (1 − 4) = −3 mL/min. Negative means 3 mL of pure water per minute is being returned to the body (high ADH: dehydration or SIADH). The 3 mL/min of pure water kept is called free-water reabsorption. CH₂O is near zero when the urine is isosmotic, as with loop diuretics: with the TAL disabled, the kidney can neither dilute nor concentrate.

qs.q: What range of urine osmolarity can the kidney produce?
qs.why: Urine can be as dilute as about 50 or as concentrated as about 1,200 mOsm/L, which is what lets plasma stay fixed near 300.

qs.q: Why does drinking 1 L of water raise urine flow far more than 1 L of isotonic saline?
opts: Saline lowers GFR more than water
Water lowers plasma osmolarity, so ADH shuts off
Saline raises plasma osmolarity, so ADH rises
Water expands blood volume more than saline
qs.why: Water dilutes the plasma, so ADH stops and the collecting ducts stop reabsorbing water. Isotonic saline adds volume without changing osmolarity, so ADH stays on.

qs.q: Where are the osmoreceptors that trigger ADH release and thirst?
qs.why: Osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus sense about a 1% rise in plasma osmolarity, trigger thirst, and make the posterior pituitary release ADH.

qs.q: Why does drinking alcohol increase urine output?
opts: It blocks V2 receptors in the collecting duct
qs.why: Ethanol blocks ADH release, so the collecting ducts stay water-tight and more dilute urine is made.

qs.q: Where is ADH made?
qs.why: Hypothalamic neurons make ADH; the posterior pituitary only stores it in their nerve endings and releases it into the blood.

qs.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus mainly makes ADH?
qs.why: The supraoptic nucleus mainly makes ADH and the paraventricular nucleus mainly makes oxytocin (each makes some of both).

qs.q: How does ADH get from its site of synthesis to the posterior pituitary?
opts: Down axons through the pituitary stalk
qs.why: ADH travels down the axons to nerve endings in the posterior pituitary. Portal vessels carry releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary.

qs.q: As plasma osmolarity rises, at about what levels do ADH release and thirst begin?
opts: ADH at about 260; thirst at about 300
Thirst at about 280; ADH at about 290
ADH at about 280; thirst at about 290
qs.why: ADH responds first, starting near 280 mOsm/L; thirst starts a little higher, near 290, and backs it up.

qs.q: What leaves the thin descending limb as its fluid becomes more concentrated?
qs.why: Water leaves by osmosis into the salty interstitium, so the fluid concentrates on the way down (to about 1,200). Salt leaves only from the ascending limb.

qs.q: Compared with plasma, fluid leaving the ascending limb is:
qs.why: The ascending limb pumps NaCl out but lets no water follow, so its fluid is diluted on the way up.

qs.q: Which transport step is the active engine of the medullary osmotic gradient?
opts: Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransport in the early distal tubule
Urea transporters in the inner medulla
qs.why: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb is the only active step; furosemide blocks it, so the kidney can no longer concentrate urine.

qs.q: How does water leave the collecting duct when ADH is present?
opts: Passively by osmosis through water channels
Actively, pumped by a water ATPase
qs.why: Water is never pumped; it moves by osmosis through the water channels ADH inserts, drawn out by the salty interstitium.

qs.q: In countercurrent multiplication, what osmotic difference does the TAL pump create between the limbs at each level?
qs.why: This 200 mOsm 'single effect', repeated with each cycle of pumping and flow, multiplies into the 1,200 mOsm/L gradient.

qs.q: How does NaCl leave the thin ascending limb?
qs.why: In the thin ascending limb NaCl leaks out passively, down its concentration gradient; the active pumping happens in the thick ascending limb.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly describes countercurrent multiplication and countercurrent exchange?
opts: Loop builds the gradient; vasa recta preserve it
Loop builds the gradient; collecting duct preserves it
Collecting duct builds the gradient; loop preserves it
Vasa recta build the gradient; loop preserves it
qs.why: Multiplication is active and done by the loop of Henle; exchange is passive and done by the vasa recta, which keep the gradient from washing out.

qs.q: In which part of the collecting duct does ADH increase urea reabsorption?
qs.why: Urea transporters (UT-A1, UT-A3) exist only in the inner medullary collecting duct; in the cortex and outer medulla ADH raises only water permeability.

qs.q: With ADH, why does urea concentration rise inside the cortical and outer medullary collecting duct?
opts: Duct cells secrete urea into the lumen
Urea diffuses in from the interstitium
Water leaves while urea stays behind
qs.why: That part of the duct has water channels but no urea channels, so removing water concentrates the urea, which then leaves in the inner medulla.

qs.q: Dialysis clears urea from blood mainly by what process?
opts: Osmosis of water into the blood
Binding to proteins in the dialysate
qs.why: Small molecules like urea pass the membrane pores down their concentration gradient into the dialysate; proteins and blood cells are too large to pass.

qs.q: About what fraction of filtered Na⁺ does the thick ascending limb reabsorb?
qs.why: The loop takes about 25% of filtered Na⁺ (and about 20% of K⁺); the proximal tubule takes about 67%.

qs.q: For which ion is the loop of Henle the main reabsorption site?
qs.why: The loop reabsorbs about 60% of filtered Mg²⁺; for Na⁺, Ca²⁺ and K⁺ the proximal tubule takes the largest share.

qs.q: Why is it useful that only about 5% of renal blood flow, flowing slowly, reaches the medulla?
opts: Fast flow would wash out the medullary gradient
Slow flow concentrates plasma proteins for filtration
Slow flow lets the vasa recta pump NaCl
Slow flow raises medullary oxygen delivery
qs.why: Fast flow would carry away the salt and urea that make up the gradient. The vasa recta have no pumps; their exchange is passive.

qs.q: Blood entering the descending vasa recta at 300 mOsm/L leaves the ascending vasa recta at about what osmolarity?
qs.why: Blood gains solute and loses water going down, then reverses going up, so it leaves only slightly above where it started, carrying off reabsorbed water without the gradient.

qs.q: Which ADH receptor on collecting duct cells raises cAMP and inserts water channels?
qs.why: V2 on principal cells retains water (the antidiuretic action); V1 on vascular smooth muscle constricts arterioles (the vasopressin action).

qs.q: ADH release responds to about a 1% change in what?
qs.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors react to about a 1% rise in osmolarity; baroreceptors need about a 10% fall in volume or pressure.

qs.q: Which collecting duct cells are the main site of ADH action?
qs.why: Principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct carry the V2 receptors and become water-permeable with ADH.

qs.q: With ADH present, final urine osmolarity equals what?
opts: Osmolarity of fluid leaving the ascending limb
Interstitial osmolarity at the papilla tip
qs.why: Water leaves the duct at every level until the urine matches its surroundings, so it ends equal to the deepest medulla, about 1,200 mOsm/L.

qs.q: After ADH binds its V2 receptor, which signal moves water channels to the luminal membrane?
qs.why: V2 → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A, which drives aquaporin vesicles to fuse with the luminal membrane.

qs.q: Which water channel does ADH insert into the luminal membrane of principal cells?
qs.why: Aquaporin-2 waits in vesicles and fuses with the luminal membrane when ADH acts; it is pulled back when ADH falls.

qs.q: Why is fluid reaching the late distal tubule dilute (50–100 mOsm/L) whether or not ADH is present?
opts: The proximal tubule removes salt without water
The collecting duct removes salt without water
The descending limb removes salt without water
The TAL and early distal tubule remove salt without water
qs.why: The TAL and early distal tubule are the diluting segments: they reabsorb NaCl but are water-tight, before ADH's site of action.

qs.q: How does a loop diuretic affect the kidney's ability to dilute and concentrate urine?
qs.why: The TAL is both a diluting segment and the engine of the medullary gradient, so disabling it limits both the minimum and the maximum urine osmolarity.

qs.q: SIADH produces which pattern?
opts: Low plasma Na⁺, low urine osmolality
High plasma Na⁺, low urine osmolality
Low plasma Na⁺, high urine osmolality
High plasma Na⁺, high urine osmolality
qs.why: ADH keeps reabsorbing water despite dilute plasma, so plasma Na⁺ falls while the urine stays inappropriately concentrated.

qs.q: Which cancer classically makes ADH itself, causing SIADH?
qs.why: Small-cell lung cancer secretes ADH ectopically.

qs.q: Why is urine Na⁺ high in SIADH?
opts: Low plasma Na⁺ raises the filtered Na⁺ load
ADH directly blocks distal Na⁺ reabsorption
Mild volume expansion lowers aldosterone and raises ANP
qs.why: The retained water expands volume a little, which turns aldosterone down and ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) up, so Na⁺ is excreted.

qs.q: Which stimulus can appropriately drive ADH high even when plasma is dilute?
qs.why: Volume loss beyond about 10% drives ADH far higher than osmolarity does, overriding low osmolarity. Measurable ADH below 280 is SIADH only if low volume doesn't explain it.

qs.q: How does a desmopressin (dDAVP) test separate central from nephrogenic DI?
opts: Urine concentrates only in central DI
Urine concentrates only in nephrogenic DI
qs.why: Central DI lacks ADH, so replacing it works; in nephrogenic DI the principal cells can't respond, so nothing changes.

qs.q: In diabetes insipidus, what are serum Na⁺ and urine osmolarity?
opts: Serum Na⁺ high, urine osmolarity high
Serum Na⁺ low, urine osmolarity low
Serum Na⁺ low, urine osmolarity high
Serum Na⁺ high, urine osmolarity low
qs.why: Pure water is lost and salt stays behind, so serum Na⁺ rises while the urine is dilute. SIADH is the opposite pattern.

qs.q: Which electrolyte disorders cause nephrogenic DI?
qs.why: High Ca²⁺ and low K⁺ both reduce aquaporin-2 and the collecting duct's response to ADH.

qs.q: Which drug reduces urine volume in nephrogenic DI?
qs.why: Thiazides block NaCl reabsorption in the early distal diluting segment and shrink ECF volume, so the proximal tubule reabsorbs more water. Desmopressin fails because the kidney can't respond to ADH.

qs.q: How is plasma osmolarity estimated (Na⁺ in mEq/L; BUN and glucose in mg/dL)?
qs.why: Na⁺ is doubled because each Na⁺ travels with an anion; dividing BUN by 2.8 and glucose by 18 converts mg/dL to mOsm/L.

qs.q: When serum osmolarity is low, what should a normal kidney's urine look like?
qs.why: ADH should shut off, so urine is dilute, and the body holds on to Na⁺. In SIADH both urine osmolarity and urine Na⁺ are high.

qs.q: Why does severe hyponatremia cause confusion, stupor and coma?
opts: Na⁺ floods into neurons and depolarizes them
Water moves into brain cells and they swell
Water moves out of brain cells and they shrink
qs.why: A dilute ECF pulls water into brain cells (cerebral edema). Shrinking of brain cells is what happens in hypernatremia.

qs.q: Free-water clearance equals urine flow minus what?
qs.why: CH₂O = V − Cosm, where V = urine flow rate. Osmolar clearance Cosm = V × Uosm ÷ Posm (Uosm, Posm = urine and plasma osmolarity).

qs.q: In which condition is free-water clearance negative?
qs.why: Negative means urine osmolarity exceeds plasma, so pure water is being kept (high ADH). DI and water drinking give dilute urine and positive values.

qs.q: Why is free-water clearance near zero on a loop diuretic?
opts: Urine stays near isosmotic to plasma
qs.why: With the TAL disabled the kidney can neither dilute nor concentrate, so urine osmolarity stays close to plasma and CH₂O is about zero.

slides.note: Normal blood H⁺ concentration is only 40 nEq/L (40 × 10⁻⁹ equivalents per liter; nEq = nanoequivalent, one billionth of an equivalent). That is over a million times lower than Na⁺ (140 mEq/L), so even small amounts of added acid matter. Because such numbers are awkward, we use pH = −log[H⁺], the negative logarithm of the H⁺ concentration. An [H⁺] of 40 × 10⁻⁹ gives a pH of 7.40. In the cartoon, adding acid tips the needle toward 0 and adding base tips it toward 14.

Normal arterial pH is 7.40, just on the alkaline side of neutral (7.0). The normal range is narrow: 7.37–7.42. Below that range the blood is too acidic (acidemia); above it, too alkaline (alkalemia). Strictly, '-emia' describes the blood pH itself, and '-osis' (acidosis, alkalosis) describes the process that adds acid or base.

Enzymes and other proteins work only in a narrow pH range, so blood H⁺ is held almost constant. The pH range compatible with life is only about 6.8–8.0. Other body fluids are allowed very different pH: the stomach secretes HCl to reach pH 1–2, and the pancreas secretes HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) to reach pH 8 and neutralize that acid in the duodenum. Acid = gives away H⁺; base = takes up H⁺.

Strength means how completely an acid gives up its H⁺ in water. A strong acid such as HCl splits almost entirely into H⁺ + Cl⁻, so all its H⁺ is free at once. A weak acid such as carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) releases only part of its H⁺; most of it stays as the intact acid. Each acid's strength is summed up by one number, its pK (see the pK slide): the lower the pK, the stronger the acid.

For a base, strength means how eagerly it grabs H⁺. Hydroxide (OH⁻) grabs H⁺ almost completely to make water. Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) takes up H⁺ only partly and reversibly. That is why buffers are weak acids and bases: a weak acid and its base exist side by side, so the pair can soak up added H⁺ or release H⁺ when it is removed. A strong acid or base reacts all the way and can't swing back.

Because pH = −log[H⁺], pH moves opposite to H⁺ and on a log scale, so equal pH steps are not equal H⁺ steps. Worked example: pH 7.4 = 40 nEq/L of H⁺. pH 7.6 = 25 nEq/L, a drop of 15. pH 7.2 = 63 nEq/L, a rise of 23. So a 0.2-unit fall in pH adds more H⁺ (23 nEq/L) than a 0.2-unit rise removes (15 nEq/L). Arterial pH below 7.37 is acidemia; above 7.42 is alkalemia.

The body defends pH in three lines, from fastest to slowest. (1) Chemical buffers bind added H⁺ within seconds ('acute conversion'). They limit the pH change but don't remove the acid. (2) The lungs adjust breathing within minutes to hours. Breathing faster blows off CO₂, which removes acid. (3) The kidneys act over hours to days. They excrete H⁺ in urine and reabsorb or make new HCO₃⁻, which finally fixes the problem.

Axes: x = moles of HCl added per liter, on a log scale (each step is 10 times more acid); y = pH. Blue line, pure water: pH falls one full unit for every 10-fold increase in HCl, because nothing takes up the H⁺. Pink line, buffer: pH stays flat near 4.7, because the buffer's base form soaks up each added H⁺. Only at very large amounts of acid (10⁻² to 10⁻¹ mol/L) does the base form run out, and then pH starts to fall. A buffer blunts pH change until it is used up.

Volatile means it can turn into a gas. CO₂ is a gas, so the lungs can exhale it, and the acid it forms leaves the body within minutes. Sulfuric acid (like phosphoric acid) can't become a gas, so the lungs can't remove it; it must be buffered and then excreted by the kidneys. This splits the body's acid into two kinds: volatile acid (CO₂) and fixed acid (everything else).

CO₂ comes from burning fuel with O₂ in mitochondria, about 200 mL per minute (13,000–20,000 mmol per day; mmol = millimole). CO₂ is not an acid itself, but it reacts with water: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Carbonic anhydrase (CA), an enzyme in red blood cells and kidney cells, speeds the first step enormously. Because the lungs exhale CO₂, this huge acid load never builds up as long as breathing keeps pace.

Follow the blue arrows. CO₂ diffuses from the tissue cell into the red blood cell. There, carbonic anhydrase turns CO₂ + H₂O into H₂CO₃, which splits into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. Hemoglobin (Hb) binds the H⁺ (and some CO₂ directly), so the H⁺ barely lowers blood pH. HCO₃⁻ leaves the red cell in exchange for Cl⁻ moving in (the chloride shift, bottom-right arrow). About 90% of CO₂ travels this way, as HCO₃⁻ in plasma. In the lungs every step runs backward and the CO₂ is exhaled.

Answer: C (pH 7.35). Step 1: PCO₂ (partial pressure of CO₂ in arterial blood; normal 40 mm Hg) is 70, so CO₂ is retained. That is respiratory acidosis. Step 2: he has had COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) for years, so it is chronic. The kidneys have had days to compensate by reabsorbing and making more HCO₃⁻. Step 3: HCO₃⁻ rises to about 36 mEq/L (12 above normal), which pulls pH back to just below normal. pH 7.15 fits an acute rise with no time for kidney help. 7.65 is alkaline. HCO₃⁻ is high, not low (D). Chronic low O₂ raises the red cell count, not anemia (E).

CO₂ added to blood takes three forms. Some stays dissolved. Some binds amino groups on proteins, mainly hemoglobin, as carbamino-CO₂. Most is turned by carbonic anhydrase into H₂CO₃, which splits into HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. Every HCO₃⁻ made this way comes with one H⁺. That H⁺ must be buffered right away, mostly by hemoglobin inside the red cell, or venous blood would become very acidic.

Follow the numbered steps in a tissue capillary. (1) CO₂ made by metabolism diffuses out of the tissue cells, across the capillary wall and into the red blood cell. (2) Carbonic anhydrase in the red cell joins CO₂ and H₂O into H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid). (3) H₂CO₃ splits into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. (4) The H⁺ stays in the red cell and binds hemoglobin (Hb-H = hemoglobin carrying an H⁺), so it barely lowers pH. (5) HCO₃⁻ moves out of the red cell into the plasma while Cl⁻ moves in (the chloride shift). Plasma carries this HCO₃⁻ to the lungs. Over 90% of CO₂ travels this way. Two small routes are not drawn: some CO₂ stays dissolved in plasma, and some binds hemoglobin directly as carbaminohemoglobin (CO₂·Hb).

Fixed acids are made every day by normal metabolism. Phospholipids break down to phosphoric acid; the sulfur-containing amino acids in protein break down to sulfuric acid. These can't be exhaled, so they are handled in two steps. Step 1: their H⁺ is buffered in blood, mainly by HCO₃⁻, which is used up (H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O). Step 2: the kidneys excrete the H⁺ in urine and make new HCO₃⁻ to replace what was used.

Every acid except CO₂/carbonic acid is 'fixed', because the lungs can't get rid of it; only the kidneys can. 'Incomplete metabolism' means the molecule isn't burned all the way to CO₂ + water, so an acid is left over (sulfate from amino acids, lactate when O₂ runs short). Fixed acid is made at 1–1.5 mmol per kg of body weight per day (roughly 50–100 mmol a day in an adult). That is tiny next to CO₂, at 13,000–20,000 mmol a day. But because only the kidneys remove fixed acid, kidney failure lets it pile up.

Which amino acids make which acid: the sulfur-containing ones (methionine, cysteine, cystine) are broken down to sulfate, giving sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). The positively charged (basic) amino acids, lysine and arginine, release HCl when they are metabolized. Phosphate-containing foods give phosphoric acid. So a high-protein diet raises the daily fixed-acid load, and the kidneys must excrete more acid.

Answer: A (metabolic acidosis). Step 1: ESRD (end-stage renal disease) means the kidneys no longer work, so dialysis is what removes the daily fixed acid. Step 2: with no dialysis for 2 weeks, sulfuric and phosphoric acid keep being made but are not excreted. Step 3: their H⁺ is buffered by HCO₃⁻, so HCO₃⁻ falls and pH falls. A fall in HCO₃⁻ is metabolic acidosis. Respiratory acidosis (C) needs a high PCO₂ from poor breathing. D and E have pH 7.45, which is alkaline.

These are fixed acids made in excess in disease, or taken in as poisons. Each adds H⁺ that uses up HCO₃⁻, causing metabolic acidosis.
  • Diabetes: without insulin, the liver turns fat into the ketoacids β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetoacetic acid (diabetic ketoacidosis).
  • Lactic acid: tissues short of O₂ (very hard exercise, sepsis, shock) switch to anaerobic glycolysis.
  • Poisons: aspirin gives salicylic acid; methanol gives formic acid; ethylene glycol (antifreeze) gives glycolic and oxalic acids.

A buffer is a conjugate pair: a weak acid (HA, the H⁺ donor) and its base (A⁻, the H⁺ acceptor). They are the same molecule with and without one H⁺. Add H⁺: it binds A⁻ and becomes HA, so free H⁺ barely rises. Remove H⁺ (or add OH⁻): HA releases H⁺ and becomes A⁻. This works because the reaction sits at equilibrium.
