By the law of mass action, adding something to one side pushes the reaction toward the other side, like a seesaw rebalancing.

The seesaw applies mass action to the CO₂ reaction. When PCO₂ rises (yellow, up arrow), there is more CO₂ on the left side, so the reaction is pushed to the right (red arrow): CO₂ + H₂O → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. More H⁺ means pH falls (green). HCO₃⁻ also rises a little (purple). The reverse also holds: when PCO₂ falls, as with fast breathing, the reaction runs left, H⁺ is used up, and pH rises. CA = carbonic anhydrase, which speeds the reaction in both directions.

Answer: B (decrease of PCO₂). Step 1: ethylene glycol makes fixed acids; HCO₃⁻ of 12 (normal 24) means metabolic acidosis. Step 2: the low pH stimulates chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies within minutes, so the person breathes faster and deeper. Step 3: this blows off CO₂, so PCO₂ falls. By mass action, less CO₂ pulls H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ toward CO₂ + H₂O, so H⁺ falls and pH moves back toward normal. A and C would make the acidosis worse. In acidemia, H⁺ pushes Ca²⁺ off albumin, not on (D). Breathing compensation starts at once, not after 12 hours (E); the kidneys are the slow part.

pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so each drop of 1 pH unit means 10 times more H⁺. pH 6 has 10× the H⁺ of pH 7; pH 5 has 10 × 10 = 100×. pH 1 is 6 units lower than 7, so it has 10⁶ = one million times more H⁺. This is why a pH change that looks small on paper is big: going from 7.4 to 7.1 means about twice as much H⁺ (40 → 80 nEq/L).

K is the dissociation constant: how much of an acid splits into H⁺ + A⁻. pK = −log K. In practice, pK is the pH at which half of the buffer is in the acid form (HA) and half in the base form (A⁻); that is the 'balance point'. A buffer works well only within about 1 pH unit of its pK, because there both forms are plentiful. A strong acid (HCl) gives up its H⁺ even at very low pH, so its pK is very low. A weak acid such as H₂CO₃ holds its H⁺ more, so its pK is higher (6.1).

The equation itself, in words: pH equals the pK plus the log of (base form ÷ acid form). Symbols: pH = pK + log([A⁻]/[HA]), where [A⁻] = concentration of the base form and [HA] = concentration of the acid form. For blood: pH = 6.1 + log(HCO₃⁻ ÷ (0.03 × PCO₂)). The 0.03 converts PCO₂ (mm Hg) into dissolved CO₂ (mmol/L). Worked example with normal values: 0.03 × 40 = 1.2; 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20; log 20 = 1.3; 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4. So pH depends on the ratio of HCO₃⁻ to CO₂ (normally 20 to 1). The kidneys control HCO₃⁻; the lungs control CO₂.

ECF (extracellular fluid) = plasma plus the fluid between cells. In the bicarbonate buffer, dissolved CO₂ counts as the acid form (HA), because with water it becomes H₂CO₃ and releases H⁺. HCO₃⁻ is the base form (A⁻) that takes up H⁺. Phosphate is the other ECF buffer, but it helps less in blood for two reasons: its concentration is low (1–2 mmol/L vs 24 for HCO₃⁻), and its acid form (H₂PO₄⁻) can't be exhaled. So the H⁺ it takes up stays in the blood, and the buffer is soon used up.

Answer: E. Two rules decide it. (1) A buffer must be weak: a strong acid splits completely and can't take H⁺ back, so C is out. (2) Its pK must be near the pH it has to hold (7.4), within about 1 unit, because there both HA and A⁻ are plentiful. pK 2, 3 and 10 are far from 7.4. At pH 7.4 those buffers would sit almost entirely in one form, so they could only work in one direction. pK 7 is the closest.

Why HCO₃⁻/CO₂ is the main ECF buffer even though its pK (6.1) is 1.3 units from 7.4: (1) Its base form, HCO₃⁻, is plentiful at 24 mEq/L (milliequivalents per liter). (2) Its acid form, CO₂, is volatile. When HCO₃⁻ soaks up H⁺, it forms H₂CO₃, which becomes CO₂ + H₂O, and the CO₂ is exhaled instead of piling up. So the buffer doesn't fill up ('saturate'), and the lungs widen its useful range. H₂CO₃ itself is tiny (about 1 molecule per 400 of dissolved CO₂), so the equation uses CO₂ instead.

HPO₄²⁻ is the base form (takes up H⁺); H₂PO₄⁻ is the acid form. Its pK of 6.8 is closer to 7.4 than bicarbonate's 6.1, so molecule for molecule it is a better buffer. But blood phosphate is low (1–2 mmol/L), so it does little in blood. Phosphate matters in the kidney: it is filtered and concentrated in urine, where it picks up H⁺ that tubule cells secrete into the tubule fluid (HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻) and carries it out of the body in urine. This route is slow because kidney acid excretion takes hours to days.

Negative sites on albumin can hold either H⁺ or Ca²⁺, so the two compete. About 40% of blood Ca²⁺ is bound to protein; only free (ionized) Ca²⁺ acts on nerves and muscle. Acidemia: extra H⁺ takes the sites and pushes Ca²⁺ off, so free Ca²⁺ rises. Alkalemia: H⁺ leaves the sites and more Ca²⁺ binds, so free Ca²⁺ falls. Total calcium stays the same; only the free part changes. So 'hypercalcemia' and 'hypocalcemia' here mean high and low free Ca²⁺. Low free Ca²⁺ makes nerves fire too easily: tingling, numbness around the mouth, muscle spasms (tetany).

Answer: A (pH 7.10, HCO₃⁻ 12). Step 1: 30 minutes of nonstop seizing makes the muscles work so hard that O₂ supply falls short. Step 2: the muscles switch to anaerobic glycolysis and make lactic acid, a fixed acid. Step 3: its H⁺ uses up HCO₃⁻, so HCO₃⁻ falls (24 → 12) and pH falls: metabolic acidosis. B has low pH with high HCO₃⁻, which fits respiratory acidosis with kidney compensation. C is alkalosis. D is normal; the acid doesn't vanish the moment the seizure stops.

Answer: A. The fastest defense is the HCO₃⁻ buffer itself. Excess H⁺ joins HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃, and carbonic anhydrase turns that into CO₂ + H₂O within seconds; the CO₂ is then exhaled. Why not the others: urinary acid excretion (B) and proximal tubule HCO₃⁻ reabsorption (E) are kidney steps that take hours to days. Phosphate (C) is too scarce in blood. The helpful breathing response lowers PCO₂; raising PCO₂ (D) would make the acidosis worse.

Correction: CO₂ bound to hemoglobin is carbaminohemoglobin. Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide (CO). Intracellular buffers handle H⁺ inside cells. Proteins buffer mainly by binding H⁺ on histidine side chains (pK 6.4–7.0); hemoglobin is the most important one. Organic phosphates bind H⁺ on their phosphate groups: AMP, ADP and ATP (adenosine mono-, di- and triphosphate) and 2,3-DPG (2,3-diphosphoglycerate, made in red cells). Their pKs (6.0–7.5) suit body pH.

Don't mix up the two roles of protein. Protein you eat is broken down, and its sulfur-containing and basic amino acids produce sulfuric acid and HCl, so diet protein is a source of acid. Proteins already in the body, albumin in plasma and hemoglobin in red cells, stay intact and hold H⁺ on their histidine side chains, so they are buffers.

Hemoglobin has 36 histidines, whose side chains bind H⁺. Its pK changes with O₂: oxyhemoglobin pK 6.7, deoxyhemoglobin pK 7.9. A higher pK means it holds H⁺ more tightly. Step by step: in tissue capillaries, Hb releases O₂ and becomes deoxyhemoglobin. At the same moment CO₂ enters the red cell and makes H⁺. The newly deoxygenated Hb grabs that H⁺. This extra H⁺ and CO₂ carried by deoxygenated Hb is the Haldane effect. Result: venous pH is 7.37, only 0.03 below arterial 7.40, despite the large CO₂ load.

Answer: D. Step 1: in a panic attack she hyperventilates and blows off CO₂, so PCO₂ falls. Step 2: less CO₂ pulls the reaction to the left, H⁺ falls and pH rises: respiratory alkalosis. Step 3: with less H⁺ on albumin, more Ca²⁺ binds albumin, so free (ionized) Ca²⁺ falls. Step 4: low free Ca²⁺ makes nerves fire easily, causing numbness and tingling around the mouth and in the fingers. Breathing into a paper bag raises PCO₂ and relieves it. Alkalosis lowers K⁺ (it moves into cells), so A is wrong.

qs.q: Normal arterial blood H⁺ concentration is about how much?
qs.why: pH 7.40 corresponds to 40 × 10⁻⁹ Eq/L, or 40 nanoequivalents per liter. That is over a million times lower than Na⁺ at 140 mEq/L.

qs.q: What makes HCl a strong acid and carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) a weak acid?
opts: HCl dissociates almost completely; H₂CO₃ only partly
HCl is volatile; H₂CO₃ is not
HCl has a higher pK than H₂CO₃
HCl accepts H⁺; H₂CO₃ donates H⁺
qs.why: Acid strength is how completely an acid gives up its H⁺. HCl releases nearly all of it at once. A strong acid has a LOW pK, not a high one.

qs.q: Why are buffers weak acids and bases rather than strong ones?
opts: They react reversibly, so they can take up or release H⁺
They are present at higher concentration than strong acids
They react completely, so they remove all added H⁺
They can be exhaled by the lungs as a gas
qs.why: A weak acid and its base exist side by side, so the pair can soak up added H⁺ or give H⁺ back. A strong acid or base reacts all the way and can't swing back.

qs.q: pH 7.4 → 7.2 raises H⁺ by about 23 nEq/L. By about how much does pH 7.4 → 7.6 lower H⁺?
qs.why: pH is a log scale, so equal pH steps are not equal H⁺ steps. pH 7.6 is 25 nEq/L, 15 below 40; the acid side changes more (40 → 63).

qs.q: Which defense against a pH change acts within seconds but does not remove acid from the body?
opts: Faster breathing to blow off CO₂
qs.why: Buffers bind added H⁺ almost instantly, limiting the pH change. The lungs act in minutes to hours and the kidneys in hours to days; only they remove acid.

qs.q: As strong acid is added to a buffered solution, when does pH start to fall steeply?
opts: As soon as the first acid is added
When the buffer's acid form is used up
When the buffer's base form is used up
qs.why: The base form soaks up each added H⁺, so pH stays flat. Once the base form runs out, added H⁺ stays free and pH falls.

qs.q: Why must sulfuric acid be removed by the kidneys rather than the lungs?
opts: It is not volatile, so it can't be exhaled
It is made only inside the kidney
It stays bound to hemoglobin in red cells
It is a weak acid that dissociates slowly
qs.why: Volatile means able to become a gas. CO₂ can be exhaled; sulfuric and phosphoric acid cannot, so they are fixed acids that only the kidneys excrete.

qs.q: CO₂ is not itself an acid. How does it produce H⁺?
opts: It is oxidized to an acid in mitochondria
It binds hemoglobin and displaces H⁺
It combines with water to form carbonic acid
It releases H⁺ directly when it dissolves
qs.why: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Carbonic anhydrase greatly speeds the first step.

qs.q: In what form is most (about 90%) of the CO₂ in blood carried?
qs.why: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells turns CO₂ into H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, and the HCO₃⁻ moves out into plasma. Only small amounts stay dissolved or bound to hemoglobin.

qs.q: As HCO₃⁻ leaves a red cell in a tissue capillary, which ion moves in?
qs.why: HCO₃⁻ is exchanged for Cl⁻: the chloride shift. The H⁺ stays inside the cell, buffered by hemoglobin.

qs.q: Inside the red cell, what mainly buffers the H⁺ made from CO₂?
qs.why: Each HCO₃⁻ made comes with one H⁺, which hemoglobin binds at once so venous pH barely falls. HCO₃⁻ can't be the buffer here: joining that H⁺ back onto HCO₃⁻ would just turn them back into CO₂ + H₂O.

qs.q: CO₂ bound directly to amino groups on hemoglobin is called what?
qs.why: CO₂ on hemoglobin is carbaminohemoglobin. Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide (CO).

qs.q: Breakdown of the sulfur-containing amino acids (methionine, cysteine) produces which acid?
qs.why: Their sulfur is oxidized to sulfate, giving H₂SO₄. Phosphoric acid comes from phospholipids; HCl comes from lysine and arginine.

qs.q: When fixed acid enters the blood, which buffer is mainly used up?
qs.why: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O, so plasma HCO₃⁻ falls. The kidneys must then excrete the H⁺ and make new HCO₃⁻ to replace it.

qs.q: Methanol poisoning produces which acid?
qs.why: Methanol is metabolized to formic acid. Ethylene glycol gives oxalic (and glycolic) acid; aspirin gives salicylic acid.

qs.q: Which acids build up in diabetic ketoacidosis?
qs.why: Without insulin the liver turns fat into the ketoacids β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetoacetic acid. Lactic acid comes from tissues short of O₂.

qs.q: In CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, what does a rise in PCO₂ do?
opts: Shifts right; H⁺ falls and pH rises
Shifts right; H⁺ rises and pH falls
Shifts left; H⁺ falls and pH rises
Shifts left; H⁺ rises and pH falls
qs.why: By the law of mass action, more CO₂ on the left pushes the reaction to the right, making more H⁺ (and a little more HCO₃⁻), so pH falls.

qs.q: pH 5 has how many times more H⁺ than pH 7?
qs.why: pH = −log[H⁺], so each 1-unit drop is 10 times more H⁺. Two units lower is 10 × 10 = 100 times.

qs.q: A buffer's pK is the pH at which what is true?
opts: The buffer is completely used up
Only the base form is present
Only the acid form is present
Acid form and base form are equal
qs.why: pK is the balance point: half the buffer is HA and half is A⁻. A buffer works best within about 1 pH unit of its pK.

qs.q: At normal blood pH 7.4, what is the ratio of HCO₃⁻ to dissolved CO₂?
qs.why: Dissolved CO₂ = 0.03 × PCO₂ = 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L. pH = 6.1 + log(24 ÷ 1.2) = 6.1 + log 20 = 7.4. The kidneys set HCO₃⁻ and the lungs set CO₂.

qs.q: In the bicarbonate buffer, which counts as the acid form (H⁺ donor)?
qs.why: Dissolved CO₂ forms H₂CO₃ with water and releases H⁺, so it is the acid form. H₂CO₃ itself is so scarce that CO₂ stands in for it; HCO₃⁻ is the base form.

qs.q: Why is HCO₃⁻/CO₂ the main ECF buffer even though its pK is only 6.1?
opts: Its pK is the closest to 7.4
It is a strong acid–base pair
It is the only buffer in red cells
HCO₃⁻ is plentiful and CO₂ can be exhaled
qs.why: HCO₃⁻ is 24 mEq/L, and the CO₂ formed when it takes up H⁺ is breathed off, so the buffer doesn't saturate. Phosphate's pK (6.8) is actually closer to 7.4.

qs.q: Why does phosphate (pK 6.8) do little buffering in blood?
opts: It is exhaled by the lungs
Its pK is too far from 7.4
qs.why: Blood phosphate is only 1–2 mmol/L versus 24 for HCO₃⁻. Its main buffering role is in urine, where it is concentrated.

qs.q: In alkalemia, what happens to free (ionized) Ca²⁺?
opts: Stays the same, as albumin binds only H⁺
Rises, as H⁺ pushes Ca²⁺ off albumin
Falls, as more Ca²⁺ binds albumin
qs.why: H⁺ and Ca²⁺ compete for albumin's negative sites. With less H⁺, more Ca²⁺ binds, so free Ca²⁺ falls while total calcium is unchanged; low free Ca²⁺ causes tingling and tetany.

qs.q: Which amino acid's side chains let hemoglobin and other proteins buffer H⁺?
qs.why: Histidine side chains (pK about 6.4–7.0) bind H⁺ near body pH. Lysine, cysteine and methionine are the dietary amino acids that produce acid.

qs.q: Protein you eat versus protein already in the body: which is correct?
opts: Eaten protein is a buffer; body proteins make acid
Eaten protein makes acid; body proteins are buffers
qs.why: Dietary protein is broken down to sulfuric acid and HCl. Albumin and hemoglobin stay intact and hold H⁺ on histidine.

qs.q: Why is venous pH (7.37) almost the same as arterial pH despite the large CO₂ load?
opts: Plasma phosphate binds the extra H⁺
Albumin releases Ca²⁺ to neutralize the H⁺
The kidneys excrete the extra H⁺
Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds the extra H⁺
qs.why: Deoxyhemoglobin has a higher pK (7.9) than oxyhemoglobin (6.7), so as Hb unloads O₂ in tissues it grabs the H⁺ made from CO₂. This is the Haldane effect.

slides.note: The kidneys have two separate acid–base jobs. Job 1, reclaim: plasma HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate, the main blood buffer) is filtered at the glomerulus, and the tubules reabsorb almost all of it (move it out of the tubule fluid back into the blood), so it is not lost in urine. This happens mostly in the proximal tubule and adds nothing new. Job 2, excrete acid: breakdown of protein and phospholipids makes about 50 mEq of fixed (non-volatile) acid a day that the lungs cannot breathe off. The distal nephron secretes this H⁺ into urine. Each H⁺ excreted creates one new HCO₃⁻ for the blood, replacing the HCO₃⁻ used up buffering that acid.

Labels: PT = proximal tubule; TAL = thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle; DT = distal tubule; CCD = cortical collecting duct; IMCD = inner medullary collecting duct. Each arrow pointing out of the tubule is HCO₃⁻ being reabsorbed (leaving the tubule fluid for the blood); its number is the share of filtered HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed there. Freely filtered means HCO₃⁻ passes the glomerulus at the same concentration as in plasma (about 24 mEq/L). So the amount filtered is huge. Filtered load = GFR (glomerular filtration rate) × plasma HCO₃⁻ = 180 L/day × 24 mEq/L ≈ 4,300 mEq/day. Losing even a few percent of that would cause acidosis, so the nephron reclaims essentially all of it, most in the proximal tubule. The downward arrow at the bottom (“~0”) is what is left in urine: almost no HCO₃⁻.

Lumen (tubule fluid) is on the left, blood on the right. Follow one H⁺ around the loop. (1) The Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger on the luminal membrane lets Na⁺ flow into the cell and pushes H⁺ out into the lumen. (2) In the lumen, H⁺ joins a filtered HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), which CA (carbonic anhydrase) splits into CO₂ + H₂O. (3) CO₂ diffuses into the cell. (4) Inside, CA runs the reaction backward: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. (5) The HCO₃⁻ exits to the blood, and the H⁺ goes back out to grab the next filtered HCO₃⁻. Net result: one filtered HCO₃⁻ reclaimed per H⁺ secreted, with no net acid excreted, because the same H⁺ keeps cycling. “Sodium avidity” means the body is holding on to Na⁺ (low volume). That speeds the exchanger, so HCO₃⁻ reabsorption speeds up too.

The same cycle, with two points added. First, what drives it: the Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase on the blood side (3 Na⁺ out to the blood, 2 K⁺ into the cell) keeps Na⁺ low inside the cell. Na⁺ then flows in from the lumen, and the exchanger uses that flow to push H⁺ out against its gradient. Second, brush-border CA (carbonic anhydrase on the luminal surface) turns luminal H₂CO₃ into CO₂, the form that can cross into the cell. Acetazolamide (a CA inhibitor) blocks this step, so HCO₃⁻ stays in the tubule and is lost in urine. Tubule fluid pH barely changes because every secreted H⁺ is used up by a filtered HCO₃⁻ instead of staying free.

Lumen (tubule fluid) is on the left, blood on the right. This is the proximal-tubule cycle that reclaims filtered HCO₃⁻. The Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger (pink) lets Na⁺ into the cell and pushes H⁺ out into the lumen. There H⁺ joins filtered HCO₃⁻, and carbonic anhydrase turns the H₂CO₃ into CO₂ + H₂O. CO₂ diffuses into the cell and becomes H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ again. The HCO₃⁻ crosses into the blood with Na⁺ (orange) or in exchange for Cl⁻ (peach). Filtered load of HCO₃⁻ (amount filtered per minute) = GFR × plasma HCO₃⁻. Normal plasma HCO₃⁻ is 24 mEq/L; if it rises, more is filtered and more is reabsorbed. But above about 40 mEq/L the proximal tubule is saturated, and every extra mEq filtered spills into urine, because these transporters have a maximum rate, like glucose's Tm (transport maximum). This is how the kidney gets rid of excess HCO₃⁻ in metabolic alkalosis.

ECF = extracellular fluid; ATII = angiotensin II. Volume changes HCO₃⁻ reabsorption in two ways. (1) Starling forces: HCO₃⁻ is part of the bulk, isosmotic reabsorption in the proximal tubule (salt and water reabsorbed together, in the same proportion). When ECF volume shrinks, peritubular capillary forces favor reabsorption, so more Na⁺, water and HCO₃⁻ are reabsorbed from the tubule fluid into the blood. ECF expansion does the opposite. (2) Angiotensin II: low volume turns on renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone. Angiotensin II directly speeds the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger (red arrows). More H⁺ secreted means more filtered HCO₃⁻ reclaimed, so blood HCO₃⁻ rises.

Contraction alkalosis = metabolic alkalosis caused by losing ECF volume. Step by step: volume falls → angiotensin II rises → it stimulates the proximal Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger → more filtered HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed → blood HCO₃⁻ rises → pH rises. Loop and thiazide diuretics cause it because they make you lose salt and water, which shrinks ECF volume. The same mechanism keeps the alkalosis of vomiting going. Because the cause is low volume, the treatment is isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl). Restoring volume shuts off angiotensin II, and the kidney then excretes the extra HCO₃⁻.

PCO₂ = partial pressure of CO₂ in arterial blood. The kidney compensates for lung problems by changing how much HCO₃⁻ it keeps, with CO₂ as the signal. High PCO₂ (respiratory acidosis): more CO₂ enters tubule cells → more H⁺ is made and secreted → more HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed → blood HCO₃⁻ rises → pH moves back up toward normal. Low PCO₂ (respiratory alkalosis): less CO₂ in the cells → less H⁺ secreted → filtered HCO₃⁻ escapes into urine → blood HCO₃⁻ falls → pH moves back down. This takes days, so it is seen in chronic respiratory disorders.

Titratable acid = H⁺ excreted bound to a filtered buffer, mainly phosphate: HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻. The name comes from how it is measured: the amount of base needed to titrate the urine back to pH 7.4. Phosphate works well for two reasons. Only 85% of filtered phosphate is reabsorbed, so 15% stays in the tubule to carry H⁺. And its pK (the pH at which a buffer works best) is 6.8, close to tubule pH. The H⁺ is pumped from the cell into the tubule fluid mainly by α-intercalated cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct. Last bullet: aldosterone makes principal cells reabsorb Na⁺ and secrete K⁺, and makes α-intercalated cells secrete H⁺.

Lumen (tubule fluid) is on the left, blood on the right. Follow H⁺ out to the lumen and HCO₃⁻ out to the blood. (1) Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase turns CO₂ + H₂O into H₂CO₃, which splits into H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. (2) Two pumps push H⁺ into the lumen: the H⁺-ATPase (blue), which aldosterone stimulates, and the H⁺–K⁺-ATPase (purple), which takes K⁺ from the lumen into the cell in exchange. (3) In the lumen, filtered HPO₄²⁻ catches the H⁺ and becomes H₂PO₄⁻, the titratable acid that is excreted. NH₃ catches H⁺ the same way, becoming NH₄⁺ (not drawn here). (4) HCO₃⁻ leaves to the blood on the Cl⁻–HCO₃⁻ exchanger (pink; called AE1, anion exchanger 1), swapping for Cl⁻. “New HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed” means this HCO₃⁻ was made in the cell, not reclaimed from the filtrate. The proximal tubule, by contrast, only reclaims filtered HCO₃⁻ and excretes no acid.

Why buffers are essential. The H⁺ pump can make urine H⁺ at most 1000 times blood H⁺. That is 3 pH units (each unit is a 10-fold step), so the lowest urine pH is 7.4 − 3 = 4.4. At pH 4.4, free H⁺ is only about 0.04 mEq/L. With about 1.5 L of urine a day, that is under 0.1 mEq of free H⁺, against roughly 50 mEq of fixed acid to remove. So almost all H⁺ must leave bound to a buffer. A buffered H⁺ (as H₂PO₄⁻) is no longer free, so it does not lower urine pH, and the pump can keep secreting. That is why titratable acid depends on how much phosphate is filtered. In the diagram, “new HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed” means HCO₃⁻ made inside the cell moves out into the blood; it was never in the filtrate.

About 50 mEq of fixed acid is excreted per day: about 40% as titratable acid (H₂PO₄⁻, about 20 mEq) and 60% as NH₄⁺ (ammonium, about 30 mEq). NH₄⁺ is called “non-titratable” because of its pK of about 9.2. At pH 7.4 it stays almost entirely as NH₄⁺, so titrating urine back to 7.4 does not pull its H⁺ off. The titration test misses it, and it must be measured separately. NH₄⁺ is the system that can be turned up a lot in acidosis, because the kidney can make more NH₃. Phosphate excretion is limited by how much phosphate is filtered.

Where NH₃ comes from and why it stays in the urine. (1) Proximal tubule cells break down glutamine (enzyme glutaminase) → NH₄⁺ + glutamate. The glutamate is metabolized to a new HCO₃⁻, which goes to the blood. (2) NH₄⁺ is secreted from the cell into the lumen on the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger, in place of H⁺. In the thick ascending limb, part of it is reabsorbed: it leaves the tubule fluid on the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (taking K⁺'s place) and builds up in the medullary interstitium (the tissue fluid around the deep tubules). (3) From there, uncharged, lipid-soluble NH₃ diffuses into the collecting duct fluid. (4) There it meets H⁺ secreted by α-intercalated cells and becomes NH₄⁺. (5) Charged NH₄⁺ cannot diffuse back across membranes, so it is trapped and excreted. This is called diffusion trapping.

The first bullet follows from diffusion trapping; the second from making more NH₃. Low urine pH → more NH₃ enters the urine: the more H⁺ in the lumen, the faster NH₃ turns into NH₄⁺. Luminal NH₃ stays near zero, so the gradient for NH₃ to diffuse in from the interstitium stays steep. This helps exactly when there is the most acid to remove. Blood acidosis → more NH₃ is made: chronic acidosis lowers pH inside proximal cells, which induces the enzymes that break down glutamine. This takes several days. It is the kidney's main way to handle a big acid load, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Potassium matters too: high K⁺ blocks NH₃ synthesis (causing type 4 renal tubular acidosis), and low K⁺ stimulates it.

Correction: the phosphate buffer is HPO₄²⁻ (filtered phosphate), which accepts H⁺ to become H₂PO₄⁻. It is not phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), which cannot accept another H⁺. Aldosterone acts on both cell types of the late distal tubule and collecting duct. In principal cells it raises Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion. In α-intercalated cells it raises H⁺ secretion, and each H⁺ buffered by NH₃ or HPO₄²⁻ leaves one new HCO₃⁻ in the blood. So high aldosterone gives low K⁺ and metabolic alkalosis, and low aldosterone gives high K⁺ and metabolic acidosis.

Where each diuretic acts, and what it does to acid–base balance. The two jobs map onto the nephron: the proximal tubule reclaims filtered HCO₃⁻, and the distal nephron secretes H⁺ and makes new HCO₃⁻. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (blue; acetazolamide, proximal tubule) block HCO₃⁻ reclaiming → HCO₃⁻ lost in urine → metabolic acidosis. Loop (orange, thick ascending limb) and thiazide (green, early distal tubule) diuretics shrink ECF volume and send more Na⁺ to the late distal nephron → more H⁺ and K⁺ secreted into urine → metabolic alkalosis with low K⁺. K⁺-sparing diuretics (purple, late distal tubule and collecting duct) block aldosterone or its Na⁺ channel → less H⁺ and K⁺ secreted → high K⁺ and mild acidosis. Red = osmotic diuretics (such as mannitol).

qs.q: Where is most filtered HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed?
qs.why: The proximal tubule reclaims 80–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻; the thick ascending limb takes about 15% and the late distal/early collecting duct about 5%.

qs.q: Which luminal transporter secretes the H⁺ that reclaims filtered HCO₃⁻ in the proximal tubule?
qs.why: The Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase on the blood side keeps Na⁺ low inside the cell. So Na⁺ flows from the lumen into the cell on the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger, which pushes H⁺ out into the lumen in return. The same H⁺ recycles, so no net acid is excreted.

qs.q: What does brush-border carbonic anhydrase do in the proximal tubule lumen?
opts: Turns H₂CO₃ into CO₂ and water
Turns CO₂ and water into H₂CO₃
Pumps HCO₃⁻ into the tubule cell
qs.why: Luminal H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ form H₂CO₃, which brush-border CA splits into CO₂ + H₂O; CO₂ then diffuses into the cell. Blocking it with acetazolamide leaves HCO₃⁻ in the urine.

qs.q: What happens once plasma HCO₃⁻ rises above about 40 mEq/L?
opts: The distal nephron reabsorbs all the extra
Extra filtered HCO₃⁻ spills into urine
qs.why: Above about 40 mEq/L the proximal Na⁺–H⁺ machinery is saturated, so every extra mEq filtered is excreted. This is how the kidney gets rid of excess HCO₃⁻ in metabolic alkalosis.

qs.q: Which hormone, raised by low ECF volume, directly stimulates the proximal Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger?
qs.why: Low volume turns on renin → angiotensin II, which speeds the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger, so more filtered HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed and plasma HCO₃⁻ rises.

qs.q: Why do loop and thiazide diuretics cause metabolic alkalosis?
opts: They lower PCO₂ by stimulating breathing
Volume loss raises angiotensin II and HCO₃⁻ reabsorption
They block carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
They add HCO₃⁻ directly to the blood
qs.why: Salt and water loss shrinks ECF volume (contraction alkalosis). Isotonic saline fixes it by turning off angiotensin II so the extra HCO₃⁻ is excreted.

qs.q: In chronic respiratory acidosis (high PCO₂), how does the kidney compensate?
opts: Secretes less H⁺, lowering plasma HCO₃⁻
Reabsorbs more HCO₃⁻, raising plasma HCO₃⁻
Excretes more HCO₃⁻, lowering plasma HCO₃⁻
Does nothing; only the lungs compensate
qs.why: More CO₂ in tubule cells makes more H⁺ to secrete, so more HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed and pH moves back up. Low PCO₂ does the opposite. This takes days.

qs.q: Titratable acid in urine is mainly H⁺ carried by which buffer?
qs.why: Filtered HPO₄²⁻ picks up secreted H⁺ to become H₂PO₄⁻. About 15% of filtered phosphate escapes reabsorption to carry it, and its pK of 6.8 suits tubule pH.

qs.q: Which cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct secrete H⁺?
qs.why: α-intercalated cells pump H⁺ into the lumen by H⁺-ATPase (stimulated by aldosterone) and H⁺–K⁺-ATPase. Principal cells reabsorb Na⁺ and secrete K⁺.

qs.q: Each H⁺ that an α-intercalated cell secretes and the urine excretes adds what to the blood?
qs.why: The HCO₃⁻ is made inside the cell from CO₂ + H₂O and leaves via AE1 (swapping for Cl⁻). It is new, unlike proximal HCO₃⁻, which is only reclaimed from the filtrate.

qs.q: Why must almost all excreted H⁺ be bound to a urinary buffer?
opts: Free H⁺ is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
Free H⁺ is exhaled as CO₂
Urine pH can't fall below about 4.4
qs.why: The pump can make urine H⁺ at most 1000 times blood H⁺, which is 3 pH units (7.4 − 3 = 4.4), so urine can hold very little free H⁺. Buffered H⁺ doesn't lower urine pH, so secretion can continue.

qs.q: About what share of daily fixed acid is excreted as NH₄⁺ (ammonium)?
qs.why: Of about 50 mEq/day, roughly 60% leaves as NH₄⁺ and 30–40% as titratable acid (H₂PO₄⁻).

qs.q: From what molecule do proximal tubule cells make NH₄⁺?
qs.why: Glutaminase splits glutamine into NH₄⁺ + glutamate. The glutamate is then metabolized to a new HCO₃⁻ for the blood.

qs.q: Why does NH₄⁺ stay in the collecting duct urine instead of diffusing back?
opts: It is charged and can't cross membranes
It is actively secreted by principal cells
qs.why: Uncharged NH₃ diffuses into the lumen, meets secreted H⁺ and becomes charged NH₄⁺, which is trapped and excreted: diffusion trapping.

qs.q: In chronic acidosis, which acid-excretion route can be increased the most?
opts: H⁺ recycled in the proximal tubule
qs.why: Acidosis induces the glutamine-breaking enzymes over several days, so NH₃ production rises a lot. Titratable acid is limited by how much phosphate is filtered.

qs.q: High aldosterone produces which combination?
qs.why: Aldosterone makes principal cells secrete K⁺ and α-intercalated cells secrete H⁺, adding new HCO₃⁻. Low aldosterone gives the reverse: high K⁺ and acidosis.

qs.q: Besides NH₃, which filtered buffer accepts H⁺ in the distal nephron?
qs.why: HPO₄²⁻ takes up H⁺ to become H₂PO₄⁻. Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) is already fully protonated and can't accept another H⁺.

qs.q: Which diuretic class causes metabolic acidosis by blocking proximal HCO₃⁻ reclaiming?
qs.why: Without carbonic anhydrase, filtered HCO₃⁻ is lost in urine. K⁺-sparing diuretics cause mild acidosis by cutting distal H⁺ secretion, not proximally; loop and thiazide diuretics cause alkalosis.

slides.note: pCO₂ = partial pressure of CO₂ in arterial blood (mm Hg); the lungs set it. HCO₃⁻ = bicarbonate (mEq/L); the kidneys set it. In words: pH depends on the ratio of base (HCO₃⁻) to acid (dissolved CO₂). In symbols (Henderson–Hasselbalch): pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻ / (0.03 × pCO₂)]. Here 6.1 is the pK of the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ buffer (the pH at which HCO₃⁻ and dissolved CO₂ are equal). 0.03 is how much CO₂ dissolves per mm Hg, so 0.03 × pCO₂ gives dissolved CO₂ in mmol/L. Worked example: 24 / (0.03 × 40) = 24 / 1.2 = 20; log 20 = 1.3; 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.40. So more HCO₃⁻ raises pH, and more CO₂ lowers it.

Acidemia means blood pH below 7.40. There are two ways to get there. Metabolic: the problem starts with HCO₃⁻. Acid is added or base is lost, so HCO₃⁻ falls. Respiratory: the problem starts with breathing. Too little ventilation lets CO₂ build up, so pCO₂ rises. The body then pushes pH back up with the other system: the lungs blow off CO₂, or the kidneys reabsorb more HCO₃⁻ and make new HCO₃⁻ for the blood. That opposite push is the “compensating alkalosis.”

This is the mirror image of acidemia. Metabolic alkalosis: HCO₃⁻ rises, because acid is lost (vomiting) or base is added. Respiratory alkalosis: fast breathing blows off CO₂, so pCO₂ falls. Compensation pushes pH back down. Slower breathing keeps CO₂ (pCO₂ rises), or the kidneys excrete HCO₃⁻ (HCO₃⁻ falls). Strictly, “-emia” names the blood pH and “-osis” names the process causing it, but the two are used as synonyms.

Read each line as: a primary disorder is offset by the opposite process in the other system (an acidosis by an alkalosis; metabolic by respiratory). The numbers, though, move in the same direction. Example: in metabolic acidosis HCO₃⁻ falls from 24 to 12. The compensating respiratory alkalosis is faster breathing, which lowers pCO₂ from 40 to about 24. Both values fall, so their ratio, and the pH, move back toward normal. “Metabolic” compensation means the kidney changing how much H⁺ it secretes into the urine and how much HCO₃⁻ it reabsorbs into the blood. The lungs compensate within minutes to hours; the kidneys need several days. Compensation pulls pH toward 7.40 but never past it, so the side of 7.40 tells you the primary disorder.

HCO₃⁻ falls in three ways. (1) Acid is added (made or swallowed): each H⁺ uses up one HCO₃⁻ as it is buffered. (2) HCO₃⁻ is lost from the gut or the kidney. (3) The kidney can't excrete the daily acid load. The low pH is sensed mainly by the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies. They stimulate the central (brainstem) respiratory center, which speeds up breathing. Faster breathing lowers pCO₂, which pulls pH back toward 7.40. The final fix is the kidney excreting the extra H⁺ and making new HCO₃⁻, which takes days.

Follow the steps with numbers. (1) An acid is added. (2) Its H⁺ joins HCO₃⁻: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ → CO₂ + H₂O, and the CO₂ is breathed out. Each H⁺ buffered costs one HCO₃⁻, so HCO₃⁻ drops, for example 24 → 12. (3) The HCO₃⁻/CO₂ ratio falls, so pH drops. (4) Low pH stimulates the carotid-body chemoreceptors. (5) Faster breathing lowers pCO₂. Rule: pCO₂ falls about 1.3 mm Hg for each 1 mEq/L fall in HCO₃⁻. Here HCO₃⁻ fell by 24 − 12 = 12 mEq/L, so pCO₂ falls about 1.3 × 12 ≈ 16 mm Hg: 40 − 16 = 24. That low pCO₂ is compensation, not a second disease.

A fixed (nonvolatile) acid is any acid other than CO₂. CO₂ is the volatile acid, and the lungs breathe it out. A fixed acid can't be exhaled. It must be buffered by HCO₃⁻ and then excreted by the kidney. Each cause here adds one. DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis) adds ketoacids; shock adds lactic acid; aspirin adds salicylic acid (and lactic acid); methanol becomes formic acid; ethylene glycol becomes glycolic and oxalic acid. Their leftover anions (ketoanions, lactate, formate …) are not measured by the lab, which is why they raise the anion gap (explained under Anion Gap).

Without insulin, glucose can't enter muscle and fat cells, so the cells starve even though blood glucose is high. Fat cells break down their stored fat and release free fatty acids. The liver burns these and turns the excess into ketoacids: acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid. Their H⁺ uses up HCO₃⁻, causing a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with fast, deep breathing as compensation. The high glucose also spills into urine and drags water and NaCl with it, so the patient becomes dehydrated.

Cells need O₂ to burn pyruvate in the mitochondria. When O₂ delivery falls, cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis. Pyruvate is turned into lactic acid so glycolysis can keep making a little ATP. Anything that lowers blood flow to tissues (hypoperfusion) does this: shock from blood loss, sepsis (infection with low blood pressure), any severe hypotension, and hard exercise in working muscle. Lactic acid adds H⁺, which lowers HCO₃⁻, and lactate, which raises the anion gap.

In overdose, aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, so mitochondria can't make ATP from O₂. Cells switch to glycolysis and make lactic acid, causing metabolic acidosis. Aspirin also blocks prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandins normally dilate the afferent arteriole (the arteriole carrying blood into the glomerulus), so without them kidney blood flow falls and the kidney is injured. Other effects: ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome, leaky lungs filling with fluid), confusion (encephalopathy), and ringing in the ears (tinnitus), an early clue. Salicylate also directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center, so the patient hyperventilates even before acid builds up.

Aspirin overdose causes two primary disorders at once. (1) Respiratory alkalosis, because salicylate drives the brainstem to breathe fast; this comes first. (2) High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from lactic and salicylic acid, which comes later. Because they push pH in opposite directions, pH can be near normal while both pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are low. Giving bicarbonate makes the urine alkaline, which speeds excretion by ion trapping. In alkaline urine, salicylic acid gives up its H⁺ and becomes charged salicylate. Charged molecules can't diffuse back across tubule cells into blood, so more salicylate stays in the urine and is excreted.

Methanol itself does little harm; its products are toxic. Alcohol dehydrogenase turns methanol into formaldehyde, and aldehyde dehydrogenase turns that into formic acid. Formic acid adds H⁺ (high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis) and damages the retina and optic nerve, causing blindness (“blind drunk” from bootleg alcohol). Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, so no new formic acid is made. Dialysis pulls methanol and formate out of the blood. Methanol is a small molecule, so it also raises the osmolar gap (measured minus calculated osmolarity; explained under Osmolar Gap).

Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) is also harmless until alcohol dehydrogenase starts breaking it down. The products are glycolic acid and oxalic acid, which add H⁺ and cause a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Oxalate binds calcium and forms calcium oxalate crystals. These show up in urine, block and injure the kidney tubules (acute kidney failure), and use up blood Ca²⁺, so serum calcium falls. Treatment is the same as for methanol: fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, and dialysis removes the parent compound and its acids. Ethylene glycol also raises the osmolar gap.

Answer: C. Step 1: the primary problem is low HCO₃⁻. Step 2: the fast fix is the lungs. Low pH drives hyperventilation, which lowers pCO₂. A process that lowers pCO₂ is a respiratory alkalosis, so that is the compensation. Why not the others: (a) raising CO₂ would make the acidosis worse; (b) low HCO₃⁻ is the disorder itself, not the fix; (d) the kidney corrects acidosis by keeping and making HCO₃⁻, not by excreting it, and that takes days, so it isn't the acute response; (e) the anion gap is a lab clue, not a compensation.

Answer: B. DKA adds ketoacids, so HCO₃⁻ falls (12) and pH falls (7.32). Fast breathing lowers pCO₂ (26) as compensation. Check with the 1.3 rule: HCO₃⁻ fell by 24 − 12 = 12, so pCO₂ should fall about 1.3 × 12 ≈ 16, to 40 − 16 = 24. The measured 26 is close enough. How to read this table (it returns in later questions): columns are pH, pCO₂ (mm Hg) and HCO₃⁻ (mEq/L); normal is 7.40 / 40 / 24. Look at pH first, then ask which value explains it.
  • a: low pH, high pCO₂, high HCO₃⁻ = respiratory acidosis with kidney compensation (chronic, e.g., COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).
  • b: metabolic acidosis.
  • c: high pH, high HCO₃⁻ = metabolic alkalosis (slow breathing raised pCO₂).
  • d: high pH, low pCO₂, HCO₃⁻ still normal = acute respiratory alkalosis.
  • e: low pCO₂, low HCO₃⁻, pH 7.44 (just above 7.40) = chronic respiratory alkalosis; the kidney has compensated.

Answer: B. Septic shock is infection with very low blood pressure. Step 1: low pressure means tissues get too little O₂. Step 2: cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis and make lactic acid. Step 3: the H⁺ uses up HCO₃⁻ (12), so pH falls (7.32). Step 4: chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation, which lowers pCO₂ (26). That is metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, the same blood gas as DKA. Only the anion gap and the history tell these causes apart.

Answer: B. Alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethylene glycol into glycolic and oxalic acid. These fixed acids use up HCO₃⁻ (12) and lower pH (7.32). Hyperventilation lowers pCO₂ (26) to compensate. So every “acid added” cause (DKA, lactic acid, toxic alcohols) gives the same blood gas: low pH, low HCO₃⁻, low pCO₂. What sets ethylene glycol apart lies outside the blood gas: a high anion gap plus a high osmolar gap, oxalate crystals in the urine, and kidney failure.

Answer: D. One minute of fast breathing blows off CO₂, so pCO₂ falls (20) and pH rises sharply (7.56). This is acute respiratory alkalosis. The kidney needs several days to lower HCO₃⁻ by secreting less H⁺, so HCO₃⁻ is still about normal (24). Compare e (7.44 / 20 / 18): same low pCO₂, but after days of hyperventilation the kidney has lowered HCO₃⁻ to 18. That brings pH almost back to normal, which is chronic respiratory alkalosis. Time decides between d and e.

The colon secretes HCO₃⁻: it moves HCO₃⁻ from the blood into the gut lumen and absorbs Cl⁻ from the lumen into the blood in exchange. Diarrhea flushes this HCO₃⁻-rich fluid, and K⁺, out of the body. So blood HCO₃⁻ falls, pH falls, and K⁺ falls (hypokalemia). Blood must keep equal positive and negative charges. As HCO₃⁻ is lost, the gut and kidney reabsorb more Cl⁻ into the blood, so Cl⁻ rises about one-for-one as HCO₃⁻ falls. Example: HCO₃⁻ 24 → 14 while Cl⁻ 104 → 114. Both are measured anions, and their sum stays 128 (104 + 24 = 114 + 14). So the anion gap (Na⁺ minus the measured anions Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻) does not change. This is a hyperchloremic (high blood Cl⁻), normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

RTA (renal tubular acidosis) is a tubule defect that causes metabolic acidosis even though filtration (GFR, glomerular filtration rate) is normal. The proximal tubule normally reabsorbs most of the filtered HCO₃⁻ (moves it out of the tubule fluid back into the blood). In proximal (type 2) RTA it can't, so HCO₃⁻ spills into urine and blood HCO₃⁻ falls. As in diarrhea, the tubule reabsorbs more Cl⁻ into the blood, so Cl⁻ takes the place of the lost HCO₃⁻. Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride + bicarbonate): AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Normal example: 140 − (104 + 24) = 140 − 128 = 12. If HCO₃⁻ drops to 14 and Cl⁻ rises to 114, the gap is still 140 − (114 + 14) = 140 − 128 = 12.

Metabolism makes about 1 mEq of fixed acid per kg of body weight per day (about 70 mEq for a 70-kg adult). The kidney removes it by secreting H⁺ into urine, carried as NH₄⁺ (ammonium, made from glutamine by tubule cells) and as titratable acid (H⁺ bound to phosphate). Each H⁺ excreted adds one new HCO₃⁻ to blood. Renal failure: too few working nephrons make too little NH₄⁺, so acid builds up. Phosphate, sulfate and urate are retained too, which raises the anion gap. Distal (type 1) RTA: the α-intercalated cells of the collecting duct can't secrete H⁺ (pump it out of the cell into the tubule fluid), so the urine can't be acidified (urine pH stays above 5.5). More Cl⁻ is reabsorbed into the blood instead, so the anion gap stays normal.

Answer: B. Diarrhea loses HCO₃⁻-rich intestinal fluid. HCO₃⁻ falls (12) and pH falls (7.32), and the lungs compensate by lowering pCO₂ (26). The blood gas is identical to DKA, sepsis and ethylene glycol. A blood gas alone only tells you “metabolic acidosis.” To find the cause, calculate the anion gap. It is normal in diarrhea, because Cl⁻ replaces HCO₃⁻. It is high when an acid has been added.

Answer: A. Step 1: HCO₃⁻ is low (14), so this is metabolic acidosis, and the fast breathing is the lungs compensating. Step 2: O₂ saturation is 98% on room air, so he is not hypoxic. The fast breathing is not from lung disease, which rules out pneumonia, and he didn't need oxygen. Step 3: anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 140 − (106 + 14) = 140 − 120 = 20, above the normal of about 12. Step 4: a high gap means an acid was added. Of the choices, only urinary sepsis adds acid (lactic acid from poor perfusion). RTA and diarrhea give a normal gap, and vomiting causes alkalosis.

Answer: B. Fever plus white cells in the urine means a urinary tract infection. A pressure of 80/40 means shock. Together this is urosepsis with septic shock. The low pressure starves tissues of O₂, so they make lactic acid. The acid uses up HCO₃⁻ (12) and lowers pH (7.32). Chemoreceptors then drive hyperventilation, which lowers pCO₂ (26). This is the same kind of patient as Q7, now shown as a blood gas.

Blood is electrically neutral: total positive charge equals total negative charge. Labs measure only the main cation (Na⁺) and the two main anions (Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻). Na⁺ is larger than Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻. The difference is the anion gap, made of unmeasured anions: mostly albumin, plus phosphate, sulfate and citrate. AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normally 140 − (104 + 24) = 140 − 128 = 12. When an acid like lactic acid is added, its H⁺ uses up HCO₃⁻ but its anion (lactate) stays in blood, unmeasured. The gap rises: 140 − (104 + 12) = 140 − 116 = 24. When HCO₃⁻ is lost and Cl⁻ replaces it, the gap stays normal. Low albumin lowers the gap.

A high anion gap means an acid with an unmeasured anion was added. Match each cause to its anion: DKA → acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate; lactic acidosis → lactate; aspirin → salicylate (plus lactate); methanol → formate; ethylene glycol → glycolate and oxalate; renal failure → retained phosphate, sulfate and urate. In each, HCO₃⁻ falls while Cl⁻ stays normal, and the gap rises by about as much as HCO₃⁻ falls.

A normal gap with low HCO₃⁻ means HCO₃⁻ was lost, or the kidney failed to make new HCO₃⁻ because it can't excrete H⁺. In both cases Cl⁻ takes HCO₃⁻'s place, so this is also called hyperchloremic acidosis. Diarrhea loses HCO₃⁻ from the gut. Proximal (type 2) RTA loses it in the urine. Distal (type 1) RTA can't secrete H⁺. Quick test: high Cl⁻ with a normal gap points to diarrhea or RTA; normal Cl⁻ with a high gap means an acid was added.

Osmolarity is the number of dissolved particles per liter of plasma (mOsm/L, milliosmoles per liter); Sosm = serum osmolarity. In words, it is estimated as twice the sodium, plus glucose divided by 18, plus BUN divided by 2.8: calculated osmolarity = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8. Na⁺ is doubled to count its partner anions (Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻). Glucose and BUN (blood urea nitrogen) come in mg/dL, and dividing by 18 and 2.8 turns them into mOsm/L. Normal example: 2 × 140 + 90/18 + 14/2.8 = 280 + 5 + 5 = 290. The lab can also measure osmolarity directly. Osmolar gap = measured − calculated, normally under about 10. In this case: calculated 280, measured 380, so the gap is 380 − 280 = 100. A small molecule that the formula doesn't count is adding particles: methanol or ethylene glycol (or ethanol). A high anion gap plus a high osmolar gap points to a toxic alcohol.

Answer: A. Step 1: pH 7.28 with HCO₃⁻ 12 is metabolic acidosis. HCO₃⁻ fell by 24 − 12 = 12, so the 1.3 rule predicts pCO₂ ≈ 40 − 1.3 × 12 ≈ 24. The measured pCO₂ is even lower (18), because the fever drives extra fast breathing. Step 2: anion gap = 136 − (118 + 12) = 136 − 130 = 6. The gap is normal (about 6–12), and Cl⁻ is high (118; normal about 104). So no acid was added; HCO₃⁻ was lost and replaced by Cl⁻. Step 3: this rules out urosepsis and the low pressure itself (both make lactic acid) and renal failure, which all raise the gap. Pneumonia causes respiratory alkalosis, not low HCO₃⁻ with high Cl⁻. Infectious diarrhea explains the fever, and the fluid loss explains the low pressure.

Answer: A. Ethylene glycol is turned into glycolic and oxalic acid. The added H⁺ lowers blood pH. Low pH stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies, which drive faster breathing to blow off CO₂. Why not the others: oxalate explains the crystals and the low Ca²⁺ (it binds calcium), not the breathing; there is no lung disease, so no hypoxia; the anion gap is high, not normal; and HCO₃⁻ is low, used up buffering the acid.

HCO₃⁻ rises when H⁺ is lost or base is added. Vomiting: stomach cells make H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ together. The H⁺ leaves the body as HCl in the vomit, and the HCO₃⁻ enters the blood. The fluid loss then raises angiotensin II and aldosterone, so the kidney reabsorbs HCO₃⁻ into the blood instead of excreting the excess (contraction alkalosis). Hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's (excess cortisol acts like aldosterone), loop and thiazide diuretics, and Bartter syndrome (inherited loss of the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ transporter in the thick ascending limb, like a built-in loop diuretic) all make the collecting duct secrete more H⁺ and K⁺ into the urine. So HCO₃⁻ rises and K⁺ falls. Milk-alkali: large amounts of calcium carbonate antacid add base. Hypokalemia: K⁺ moves out of cells into the blood, and H⁺ moves from the blood into cells in exchange. Compensation: slower breathing raises pCO₂.

Too little ventilation lets CO₂ build up, so pCO₂ rises and pH falls. Sort the causes by where breathing fails. Lungs and airways: COPD traps air and CO₂; obstructive sleep apnea blocks the airway. Brainstem drive: opiates and barbiturates depress the medullary respiratory center. Nerves and muscles: ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, loss of motor neurons) and diaphragm weakness. Breathing is the problem, so the lungs can't compensate. The kidney compensates over several days by secreting more H⁺ into the urine and adding new HCO₃⁻ to the blood. Rule: for each 1 mm Hg rise in pCO₂, HCO₃⁻ rises about 0.1 mEq/L when acute and about 0.4 mEq/L when chronic. Example: pCO₂ 40 → 60, a rise of 20. Acute: 0.1 × 20 = 2, so HCO₃⁻ ≈ 26 and pH is very low. Chronic: 0.4 × 20 = 8, so HCO₃⁻ ≈ 32 and pH is closer to normal.

Too much ventilation blows off CO₂, so pCO₂ falls and pH rises. Hypoxia (low blood O₂, from pneumonia, pulmonary embolus or high altitude) stimulates the carotid-body chemoreceptors. Pain, fever, anxiety and salicylates drive the medullary respiratory center directly. Severe anemia lowers the O₂ delivered to tissues, and the person breathes fast. Acidosis is on the list because metabolic acidosis drives hyperventilation as its compensation. The kidney compensates over days by secreting less H⁺ and excreting HCO₃⁻. Acute: HCO₃⁻ near normal, pH high. Chronic: HCO₃⁻ low, pH near normal. Low CO₂ also constricts brain arteries (light-headedness) and lowers free Ca²⁺, because alkaline blood makes albumin bind more Ca²⁺ (tingling).

Answer: C. Loss of tooth enamel (stomach acid on the teeth) and enlarged parotid glands are signs of repeated self-induced vomiting. Step 1: vomiting loses HCl, so HCO₃⁻ rises (36) and pH rises (7.46). That is metabolic alkalosis. Step 2: high pH inhibits the chemoreceptors, breathing slows, and pCO₂ rises (54) as compensation. Why not a: it also has high CO₂ and high HCO₃⁻, but its pH is low (7.36). So in a, the high CO₂ came first (respiratory acidosis). The pH tells you which change came first.

Answer: A. Vomiting lowers K⁺ in three ways. (1) A little K⁺ is lost in the vomit. (2) Alkalosis shifts K⁺ into cells as H⁺ leaves them. (3) Most important, the fluid loss raises aldosterone, which makes the principal cells of the collecting duct secrete K⁺ into urine. Severe hypokalemia disturbs the heart's repolarization and causes fatal arrhythmias. Low K⁺ also makes the kidney secrete more H⁺, which worsens the alkalosis. Hyperkalemia is the opposite of what vomiting causes.

Answer: C. Step 1: pH 7.34 is below 7.40, so this is acidosis. Step 2: which value explains it? pCO₂ 60 is high (normal 40), and CO₂ is an acid, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis. HCO₃⁻ 38 (normal 24) would raise pH, so it is the compensation. Step 3: pCO₂ rose 60 − 40 = 20 mm Hg. If acute, HCO₃⁻ would rise only 0.1 × 20 = 2, to about 26. It rose 38 − 24 = 14, far more. Only several days of kidney compensation raise HCO₃⁻ that much, so the disorder is chronic, as in COPD. Why not the others: methanol, diarrhea and DKA lower HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis); a pulmonary embolus causes hypoxia and hyperventilation, which lowers pCO₂.

Answer: A. Hematocrit is the percent of blood volume made of red cells. A hematocrit of 15 (normal about 40) is severe anemia from bleeding. With so little hemoglobin, tissues get less O₂. The patient breathes fast and blows off CO₂, causing respiratory alkalosis. The pulse of 110 is the heart compensating for the anemia. Blood pressure is normal (120/80), so there is no shock yet and no lactic acidosis. Why not the others: nothing here causes hypoventilation (b); no H⁺ is lost and no base is added, so HCO₃⁻ doesn't rise (c, d); a low anion gap comes from low albumin, not bleeding.

qs.q: Which organ sets plasma HCO₃⁻, and which sets arterial pCO₂?
opts: Lungs set HCO₃⁻; kidneys set pCO₂
Kidneys set HCO₃⁻; lungs set pCO₂
Liver sets HCO₃⁻; lungs set pCO₂
Kidneys set both HCO₃⁻ and pCO₂
qs.why: Breathing controls how much CO₂ stays in blood, while the kidneys reclaim and make HCO₃⁻. pH depends on the ratio of HCO₃⁻ to dissolved CO₂.

qs.q: Metabolic alkalosis is compensated by which process?
qs.why: Slower breathing keeps CO₂, so pCO₂ rises (a respiratory acidosis) and pH is pulled back down. Compensation always comes from the other system.

qs.q: When one value (HCO₃⁻ or pCO₂) changes first, which way does the other value move as compensation?
opts: It moves only after pH normalizes
Opposite direction to the first value
It stays at its normal value
Same direction as the first value
qs.why: pH depends on the HCO₃⁻/CO₂ ratio, so the ratio comes back toward normal only if both values move together: when HCO₃⁻ falls, pCO₂ falls too. The process is the opposite (an acidosis is offset by an alkalosis), but the numbers move the same way.

qs.q: Why does the side of 7.40 reveal the primary disorder?
opts: Compensation always returns pH exactly to 7.40
Only the primary value can change pH
qs.why: Compensation pulls pH toward 7.40 but not beyond it. So pH below 7.40 means the primary process is an acidosis, and above 7.40 an alkalosis.

qs.q: Why does adding a fixed acid lower plasma HCO₃⁻?
opts: The kidney excretes HCO₃⁻ in response
Each buffered H⁺ uses up one HCO₃⁻
qs.why: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ → CO₂ + H₂O, and the CO₂ is breathed out. Every H⁺ buffered costs one HCO₃⁻.

qs.q: In metabolic acidosis, what mainly senses the low pH and drives faster breathing?
qs.why: The carotid-body chemoreceptors respond to the low pH and drive the brainstem respiratory center, so pCO₂ falls as compensation.

qs.q: In metabolic acidosis, pCO₂ falls about how much for each 1 mEq/L fall in HCO₃⁻?
qs.why: Example: HCO₃⁻ 24 → 12 is a 12 mEq/L fall, so pCO₂ falls about 1.3 × 12 ≈ 16 mm Hg, to 40 − 16 = 24 mm Hg. That low pCO₂ is compensation, not a second disorder.

qs.q: Which acid can the lungs remove directly?
qs.why: CO₂ is the only volatile acid. Fixed acids such as lactic, keto and formic acid can't be exhaled; they must be buffered by HCO₃⁻ and excreted by the kidney.

qs.q: Which acids build up in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
qs.why: Without insulin, glucose can't enter cells, so fat is broken down; the liver turns the free fatty acids into acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acid, which use up HCO₃⁻.

qs.q: What links sepsis, hypovolemic shock and severe hypotension to lactic acidosis?
qs.why: Low blood flow means too little O₂, so pyruvate is turned into lactic acid to keep glycolysis running. The H⁺ lowers HCO₃⁻ and the lactate raises the anion gap.

qs.q: Aspirin overdose causes which two primary disorders?
qs.why: Salicylate directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center (respiratory alkalosis, first), and poisoned mitochondria make lactic acid (high-gap metabolic acidosis, later). pH can end up near normal.

qs.q: Why does giving bicarbonate speed salicylate excretion?
opts: Bicarbonate converts salicylate to exhaled CO₂
Bicarbonate raises GFR, filtering more salicylate
Acidic urine traps uncharged salicylic acid in the tubule
Alkaline urine traps charged salicylate in the tubule
qs.why: In alkaline urine, salicylic acid (a weak acid) loses its H⁺ and becomes charged salicylate, which can't diffuse back into blood, so it stays in the urine (ion trapping).

qs.q: Which finding is typical of methanol poisoning?
qs.why: Methanol becomes formaldehyde and then formic acid, which injures the retina and optic nerve ("blind drunk"). Oxalate crystals and low Ca²⁺ belong to ethylene glycol; tinnitus to aspirin.

qs.q: How does fomepizole treat methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?
opts: Alkalinizes urine to trap the acid
qs.why: The parent alcohols do little harm; alcohol dehydrogenase starts turning them into the toxic acids. Blocking it stops new acid from forming; dialysis is what removes the alcohol.

qs.q: Why does ethylene glycol poisoning lower serum Ca²⁺?
qs.why: Alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethylene glycol into glycolic and oxalic acid. Oxalate binds Ca²⁺ as calcium oxalate crystals, which appear in urine and injure the tubules.

qs.q: In metabolic acidosis, how does the kidney eventually correct pH?
opts: Excretes H⁺ and makes new HCO₃⁻
qs.why: The kidney secretes the extra H⁺ into the urine and adds new HCO₃⁻ to the blood, but this takes days. The fast (acute) compensation is hyperventilation, a respiratory alkalosis.

qs.q: Low pH, low pCO₂ and low HCO₃⁻ indicate which disorder?
qs.why: Low pH means acidosis, and the low HCO₃⁻ explains it. The low pCO₂ would raise pH, so it is the compensation (hyperventilation).

qs.q: How does chronic respiratory alkalosis differ from acute on a blood gas?
opts: Lower HCO₃⁻ and pH nearer normal
qs.why: In the first minutes pCO₂ falls but HCO₃⁻ is still about 24, so pH is high. After days the kidney secretes less H⁺, HCO₃⁻ falls (e.g., to 18), and pH comes back near 7.40.

qs.q: Which lab finding sets ethylene glycol poisoning apart from DKA and lactic acidosis?
qs.why: All three give the same blood gas and a high anion gap. Ethylene glycol is a small unmeasured molecule, so it also raises the osmolar gap.

qs.q: In diarrhea, as plasma HCO₃⁻ falls, which anion rises to replace it?
qs.why: Intestinal fluid is rich in HCO₃⁻. As HCO₃⁻ is lost in the stool, the gut and kidney reabsorb Cl⁻ into the blood about one-for-one. Both are measured anions, so the anion gap stays normal (hyperchloremic acidosis).

qs.q: What is the defect in proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis (RTA)?
opts: Can't filter HCO₃⁻ at the glomerulus
qs.why: The proximal tubule normally reabsorbs most filtered HCO₃⁻ (returns it from the tubule fluid to the blood). In type 2 RTA it spills into urine, blood HCO₃⁻ falls, and Cl⁻ takes its place, so the gap stays normal.

qs.q: Which cells fail in distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis?
opts: Principal cells of the collecting duct
α-intercalated cells of the collecting duct
qs.why: α-intercalated cells can't pump H⁺ into urine, so urine can't be acidified (pH stays above 5.5). Cl⁻ is retained, so the anion gap stays normal.

qs.q: Why does renal failure raise the anion gap?
opts: Cl⁻ is retained in place of HCO₃⁻
Albumin is lost in the urine
Phosphate, sulfate and urate are retained
qs.why: Too few nephrons make too little NH₄⁺, so the daily ~1 mEq/kg acid load builds up with its unmeasured anions (phosphate, sulfate, urate). Extra Cl⁻ reabsorbed into the blood is the RTA pattern, which keeps the gap normal.

qs.q: Which unmeasured anion makes up most of the normal anion gap?
qs.why: The lab measures Na⁺, Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻; the leftover negative charge is mostly albumin, with some phosphate, sulfate and citrate. So low albumin lowers the gap.

qs.q: Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 100, HCO₃⁻ 10 (mEq/L). What is the anion gap?
qs.why: Anion gap (AG) = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 138 − (100 + 10) = 138 − 110 = 28, well above the normal ~12, so an acid with an unmeasured anion was added.

qs.q: Why does lactic acidosis raise the anion gap?
opts: Cl⁻ rises to replace lost HCO₃⁻
Lactate replaces HCO₃⁻ but isn't measured
qs.why: The H⁺ uses up HCO₃⁻, but lactate stays in blood as an unmeasured anion, so the gap rises about as much as HCO₃⁻ falls. When Cl⁻ replaces HCO₃⁻ instead, the gap stays normal.

qs.q: Which cause of metabolic acidosis has a normal anion gap?
qs.why: In RTA (as in diarrhea) HCO₃⁻ falls while Cl⁻ rises, so the gap stays normal. Renal failure, DKA and salicylates add acid whose anion is unmeasured.

qs.q: How is calculated serum osmolarity estimated (BUN = blood urea nitrogen)?
qs.why: Glucose and BUN come in mg/dL, and dividing by 18 and 2.8 turns them into mOsm/L. Normally the result is about 290.

qs.q: Why is Na⁺ doubled in the calculated osmolarity?
opts: To count K⁺ along with Na⁺
qs.why: Each Na⁺ is paired with an anion (mostly Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻), so 2 × Na⁺ estimates both. The divisors 18 and 2.8 do the unit conversion for glucose and BUN.

qs.q: A high anion gap plus a high osmolar gap points to what?
qs.why: Toxic alcohols are small unmeasured molecules (osmolar gap, normally under ~10) that become acids with unmeasured anions (anion gap). DKA and lactic acidosis raise only the anion gap.

qs.q: Why does vomiting raise plasma HCO₃⁻?
opts: Stomach loses H⁺; its paired HCO₃⁻ enters blood
Swallowed base is absorbed from the gut
Fast breathing during vomiting raises HCO₃⁻
Stomach loses HCO₃⁻; blood gains Cl⁻
qs.why: Stomach cells make H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ together; the H⁺ leaves as HCl and the HCO₃⁻ stays in blood. Volume loss then raises aldosterone, so the kidney reabsorbs the extra HCO₃⁻ into the blood instead of excreting it.

qs.q: Bartter syndrome acts like long-term use of which drug?
qs.why: Bartter syndrome is an inherited loss of the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ transporter in the thick ascending limb, the loop diuretic's target. The collecting duct then secretes more H⁺ and K⁺ into the urine: metabolic alkalosis with low K⁺.

qs.q: In chronic respiratory acidosis, HCO₃⁻ rises about how much per 1 mm Hg rise in pCO₂?
qs.why: Acutely HCO₃⁻ rises only about 0.1 per mm Hg. After several days of extra renal H⁺ secretion and new HCO₃⁻, it rises about 0.4 per mm Hg and pH moves closer to normal. Example: pCO₂ 40 → 60 (a rise of 20): acute 0.1 × 20 = 2, so HCO₃⁻ ≈ 26; chronic 0.4 × 20 = 8, so HCO₃⁻ ≈ 32.

qs.q: Which condition causes respiratory alkalosis?
qs.why: Anxiety, like pain, fever and salicylates, drives the respiratory center and blows off CO₂. Opiates and COPD cause hypoventilation (respiratory acidosis); vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis.

qs.q: Eroded tooth enamel and enlarged parotid glands point to which acid–base disorder?
qs.why: Both are signs of repeated self-induced vomiting. Losing HCl raises HCO₃⁻ and pH, and slower breathing raises pCO₂ as compensation.

qs.q: When pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are both high, what tells you which change was primary?
opts: Whether pH is above or below 7.40
Which value is further from normal
The size of the anion gap
qs.why: pH above 7.40 (e.g., 7.46) means high HCO₃⁻ came first: metabolic alkalosis. pH below 7.40 (e.g., 7.34) means high pCO₂ came first: respiratory acidosis, as in COPD.

qs.q: What is the main reason repeated vomiting lowers serum K⁺?
opts: K⁺ is lost in the vomit
Alkalosis moves K⁺ out of cells
Low K⁺ intake from not eating
qs.why: Volume loss raises aldosterone, which makes principal cells secrete K⁺ into urine; only a little K⁺ is in vomit. Alkalosis moves K⁺ into cells, not out, which also lowers serum K⁺.

qs.q: Why does severe anemia from acute bleeding cause respiratory alkalosis?
opts: Low O₂ delivery drives faster breathing
Lactic acid from shock drives breathing
qs.why: With little hemoglobin, tissues get less O₂, so the patient breathes fast and blows off CO₂. With normal blood pressure there is no shock yet, so no lactic acidosis.
